arnald-villanova-opera-1527:
Arnald of Villanova's collected works fill this Latin Opera, in a 1527 printing. Arnald served as doctor to popes and kings across the medieval West. His writings span medicine, alchemy, theology, and sharp prophecies about the end of the present age of the world.

Few minds of the Middle Ages ranged so wide or worked so boldly. He reformed medical study, courted heresy charges, and still kept royal patients. Remedies sit beside visions in the crowded Latin pages here. The volume preserves the full mind of a versatile genius, a healer and prophet whom both church and court found hard to ignore.
arxiv-2512-00027:
Robots that follow spoken directions through real rooms need to see, move, and talk back when orders are unclear. Nivedan Yakolli and four co-authors survey this field, called vision-and-language navigation, in a 2025 review. Their subject is how teams of robots can work with people in shared three-dimensional spaces.

The review gathers recent work on how robots read human instructions, plan routes, and coordinate with each other. It also points to open problems, such as handling vague commands and keeping communication clear when several machines act at once. Readers get a map of current methods and the directions the authors see as most promising for better teamwork.
arxiv-2512-00227:
Operator ideals called Schatten classes measure how close an operator is to being finite and small. Tamara Bottazzi and Cristian Conde investigate these ideals as semi-inner product spaces in 2025. Semi-inner products generalize the geometry of angles beyond ordinary inner product spaces.

The authors study angles and related geometry in the Schatten classes for exponents above one. Such geometry underlies quantum information, where Schatten norms measure distances between quantum states. Clarifying when these spaces behave like familiar Euclidean geometry helps analysts use them with confidence in proofs and applications. Angles in these spaces generalize the familiar geometry of Hilbert spaces. The authors work in the sense of Giles and Lumer, a standard reference point.
arxiv-2512-00527:
The fractional quantum Hall effect hosts some of the strangest states of matter known. Mytraya Gattu dresses composite fermions with artificial intelligence in 2025, using machine learning to improve their wavefunctions. Composite fermions are quasiparticles that already explain much of the effect's behavior.

Recent variational studies captured these ground states with machine learning starting from no prior physics knowledge. Gattu instead starts from Jain's composite-fermion wavefunctions, which are accurate in an idealized limit, and lets learning refine them. Combining a strong physical ansatz with flexible fitting could yield the most accurate descriptions yet of these exotic states. Composite fermions turn a strongly interacting problem into a weakly interacting one.
arxiv-2512-00627:
Sparse regression picks a few true predictors from a crowd of candidates, and priors must encode that sparsity. Chadi Bsila and co-authors develop a variational Bayes method for spike-and-slab regression in 2025, replacing the usual divergence objective with Rényi's alpha-divergence. Their setting is high-dimensional linear regression.

The method uses spike-and-slab Laplace priors within a mean-field approximation. The alpha parameter interpolates between zero-forcing and mass-covering behavior. Flexible methods matter because exact Bayesian computation is impossible at the dimensions genomics and economics now demand. Spike-and-slab priors put real probability on a coefficient being exactly zero. That honesty about exclusion is what variable selection needs. For folks who face wide data with few true clues, the gain is choice. One knob tunes how bold or how shy the fit will be as it picks its clues.
arxiv-2512-01127:
A 2025 machine learning paper proposes mode-conditioning to unlock better test-time scaling. Letting a model sample many answers in parallel should improve results, since the best of many tries often wins. In practice, gains are sharply limited by diversity collapse: the model concentrates on a few modes and repeats the same mistakes across samples.

The proposed ModC framework allocates test-time compute across reasoning modes on purpose. Modes can come from specialist models or from mode-specific prefixes that steer one model. Spreading samples across modes should surface different approaches and different errors. That makes parallel sampling worth its extra cost on hard problems.
arxiv-2512-01427:
Klara Reichard and co-authors work on finding odd objects in road scenes. Self-driving systems must spot both known and unknown things. Past methods can outline an unknown zone. They fail to say what that zone is in words.

The team adds language to the task. Their method gives a word label to each odd zone it finds. A label like debris or stray cart helps the car plan a reply. Word labels also help staff log and study near-miss events. The work pushes road vision from mere spotting toward real scene sense.
arxiv-2512-01727:
Benjamin Blakely and co-authors evaluate AI cybersecurity for nuclear infrastructure on real plant data. Advanced reactors face attackers who exploit cyber-physical links. They can twist control systems while dodging classic IT guards. Testbeds must reflect that real risk.

Their testbed uses operational data from Argonne's engineering test loop. AI methods are scored on that live-like data. Scores show which detectors catch stealthy attacks. Nuclear sites need that proof before any AI guard can be trusted near reactor controls. Operational data keeps the test honest, since lab-made attacks often miss the noise and quirks of a working test loop's traffic.
arxiv-2512-01827:
Yize Zhang and co-authors teach models to discover visual causes with CauSight. Humans grasp not just what is seen, but why it happens. Visual causal discovery asks models to infer cause and effect among scene entities. Mere detection of objects falls short of that goal.

Their learning frame targets that deeper skill. Models must state which entity drives which change. Causal reads help robots and safety systems predict what comes next. They also make model errors easier to explain and fix. Cause graphs can be graded directly, since each claimed arrow is right or wrong, unlike vague scene captions that resist scoring.
arxiv-2512-02127:
In the standard cosmology, the local mix of ordinary matter and dark matter can wobble slightly from place to place, frozen in from the early universe. Owen Jessop and five co-authors use the FLAMINGO galaxy formation model in 2025 to ask what those ripples do to galaxy formation.

In linear theory these compensated variations cancel out in total density while shifting the baryon share, with a small root-mean-square amplitude. Whether such a subtle shift leaves visible marks on galaxies was an open question for simulators. The answer affects how precisely galaxy surveys can be read as tests of the underlying cosmology.
arxiv-2512-02427:
Hossein Nekouyan and three co-authors study posted price selling, where items go to buyers at set prices. Posted prices are simple, easy to grasp, and give buyers no reason to lie about value. Sellers often raise prices over time to handle doubt about who will arrive next.

Moving prices carry costs, though: late buyers may pay more for the same goods, which feels unfair. Each price change also costs effort to run. The 2025 study weighs plans that change prices only a few times, and that stay sensitive to risk. The aim is most of the gain with far fewer moves. Fewer price shifts also mean less work for the staff who run the sale each day.
arxiv-2512-02627:
Chiara Calascibetta, Laëtitia Giraldi, and Jérémie Bec study how to steer swarms of tiny self propelled particles. Left alone in a channel, such particles pile at walls, clog passages, and form bands. That self organization fights any attempt to move the swarm in one chosen direction.

The team applies global control, a single steering signal for the whole swarm, tuned in an optimal way. The aim is directed migration despite the clogging tendencies. Lessons here could guide micro robots, drug carrying particles, and other active matter systems that must travel through tight spaces. A swarm that can be steered as one body is far more use than the same swarm left to clog.
arxiv-2512-02727:
Yifan Zhou and co-authors estimate hand poses in 3D when hands overlap and hide each other. Daily hand interactions often include severe occlusions, such as two hands crossing. Occluded joints must then be guessed from global context, not seen directly.

Their DF-Mamba model uses deformable state space modeling to link local image features with the whole scene. Local patches hint where a hidden joint sits; global shape keeps the guess plausible. Robust hand tracking underpins sign language tools, virtual reality, and robots that work safely beside human hands. Hands that cross and twist are the norm in sign and craft, so the test set leans on them hard.
arxiv-2512-02827:
Slobodan Filipovski and three co-authors settle a question about directed graphs with nearly unique short routes. A digraph is called k-geodetic when any two vertices are joined by at most one walk of length up to k. Graphs close to the limits of this property are counted by an excess value.

The title states the result plainly: there are no excess one digraphs. The proof rules out a whole borderline family that might have existed. Nonexistence results prune the search space for network designs built on unique routing. A clean no can save years: no team need hunt for a graph that math says can not be built at all.
arxiv-2512-02927:
P. Narayanan and A. Raghuram prove, rather than compute, a case of the congruence principle for L-function values. The principle links congruences between objects to congruences between special values of their L-functions. Eisenstein cohomology is their main machine for the proof.

After refining that machinery for integral cohomology, they prove the principle for ratios of critical values. The L-functions are Rankin-Selberg type, attached to pairs of holomorphic cuspforms. Proved cases anchor the principle that computations elsewhere can only suggest, advancing the Langlands program's arithmetic core. Proof locks the case in a way counts can not. Locked cases are the stones on which the next ring of this long chain of work will rest.
arxiv-2512-03227:
Galaxy motions reveal distances and cosmic growth. K. Douglass and a large team present a distance catalog from the DESI survey in this 2025 work. They use the Tully-Fisher relation, which links a spiral galaxy's spin speed to its brightness.

The team calibrated the relation with first-year DESI data. They measured spin speeds for more than ten thousand galaxies. Those speeds give distances that do not rely on redshift alone. The catalog supports maps of how matter moves in the nearby universe, which test dark energy models. Distance catalogs like this one feed maps of bulk flows across the nearby cosmos.
arxiv-2512-03427:
Drones in forests need depth vision that works among trees. Yida Lin, Bing Xue, Mengjie Zhang, Sam Schofield, and Richard Green evaluate stereo methods in this 2025 work. Autonomous forestry flights need robust depth estimates that generalize across domains.

Past evaluations focused on urban and indoor scenes, leaving vegetation untested. The team ran the first systematic zero-shot evaluation of eight stereo methods. The methods span iterative, foundation model, and adaptation styles. Results show which methods cope with dense foliage, guiding safer drone work in forests. Forest scenes punish weak stereo, since leaves repeat patterns and light shifts fast.
arxiv-2601-06827:
Research by Jinhan Liu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with PDR. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Detecting pre-training data in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for auditing data privacy and copyright compliance.

Yet it remains challenging in black-box, zero-shot settings where computational resources and training data are scarce. While existing likelihood-based methods have shown promise, they typically aggregate token-level scores using uniform weights, thereby neglecting the inherent information-theoretic dynamics of autoregressive generation. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07027:
Sergey A. Antonyan and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with characterizations of g g -ANR spaces and inverse limits. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Antonyan, Aura Lucina Kantún-Montiel, Jesús Eduardo Mata-Cano, Armando Mata-Romero. We prove that, for a compact group G G. A metrizable G G -space is a G G -ANR under the following asumptions.

If it dominates a G G -ANR space through a fine G G -homotopy equivalence. If it is G G -homotopy dense in a G G -ANR. If it contains a G G -ANR as a G G -homotopy dense subset; if. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07127:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Delong Jia(贾德龙) and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers hierarchical structure of the open cluster NGC 752 astropy ( 2 ; 1. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The structure of open clusters provides key insights into their evolution and the dynamics of the Milky Way. Using Gaia DR3 data, we applied a hierarchical clustering algorithm to the open cluster NGC 752 based.

On the kinematical information and identified four substructures corresponding to different stages of disintegration. The cluster exhibits a pronounced signature of mass segregation. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07327:
An arXiv preprint from 2026 deals with how to predict creativity ratings from written narratives. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step workflow for building and analysing semantic networks from short creative texts.

The authors introduce and compare two widely used text-to-network approaches: word co-occurrence networks and textual forma mentis networks (TFMNs). We also show how they can be used in machine learning to predict human creativity ratings. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07527:
Josip Kir Hromatko and colleagues study how electric cars with several motors should share the work of driving. In straight-line driving, the motors together must meet the driver's torque demand. Many splits can meet it, but they use different amounts of battery energy. Choosing the split well saves range. Their 2026 preprint offers a new approach to that allocation problem.

The team approximates electric motor losses with higher-order polynomials that have special structure. Those polynomials are pseudoconvex, a property that makes optimization easier and more reliable. With losses modeled this way, the best torque split can be found cleanly. The paper speaks to vehicle engineers chasing efficiency through software rather than bigger batteries.
arxiv-2601-07627:
Shuzo Izumi takes up a plain-sounding question in geometry: can one solid shape rotate inside another? His 2026 preprint restricts the motion to rotation only, with no sliding. Think of turning a solid object inside a solid box. If rotation is possible at all, the center and direction of the turn may still be tightly restricted.

Naive problems like this can hide sharp mathematical structure. The space of allowed rotations depends on the exact shapes of both polytopes. Izumi studies those constraints for one polytope placed inside another. The question links geometry, motion planning, and the theory of configuration spaces. Readers who enjoy concrete problems with rigorous answers will find a careful treatment of when turning is possible and around which points.
arxiv-2601-07727:
N. K. Patra and colleagues use symbolic regression to find formulas linking neutron star traits to nuclear matter. The equation of state of dense matter inside neutron stars remains uncertain. At densities above nuclear saturation, interactions grow complex and exotic matter like hyperons may appear. Their 2026 preprint searches for the relations between matter properties and star properties. The focus is on nonlinear links and interdependencies.

Symbolic regression searches for readable formulas rather than black-box predictions. A readable formula shows which matter traits drive a star's radius or mass. That insight helps observers plan measurements and theorists test models. Neutron star data from gravitational waves and X-ray timing keep improving. The paper speaks to astrophysicists who want interpretable machine learning, not just accurate fits.
arxiv-2601-07927:
Sourav Maji and Abhishek Chowdhury count the quantum states of certain black holes with computational algebra. Their note explores algebraic geometry techniques for computing a helicity trace index. The index is the fourteenth one, for four-charge, one-eighth BPS configurations of pure D-branes. These configurations are dual to dyonic black holes built from D1, D5, momentum, and KK monopole charges. The work appears as a 2026 preprint note.

Microstate counting checks whether string theory reproduces black hole entropy. Each counted index compares a brane construction against the black hole it mirrors. Computational algebraic geometry makes counts feasible that hand calculation cannot reach. The note focuses on pure D-brane systems in type IIA superstring theory. It serves string theorists who test duality with exact numbers. Short and technical, it adds one more verified case to the counting program.
arxiv-2601-08027:
Deepak Deo, Daniel McIntosh, and five co-authors study galaxies that have just stopped forming stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at recently quenched ellipticals, a short phase between active star formation and quiet old age. What shuts star formation down in these systems is still not known.

The team studies neutral hydrogen gas and star formation across many wavelengths. Their sample holds 155 recently quenched ellipticals, plus earlier precursor and later descendant systems for comparison. By tracking gas content across these stages, readers can see how a galaxy changes as quenching begins and ends. The work helps test ideas about why star formation fades.
arxiv-2601-09427:
Sung-Soo Byun, Yeong-Gwang Jung, and Guido Mazzuca deform a classic law of random matrix theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a q-deformed random unitary ensemble tied to the little-q Laguerre weight. The ensemble is a discrete cousin of the classical Laguerre ensemble.

In a double scaling regime, where q shrinks as the matrix size grows, the authors derive the limiting spectral distribution. The limit gives a q-deformation of the Marchenko-Pastur law, which describes eigenvalue spreads of sample covariance matrices. Deformed laws like this link random matrices to combinatorics and quantum groups. The result pins down exactly how the classic curve bends under the deformation.
arxiv-2601-09527:
Jonathan Knoop and Hendrik Holtmann write a practical guide to running language models in-house. Their 2026 arXiv paper shows how small and medium firms can do private LLM inference on consumer Blackwell graphics cards. Many firms want an alternative to cloud APIs, which raise privacy worries.

Dedicated cloud GPU rentals improve privacy but cost steadily and give limited guarantees. Professional on-premise cards such as the A100 and H100 are too pricey for most small firms. Consumer cards offer a middle path. The guide weighs cost against control for firms that must keep their data at home.
arxiv-2601-10227:
Lorenzo Campioni links split counts to semigroups of counts. A split of a count into parts can be refined if a part splits more. Some splits admit no such step with all parts distinct. Those are named unrefinable splits.

Campioni ties them to count semigroups. Those are sets of counts closed under sums, with gaps. He reads splits as Young diagrams with hook sets. That read gives new tests for when a split is unrefinable. Gaps in the semigroup map to parts that are absent. The link lets him sort splits with the most absent parts.
arxiv-2601-10327:
Suzuyo Komeda and co authors speed up a deep scan of live tissue. The scan is optical coherence tomography, or OCT. It maps tissue by light bounce in depth. A dynamic form tracks how cells move. The rig used here sweeps a full field at once.

Full field scans yield sharp maps but vast data. That bulk makes streams slow and holds back fast work. The team use a neural net to cut that load. It forms sharp dynamic maps at high speed. The aim is high throughput scans that clinics and labs can run live.
arxiv-2601-10627:
Rajdeep Mazumdar, Kalyan Malakar, and Kalyan Bhuyan test a modified theory of gravity against fresh survey data. The theory, called f(Q, L_m) gravity, changes the rules that link matter and spacetime. They use a nonlinear form of it to describe the late universe. The aim is to match how cosmic expansion speeds up today.

They check the model against baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI DR2, a major galaxy survey release. Such data pin down the expansion history of the universe. A model that fits them stays in the race to explain cosmic acceleration. The paper shows how new survey data can sort rival gravity theories.
arxiv-2601-10827:
Simin Liu and co-authors plan robot manipulation that uses contact everywhere, not just at the fingertips. Humans lean, brace, and slide objects with whole arms. Contact-rich manipulation copies that freedom. State-of-the-art model-based planners mostly check feasibility: can a motion work at all? They rarely chase optimality, the best motion.

The authors aim for approximately optimal plans over long horizons. Their planner works on a graph of reachable sets in the plane. Contact makes dynamics rough and nonsmooth, so planning must respect geometry at each touch. Near-optimal contact plans could let robots handle clutter and heavy objects with a natural ease that fingertip-only control cannot match.
arxiv-2601-10927:
Todd Cochrane, Andrew Granville, and Junren Zheng study mixed incomplete character sums of rational functions. Character sums are sums over number-theoretic symbols that detect patterns in whole numbers. Graham and Ringrose proved strong bounds for such sums over intervals. Their result held when the modulus was squarefree and sufficiently smooth, with the interval long enough.

The new work treats mixed sums built from rational functions, with smooth moduli. Incomplete sums, cut off mid-range, are the hard and useful kind. Sharp bounds feed cryptography, where character sums guard security, and analytic number theory, where they count primes in disguise. The paper extends a classic line of estimates to a wider family of sums.
arxiv-2601-11327:
Agata Zywot, Xinyi Chen, and Maarten de Rijke test teams of small AI agents. Their 2026 report asks if such teams can beat one big model. The test bed is GAIA, a benchmark of hard general tasks. The agents are Qwen3 models with tools in hand.

Model sizes in the tests run from 4B to 32B. The team varies three things to see what counts most. One is scale, the raw size of the model used. One is explicit thinking, from none to planner-only to full. The third is tool use: search, code, and mind-maps. Tool use gave the largest and most steady gains. That finding favors smart setups over raw size alone.
arxiv-2601-11627:
Hassan Ugail, Jan Ritch-Frel, and Irina Matuzava authenticate historical drawings. Their 2026 preprint uses handcrafted features with one-class learning. Attribution of works on paper is a persistent challenge. Reference corpora are often small for a given artist.

Style in drawings lives in line and limited tonal range. The team builds a verification-based computational framework. One-class autoencoders learn from genuine works alone. Their inputs are a compact set of handcrafted features. Those features are interpretable, not black-box embeddings. The system judges if a new drawing fits the artist. Cultural heritage gains a tool for disputed sheets. Small corpora are the norm the design respects.
arxiv-2601-12027:
Raghav Bongole, Tobias J. Oechtering, and Mikael Skoglund push a classic bound in statistics to a wider case. The Fano bound limits how well any method can do. Their case is interactive, where data come from acts that change as learning runs.

Past bounds in this case deal with mean risk. Tail risk, the odds of a very bad result, was less well tracked. They swap the hard pass-fail event for a random one-bit score tied to the loss. That swap lets the bound cover tail goals for a broad class of losses.
arxiv-2601-12227:
Yuanyun Zhang, Han Zhou, Li Feng, Yilin Hong, and Shi Li learn health traits over time from records plus wearable data. Models trained on health records do well on many clinic tasks. Yet records are sparse, irregular, and driven by visits.

Wearables give dense, steady body signals, but lack labels and clinical sense. Joining the two could give traits that are both rich and grounded. Such traits could aid long-run risk and trend calls. The work builds that joint learning frame.  Joint traits could track slow shifts in health state.
arxiv-2601-12527:
Richard Liu, Itai Lang, and Rana Hanocka work on mesh deformation in computer graphics. The classic setup uses handles: a user drags a few control points and the shape follows. Classic methods give precise, fast control of the edit. The catch is that the user must know in advance where to place the handles.

The map from handle placement to final shape is often unintuitive. It is also non semantic, meaning handles do not line up with parts a user thinks about. The team propose deep feature deformation weights as a learned fix. Learned weights could spread a sparse edit in a way that respects the shape. That would let artists edit by meaning, not by trial and error.
arxiv-2601-13227:
Laura Dietz and co-authors ask a sharp test design question. Tools that write from sources are now judged by AI judges. Fact bit tests, called nugget tests, sit in both the judge seat and in the tools. That dual role can hide a leak.

The team asks how much a tool gains if it can peek at judge secrets. Such peeks would be a form of inside knowledge. If gains are large, scores may flatter tools that game the test. The study probes that risk head on. For teams that build or buy such tools, the work is a call to guard test facts as they would guard exam keys.
arxiv-2601-13327:
Po-Yu Liang, Tibo Duran, and Jun Bai design peptide binders with no need for a shape guess first. A peptide is a short chain of amino acids. Binders that grip a set target have wide use in drugs and bio chem. Many past tools first guess the 3D shape of the pair. That step adds bulk and trims the range of chains they can make.

Their tool, PepEDiff, works from the target's chain and its pocket sites alone. It spreads a protein embedding in a diffusion run to draft new binder chains. By skip of the shape step, it can roam a wider set of chains. For drug teams, a fast binder draft tool has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13727:
Bart Jacobs works on certifying the results of a program checker called VeriFast in 2026. VeriFast checks that C and Rust code meets strict correctness claims. It runs each function on its own, guided by notes the user adds. Those notes state what must hold before and after each step, in separation logic.

Jacobs adds a path to certify VeriFast output in a foundational way. The method uses hinted mirroring to rebuild the proof in a trusted base. Users then need not trust the whole tool, just the small checker. Stronger proof chains matter for safety-critical code.
arxiv-2601-13927:
Yousef Sadegheih, Dorit Merhof, and Pratibha Kumari adapt brain lesion models to new scan types over time in 2026. Brain lesion segmentation from multi-modal MRI often assumes a fixed set of scan types. It also assumes predefined pathologies, which real cohorts break. Continual learning offers a path, but with hard limits.

Past methods impose a maximum modality configuration on the model. Or they suffer severe forgetting in buffer-free settings, with no stored old data. The team targets modality-agnostic, domain-incremental segmentation. Models that adapt without forgetting could serve hospitals with varied scanners.
arxiv-2601-14027:
Junqi Liu and a large team use a general coding agent as a formal math reasoner in 2026. Agentic systems now dominate formal theorem proving, with strong performance. They coordinate multiple models and tools to build proofs. Existing approaches often rely on task-specific pipelines and trained formal provers.

That reliance limits flexibility and reproducibility, the team argues. Their Numina-Lean-Agent is an open and general agentic reasoning system. It directly uses a general coding agent for formal mathematics in Lean. An open system lets other teams test, copy, and extend the approach.
arxiv-2601-14327:
A team at YuanLab.ai tackles a training bottleneck in this 2026 paper. Their models are Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Such models route each input to a few expert parts, so they score well with fewer active parameters. Pre-training them is still a major cost, though. Many experts sit underused, and training runs at low efficiency.

The team built LAEP, a layer-adaptive expert pruning algorithm for the pre-training stage. Pruning cuts experts that add little. Layer-adaptive means each layer is pruned by its own needs, not one global rule. The stated goal is faster, leaner pre-training without giving up the gains that make these models strong.
arxiv-2601-14627:
Tobias Schwaigert and a team of eleven co-authors strain a crystal into a new state in this 2026 paper. Epitaxial strain is a powerful means to engineer emergent phenomena in thin films and heterostructures. Their material is KTaO3, a cubic perovskite in bulk form. Grown commensurate to SrTiO3 substrates, the films feel an in-plane strain of minus two percent.

Under that strain, the team demonstrates ferroelectricity above room temperature. Ferroelectric materials hold a switchable electric polarization, useful for memory and sensors. The strained films become a highly tunable ferroelectric. Readers get a recipe for turning a non-ferroelectric bulk crystal into a working ferroelectric film.
arxiv-2601-14727:
Shuxing Fang, Ruijian Han, Yuanhang Luo, and Yiming Xu survey a classic ranking model in this 2026 paper. The Bradley-Terry model turns pairwise comparisons into ratings. It is widely used wherever items are ranked by head-to-head results, from sports to product tests. The article surveys recent progress in the model and its extensions.

The authors focus on statistical and computational aspects. They emphasize the regime in which both the number of objects and the volume of comparisons tend to infinity. That regime matches large-scale applications, where millions of comparisons feed the ratings. Readers get theory, algorithms, and applications in one review of a workhorse model.
arxiv-2601-15227:
Rafael Boto, Karim Elyaouti, and co-authors scan a two-Higgs model for signs of broken symmetry between matter and antimatter. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the complex two-Higgs-doublet model. The focus is the known 125 GeV Higgs boson and how it couples to fermions.

Large CP-violating couplings would be a major clue about the universe's matter excess. The authors explore the model's parameter space with machine learning tools. Their kit includes an evolutionary strategy algorithm and a novelty reward. Those modern tools hunt for rare corners that older scans might well miss.
arxiv-2601-15527:
Alejandro González Nevado works on Eulerian polynomials in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the classic one-variable case, these polynomials are palindromic. Their coefficients read the same forward and backward. An identity behind that fact is well known. González Nevado lifts that identity to the multivariate setting. The polynomials then depend on several variables at once.

Nice combinatorial identities follow from the generalization, he notes. They can be read off from the polynomial relation itself. The proof also uses a bijection between permutations. Such identities give exact counts for permutation patterns. Palindromicity is a strong symmetry, and it often hints at deeper structure. For combinatorics readers, the paper extends a classical result in a clean direction.
arxiv-2601-15627:
Zechun Hu, Renming Song, and Li Wang study reinforced random walks in a 2026 arXiv paper. In an edge-reinforced walk, each crossing makes an edge more likely to be crossed again. The reinforcement here is linear, with a strength parameter. The walk lives on the half-line of nonnegative integers. Edges start with weights that grow with position. For large positions, the weight follows a power of the position times a log power.

The authors study the walk's limit behavior. That means where the walk ends up spending its time as steps pile up. The work was motivated by a 2021 article they cite. Reinforced walks model memory in motion, from animal foraging to network traffic. Limit results tell us when memory traps a walker and when it still roams.
arxiv-2601-15827:
Kuntal Banerjee and three co-authors study symmetry in torus dynamics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their maps are affine automorphisms of the two-torus. Each map combines a linear part with a shift. The linear part is a matrix, and the shift is a fixed vector. All arithmetic wraps around modulo the integers. Reversibility asks whether a map can be undone by a symmetry of the system.

Strong reversibility adds stricter demands on that symmetry. The authors study both notions for these maps. Reversible systems appear in physics, where time reversal is a basic question. Torus maps are simple enough to classify yet rich enough to matter. A full account of when they are reversible gives dynamicists a clean reference case for more complex systems.
arxiv-2601-16027:
Yiran Qiao and five coauthors study risk in live streams. Their 2026 preprint notes that scams and planned bad acts can build up bit by bit. Harm can also show up again in streams that look unlinked at first. A check of one stream alone can miss that wider past. The team links proof across sessions to catch such risk.

The method pairs a large language model with search over past cases. When a new stream raises doubt, the system pulls in old proof from other streams. Past plots and tricks then help judge the new case. This past proof is the core gain of the work. It aims to help sites spot slow, spread out scams that single checks would miss.
arxiv-2601-16127:
Alphaeus Dmonte and three coauthors join tongue tuned models to cut retrain costs. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models tuned for set tasks in many tongues. To add data or a new tongue, teams oft retrain the whole model. That full run costs much time and compute. The team tests if tuned models can be merged in place.

Merging joins the weights of models tuned for each tongue. A merged model may hold all tongues with no fresh full run. The test checks scores after merge on each tongue. Low cost merge would ease care of such models. It would also speed the add of new tongues.
arxiv-2601-16227:
Sneha Pradhan and three coauthors weigh neutron star traits in a new gravity frame. Their 2026 preprint uses NICER views of neutron stars. The frame is symmetric teleparallel gravity with a form set by a value Q. Three forms of that frame are tested side by side. They are the straight, log and growth forms of the Q term.

Bayes tools weigh which traits fit the NICER views best. Star mass and size shift with the gravity form in play. Tight fits test if the new frame can match real stars. They also bound how far the frame may stray from known gravity. The work joins sky views to gravity theory.
arxiv-2601-16727:
Julian Block, Andreas Könsgen, Jens Dede, and Anna Förster measure tiny power draws with care. Small web-linked gear must run for months on one cell. To plan that life, teams must gauge sleep-state draws. Those draws are far too small for plain tools. Their 2026 preprint tests fine gauge tricks on a real node.

Their test case is MoleNet, a net of small sense nodes. Bench tools like scopes blur at such low draws. The team weighs which tricks stay true at that scale. Sharp gauges help teams fix leaks in code and gear. Long cell life then serves farms, woods, and smart homes.
arxiv-2601-16927:
Łucja Kipczak and a large team probe how spin and lattice moves tie in a layered crystal. The crystal CrCl3 stacks in sheets that cleave with ease. Its spins line up in an anti-parallel form. Such ties shape how 2D magnets act and store. Their 2026 preprint reads the crystal's hums with split light beams.

Light reads show how hums shift with spin state. Glow and soak reads add more views of the tie. Thick flakes and bulk forms both come in view. Strong ties let fields or strain steer spin states. That steer could serve thin magnet tools in years ahead.
arxiv-2601-17127:
H. Cortés-Muñoz and a team of eight co-authors map gas clouds round far galaxies at cosmic noon. That far gas, the CGM, feeds and takes from its galaxy. Its size and flow traits stay hard to pin down. Their 2026 preprint uses pairs of quasars as twin probes. Shade lines of triply-stripped carbon mark the gas. Twin lines let the team gauge how far the gas stays in step.

Step scales tell if the gas is smooth or clumped. Clumps point to flows in or out of the galaxy. Such maps test how galaxies ate and grew then. Cosmic noon is when star birth peaked most.
arxiv-2601-17327:
Francisco J. G. de Oliveira and three co-authors study a risk where wind farms meet power lines. A turbine wake is a zone of churned air behind the blades. That churn can shake overhead conductors. Shake builds fatigue damage over time. Rules for safe gaps vary by country. In the United Kingdom, lines should stay at least three rotor widths away.

The team measures how wakes change the rate of fatigue build-up. Proof like that can firm up rules that now rest on caution. Too small a gap risks line failure. Too large a gap wastes land near farms. Their work helps planners set gaps with data in hand.
arxiv-2601-17427:
Cristopher Erazo, Santiago Acevedo, and Alessandro Ingrosso measure the Hopfield model in a new way. The Hopfield model is a spin system used in physics, learning, and brain science. The team uses Binary Intrinsic Dimension. That is a geometric measure built for binary data. It reads the true shape of data that lives in bits.

With it, they characterize the phases of the model. They also track the transitions between phases. The measure proves robust where older tools strain. A clear phase map helps all three fields that share this model. It shows where memory works and where it breaks. Neural networks with Hopfield roots gain a sharper design lens.
arxiv-2601-17527:
Yu Wang and Xiangchen Liu study how language model agents update beliefs. Models now act as economic agents in tests and tools. They read mixed signals, some personal and some aggregate. How they weigh those signals was opaque. The authors run experiments with models cast as households and firm heads. They build a Behavioral Kalman Filter frame to score the updates.

A Kalman filter is a classic tool for belief updates under noise. The behavioral form adds human-like bias. Scores show if models overreact or lag. That matters as models take real economic roles. Forecast and policy tests need agents whose belief rules are known. This work makes those rules visible.
arxiv-2601-17727:
X. C. Hu, H. Y. Yuan, and X. R. Wang study how two magnetic skyrmions interact. Skyrmions are tiny swirling spin textures. Moving many of them is key to racetrack memory and logic devices. Their mutual forces were poorly understood. The team studies skyrmion pairs in chiral magnetic films. They find the interaction has intrinsic, anisotropic traits.

Anisotropic means the force depends on direction, not just distance. Device layouts must respect that direction sense. Wrong assumptions could jam or scatter stored bits. A clear force law lets engineers space skyrmions with care. It also informs how pulses should push them. The work is basic physics with direct device stakes.
arxiv-2601-18327:
M. Y. Abd-Rabbou, Irfan Siddique, Saeed Haddadi, and Cong-Feng Qiao design a repeater chain for moving energy by quantum means over long range. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum energy teleportation. The protocol can activate local vacuum energy by spending pre-shared entanglement plus classical messages. Its practice is blocked by locality: in gapped systems, ground-state correlations fade fast with distance. That fade caps how far one step can reach. The authors propose a scalable repeater architecture for gapped systems.

Repeaters broke the same wall for quantum communication. A chain of short hops could carry the energy effect across a long span. The work extends a striking protocol toward real distances.
arxiv-2601-19327:
Boon Suan Ho generalizes a key entropy bound used in a famous sets problem. The union closed sets conjecture asks whether some element lies in at least half the sets of a union closed family. A lemma by Boppana, tying the entropy of a squared chance to the entropy itself, became a key tool in recent progress.

Ho extends that inequality past its first form. The bound involves the golden ratio, a quirk that hints at hidden structure. Stronger entropy tools may push the long open conjecture closer to a proof, or at least narrow where a counterexample could hide.
arxiv-2601-19827:
Mahdi Astaraki and Mohammad Arshi Saloot test when repeated retrieval helps a language model answer hard questions. Retrieval-augmented generation fetches evidence once, then answers. Iterative variants loop: retrieve, reason, then retrieve again with sharper queries. Scientific multi-hop questions need several linked facts, so looping sounds ideal.

The authors run a diagnostic study in scientific question answering. Surprisingly, the iterative approach can beat setups given ideal evidence. That result challenges the assumption that perfect retrieval is the ceiling. Multi-hop reasoning over sparse, mixed evidence is the stress test here. Knowing when loops pay helps builders spend compute wisely. The work also maps where static retrieval remains enough.
arxiv-2601-20527:
Arpith Kumar proposes thermodynamic consistency as a reliability test for complex Langevin simulations. The method is a promising route around the sign problem in quantum field theories with complex actions, where standard sampling fails. But it can converge to wrong results even when the run looks stable, so trustworthy checks are needed.

Existing diagnostics, like watching drift distributions, are indirect. Kumar argues that checking thermodynamic relations gives a more direct test of whether the output can be believed. A sharper test matters wherever complex Langevin results feed into claims about matter that no experiment can reach.
arxiv-2601-20727:
Victor Ojewale, Harini Suresh, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian ask how large language models can be held to account. Their 2026 paper notes that these models now sit inside big decisions. They help shape choices in health care, finance, jobs, and public services. Yet when a choice goes wrong, there is often no clear record of how it was made.

The authors propose LLM audit trails as a fix. An audit trail is a durable record of the process that others can review later. They frame it as a social and technical mechanism, not just a log file. It is meant to support continuous accountability over time. The paper gives designers and regulators a concrete way to demand a paper trail from AI systems.
arxiv-2601-20927:
Jin Ming Koh and eight co-authors entangle logical qubits without touching the physical ones. Their 2026 paper addresses a core need of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Logical entangling gates are essential for scalable machines. They are limited by the error rates and overheads of physical two-qubit gates and measurements. Every physical operation is a chance for noise to strike. A gate that needs no physical operation would dodge that risk.

The authors present a route to such gates. Logical information lives spread across many physical qubits. Manipulating that encoding cleverly can enact entanglement at the logical level. The physical layer stays idle while the logic moves. Fewer operations mean fewer errors to correct later. The work joins a broad effort to cut the cost of fault tolerance. It reframes a hardware problem as a coding opportunity.
arxiv-2601-21327:
Kael Kemp, Aman Desai, and Paul Jackson forecast how well a planned future collider could measure the Higgs boson. The machine, called FCC-ee, would smash electrons and positrons together. The team studies Higgs particles that decay into pairs of W bosons, which then decay further into light particles.

They estimate the precision on the combined rate of making a Higgs with a Z boson and seeing that decay. Clean lepton-only decays give sharp signals but few events. Knowing the reach in advance helps planners set priorities. It also shows what this decay path can teach about the Higgs itself.
arxiv-2601-21427:
Barium titanate is gaining ground as a material for chips that route light. It responds strongly both to light itself and to electric fields. Recent work has made low-loss waveguides and crisp resonators from thin films of it. Laying those films on an insulator has made the material a serious platform.

Waveguide designs decide how well such a chip can change light from one color to another. Hybrid designs mix the material with other structures to do that job better. The paper reviews and develops such designs. The goals they serve include frequency conversion and quantum photonics, two uses that need light handled with great care.
arxiv-2601-21727:
M. Ambrosch and a large team hunt hot subdwarf stars in a vast set of Gaia spectra using machine learning. Hot subdwarfs are compact, evolved stars near the extreme end of the horizontal branch. They hold clues to late stellar evolution and to the ultraviolet glow of old galaxies.

The team extends earlier work to a far larger sample of low-resolution spectra. Learning methods sort true subdwarfs and their binaries from look-alikes at scale. A bigger, cleaner catalogue sharpens the statistics on how these stars form. That feeds models of binary evolution, since many subdwarfs are thought to be shaped by a companion.
arxiv-2601-21827:
Zhi-Qiu Huang and co-authors use gamma-ray bursts to check how particles gain energy at extreme shock waves. Particle-in-cell simulations are the best tool for studying acceleration at relativistic shocks. But limited computing power constrains them, and the effect of those limits is hard to judge in advance.

The team therefore turns to observations: the late-time X-ray afterglows that bursts leave behind. Those glows carry fingerprints of the acceleration process that simulations must match. Their 2026 preprint draws out what the afterglow data imply for the simulations. This kind of cross-check matters because the same physics is invoked to explain cosmic rays and the brightest explosions in the universe.
arxiv-2601-21927:
Hong Chen and co-authors attack the memory problem that makes long conversations with language models expensive. As a chat grows, the stored key-value cache grows in a straight line, and deployment costs climb with it. Existing compression methods often ignore the structure of multi-turn dialogue.

Simple eviction rules can throw away context that later turns depend on. The team's 2026 preprint proposes SONIC, a learning-based framework that compresses past segments of a conversation into compact Nexus tokens that keep the meaning. Keeping long chats affordable matters for customer support, tutoring. And any service where a model must remember an hour of back-and-forth without renting ever more memory.
arxiv-2601-22227:
William Jarvis and co-authors study black holes hidden behind dust. Active galactic nuclei, or AGN, are luminous galactic centers, but the obscured ones are veiled by gas and dust that block direct views. The team analyzes nearly two hundred X-ray luminous AGN at modest redshifts in the GOODS survey fields.

For each object they build the spectral energy distribution. That is the light output from X-rays to the far infrared. They also classify the host galaxy's shape from its light profile. Their 2026 preprint links the hidden black holes to the galaxies that host them. Obscured growth may be the main way black holes gain mass, so catalogs like this shape the census of cosmic black hole growth.
arxiv-2601-22727:
D. Trotta and a co-author describe a wide-band amplifier built to test tiny photon sensors at picosecond scale, across a wide range of cold. Future physics runs may work silicon photomultipliers at very low heat, in harsh radiation, to time single photons sharply. Their 2026 preprint presents a trans-impedance amplifier for that characterization work.

Full maps of sensor traits across heat levels let teams pick the best trade of performance and survival. The amplifier is the enabling tool for those maps. The work is lab hardware, reported for builders. It serves the next wave of detectors.
arxiv-2601-22827:
Himal Wijekoon, Pierre Hirel, and Anna Grünebohm model, atom by atom, how defects affect switching in a key material. The material is barium titanate, a ferroelectric crystal used in sensors and memory. Its useful traits depend on tiny regions flipping their electric alignment.

One class of defects, called edge dislocations, can pin or guide that flipping. No atom-level picture of their role existed before this kind of modeling. Knowing how defects steer switching could help engineers design faster, tougher electronic parts. The study is modeled at the atomic scale, so it follows individual atoms near the dislocation rather than averaged behavior.
arxiv-2601-23127:
Sung-In Kim and three co-authors study how home-care patients keep control over their own lives. Home-based care brings medical and care services into a patient's living space. It promises care centered on the patient, yet patient agency is often weakly represented in shared planning.

Through interviews with patients, clinicians, and care workers, plus long observation, they trace how agency shows up. Information practices and relationships inside care networks shape that agency. The findings can guide tools and routines that keep patients as decision makers, not bystanders.
arxiv-2601-23227:
Jan Klíma and co-authors present SpinWaveToolkit, an open-source Python package for spin-wave physics. Spin waves are ripples in the magnetization of magnetic materials, key to future fast, low-power devices. The package models them in thin ferromagnetic films and coupled magnetic bilayers.

It combines classic Kalinikos-Slavin theory with a semi-analytical dynamic-matrix method. Users can compute dispersion relations, group velocities, decay lengths, mode profiles, and equilibrium states. A shared toolkit lets labs compare results and design magnonic devices faster. Static equilibrium magnetization states are among the computed outputs, giving device designers the full operating picture of a film.
arxiv-2603-02027:
Javier Lafuente Lopez proves a rigidity result for spacetimes that share the same Ricci curvature. His 2026 work defines a viable spacetime as one that admits a complete timelike geodesic. Timelike geodesics are the paths of freely falling observers, and completeness means they extend forever.

Take two causal spacetimes linked by a map that preserves causal structure and the Ricci tensor. If either spacetime is viable, that map must be a homothety, a pure rescaling of the metric. No stranger deformation can keep both causality and Ricci curvature fixed under the viability condition. Results of this kind limit how much freedom the Einstein equations leave once curvature data are pinned down. Causal order is pinned down too, a uniqueness theme at the core of relativity.
arxiv-2603-02227:
Keston Aquino-Michaels asks whether a transformer can learn which links matter in this 2026 paper. Attention links are highly focused, and a small gate can spot the key ones after training. Yet when sparse attention trains as a whole, learned gates barely beat random ones. Aquino-Michaels names this failure routing absorption and tests it on a small transformer.

Four lines of proof point the same way: the model's core weights adapt to any mask imposed. Soft gates learned or random end at near-equal quality. Hard gates get no learning signal through the mask at all. A gate copied onto adapted weights fails badly on fresh weights. Even random masks during training fail to stop the adaptation. Sparse methods with per-query gates face this pressure in full.
arxiv-2603-02327:
E Leitinger, A Miglio, J Montalbán, and colleagues question the origin of nitrogen-rich stars in this 2026 paper. Globular clusters are ancient star groups with distinct chemical patterns. Lone stars in the galaxy with those patterns are usually assumed to be cluster escapees. The team widens the search across the Kepler field, in halo and disc regions alike.

Star vibrations yield masses and ages, which are linked to chemistry and motion. Their sample holds over a hundred red giants, most with measured masses. Of twenty enriched stars, only a few are old enough to plausibly come from clusters. Most look too young, which likely reflects binary mergers or mass transfer, not true youth. Cluster origin thus fails for most of these field stars.
arxiv-2603-02427:
Ilias Triantafyllopoulos and Panos Ipeirotis detect careless survey respondents without labels in this 2026 paper. Surveys lose value when some respondents answer randomly or with low effort. Attention checks catch some, but they cost time and work inconsistently. Their framework scores each response set for coherence, using two unsupervised views.

One view rebuilds responses with an autoencoder and flags poor rebuilds. The other models dependencies between answers with a tree structure. A new loss makes the autoencoder sturdier against odd cases. Across nine real data sets, survey design mattered more than model complexity. Surveys with coherent, overlapping question batteries let even linear models separate careless respondents well. Good measurement design and easy detection, they show, go hand in hand.
arxiv-2603-02527:
Chengkang Xu determines when certain symmetry modules can be unitary in this 2026 mathematics paper. The setting is the gap-p Virasoro algebra, a family of infinite-dimensional symmetry algebras. Modules encode how the algebra acts on a space of states. A module is unitary when its action respects a positive inner product.

Xu focuses on irreducible Harish-Chandra modules, a well-behaved class with controlled weight spaces. For any such module, the paper determines the exact condition for unitarity. That condition separates the modules that admit a consistent quantum-mechanical reading from those that cannot. Representation theory of Virasoro-type algebras leans on such classifications. Knowing precisely which modules are unitary guides both pure mathematics and conformal field theory.
arxiv-2603-02627:
Praful Gagrani, Jiwei Wang, Yannick De Decker, and David Lacoste bound growth rates in chemical reaction networks in this 2026 paper. Networks of reactions underlie prebiotic chemistry and cell metabolism alike. Growth or shrinkage is usually studied through detailed kinetics with many parameters. Their approach needs only stoichiometry, the bookkeeping of what each reaction consumes and produces.

In the balanced-growth regime, they derive constraints on how fast a network can grow. A topological quantity, the maximum amplification factor, controls those bounds. It comes from an optimization over feasible reaction fluxes. Numerical tests on random network ensembles illustrate the bounds in action. The results speak to origin-of-life chemistry, where autocatalysis enables self-maintenance and growth. Synthetic network designers can also use the bounds as a structural check.
arxiv-2603-02827:
Sabine Cornelsen, Jan Kratochvíl, Miriam Münch, and colleagues ask when a graph can be drawn as strings hanging from one line. In such a drawing, each vertex is a curve below a baseline, and curves cross exactly when vertices are linked. Their 2026 paper restricts the curves to simple L-shaped bends and studies series-parallel graphs without shortcut edges.

They prove that, for these graphs, a drawing with double-bend strings exists exactly when a plain string drawing exists. A fast linear-time test decides the question. One catch remains: they build a graph that allows the double-bend form but not the stricter single L-shape. The gap between the two drawing styles is real, and now precisely located.
arxiv-2603-02927:
Tom Reichert and Iurii Karpenko separate a true signal from a shadow in collisions of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 paper concerns elliptic flow, the sideways pattern of particles flying out of heavy-ion collisions. A tidy scaling of that flow with quark count is taken as evidence for quark-gluon plasma, the hot early-universe state.

Recent STAR results show the scaling breaks at lower collision energies, but blocking by the passing spectator nuclei muddies the reading. The authors define new measures of how much flow each direction absorbs, effectively unshadowing the emitting source. A simple ballistic toy model shows how strongly shadowing distorts the scaling. Their cleanup matters for reading STAR data and for the coming CBM experiment.
arxiv-2603-03027:
Anne-Marie Aubert and Roger Plymen describe an algebra whose representation theory is shaped like a Klein bottle. Their 2026 paper works over a local field and studies a depth-zero building block for representations of the group SL8. The block is governed by a twisted Hecke algebra built from quadratic and quartic field extensions.

They write the algebra down fully, with generators and relations, and list all its simple modules, each just two-dimensional. The algebra's spectrum is an explicit variety whose compact real form is a Klein bottle, the one-sided surface, and that bottle models a family of unitary representations. Comparing with the classical untwisted setting, the two Bernstein varieties match exactly. The Klein bottle reappears, now floating inside the tempered dual of the full group.

bacon-new-atlantis-1627:
Francis Bacon imagined an island where science ruled in peace, and left the tale unfinished at his death. New Atlantis, printed in 1627, tells of Bensalem, a land cut off from the known world. Sailors blown off course find its ports and its wise, kind rulers.

At the heart of Bensalem stands Salomon's House, a great college of men who study nature to help mankind. Its labs, gardens, and engines sketch a research state three centuries early. The tale became the model of the lost-land utopia in English. Atlantis writers have cited Bacon ever since.
bernard-experimental-medicine-greene-192:
Claude Bernard was a French physiologist whose lab work remade the study of digestion, the liver, and the nerves. His Introduction to the Study of Experimental Medicine, in Greene's 1927 translation, is physiology's founding manifesto. Bernard wrote it as a guide for young doctors entering the lab.

He argues that medicine must test ideas by controlled trials, not by authority or bedside habit alone. His key concept, the internal environment, holds that the body's inner fluids stay steady while the outside world shifts. That insight later fed Cannon's idea of homeostasis and still frames physiology. Young doctors still read it as a first lesson in how labs should think.
burden-quest-for-the-dragon-of-komodo-19:
Douglas Burden sailed to a small island east of Java in 1926 to hunt a dragon of report. The Quest for the Dragon of Komodo, his 1927 account in Natural History, tells that expedition in full. Burden was a trustee of the great New York museum and a keen field man.

His party trapped and shot the great lizards, some ten feet long, and shipped live ones back to America. The dragon proved real: a huge meat-eating monitor, swift and strong. The tale of the hunt helped spark the film King Kong some years later. Burden's piece is the dragon's debut in the West.
cather-death-comes-archbishop-1927:
Death Comes for the Archbishop, published in 1927, is often ranked as Willa Cather's finest novel. Its heroes are two French priests, Bishop Jean Latour and Father Joseph Vaillant. In 1851 they take charge of a vast new diocese in New Mexico, among desert, mesas, and scattered villages.

Latour and Vaillant ride long miles to visit missions, settle disputes, and build a cathedral of honey-colored stone. Cather tells their lives in calm, clear episodes rather than one driving plot. The book honors patience, friendship, and faith lived out quietly. It also gives one of the great portraits of the American Southwest in fiction.

River islands made natural prisons: hard to leave, easy to guard, near yet apart. A sighting there added a curious point to the Hanoi prison map. It also suggested overflow or special holding beyond the known sites. This short report preserves the island jail as observed, one of the capital system's stranger addresses.

The northern camps were run with a parade-ground precision the south never matched. Locating them fed rescue planning and the great accounting alike. For readers, the report is the northern chapter of the captivity story, pinned to one district's map.
