The document lets that test be run fairly. It also shows the American habit of leading with drafts. Paper, at Potsdam, was power in draft form.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d827:
Barnes reported from Bulgaria on July 30, 1945, in document 827. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary two days before Potsdam closed. His letters form one of the volume's most complete post records. This one entered the second Potsdam volume near the end of his run.

A closing-stage report has the air of a final entry. Barnes wrote knowing the decisions were nearly made. Readers see him placing his last facts where they would count: on the record. The document shows the dignity of the reporting craft. Influence fades; a true file endures, and his file endures.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d927:
Seymour Rubin, chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, wrote this candid letter extract to his acting deputy on July 25, 1945. He recounts the reparations talks in Moscow and at Potsdam. Basic principles had won agreement, but the Russians held back on defining war booty and restitution.

Then the Soviet booty definition, covering nearly everything, scrapped the earlier work. A new plan let Russia pay itself and Poland from its own zone. Rubin gives the agreed shares: 56 percent Soviet, 22 percent each for Britain and America. He also reports Soviet interest in two billion dollars of Ruhr equipment, and talk of trading food and potash in exchange.
frus-1961-63v07-d327: A 1961-1963 FRUS editorial note from the Arms Control volume. The disarmament talks. This note provides that context. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
frus-1981-88v04-d327: A 1981-1988 FRUS memorandum from the Secretary of State on the Soviet Union. Reagan's team wrote. This document preserves that memo. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
gao-gaoreports-b-296127: International Marine Products took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296627: Coastal Maritime Stevedoring took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298327: Praxair took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Gas giants get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298527: Technical Support Services took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298627: eFedBudget Corporation took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Budget-tech deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299227: L-3 Communications doubled its March 2007 protest — two case numbers, one fuze-products fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims at once. The firm challenged the awards as unfair, and the call weighs each claim with care. Paired filings get one careful answer from the bid court.
gao-gaoreports-b-303927: A Labor grant to New York's workers' comp board got a fiscal ruling in this June 2005 GAO call, which tests the grant. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the grant was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-311327: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Mark Whetstone-Designated Employee Agent. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-400127: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Zia Engineering & Environmental Consultants, LLC; Garrison Engineering & Maintenance Services, LLC. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-400227: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Systems Research and Applications Corporation. The July 21, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-227: Housing loan guarantee suspensions needed prevention in 2005, and GAO's report offers options to keep the FHA and RHS programs running. The review writes the safety net. The homebuyers deserved the steady programs. The options were offered. The homebuyers deserved the steady programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-327: Chemical and water plant protection got a GAO survey in 2005, and the report covers federal requirements, facility actions, and remaining gaps. The review checks the fences. The towns downstream deserved the guard. The gaps remained. The towns downstream deserved the guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-427: Defense prepositioning needed better oversight in 2005, and GAO's report says management of the stockpile programs required upgrading. The findings demand the supervision. The report warns that the forward-deployed gear deserved watching. The oversight had to improve. The forward-deployed gear deserved watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-727: Airport intermodal connections got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says potential strategies would redefine the federal role. The findings take the measure. The report shows the transit links were studied. The strategies had to be understood. The transit links were studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-927: Performance information needed better agency use in 2005, and GAO's report says enhancing the use of data for decisions was required. The findings demand the uptake. The report warns that the managers deserved working gauges. The use had to be enhanced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-27: Service contract wage determinations needed transparency in 2006, and GAO's report says the process could benefit from openness and better violation tracking. The findings demand the daylight. The report warns that the contract workers deserved fair wages. The process had to be transparent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-327: The Missile Defense Agency fielded a partial shield in 2006, and GAO's report says initial capability arrived but fell short of original goals. The findings balance the milestone and the miss. The report warns that the shield's promise needed honesty. The goals had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-427: Environmental cleanup liabilities needed long-term planning in 2006, and GAO's report says control weaknesses and uncertainties hampered the fiscal outlook. The findings demand the foresight. The report warns that the toxic bill would come due. The planning had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-627: The community services block grant needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says HHS should focus its monitoring efforts. The findings demand the attention. The report warns that the anti-poverty dollars deserved watching. The oversight had to improve. The anti-poverty dollars deserved watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-727: Empowerment zones showed mixed results in 2006, and GAO's report says communities improved, though the program's exact effect was unclear. The findings balance hope and doubt. The report warns that the revitalization dollars needed proof. The zones had to show results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1127: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that the Smithsonian was rotting from the roof down. Leaky tops, tired air systems, and thin guard coverage put the nation's attic — its priceless collections — at risk. The report is a plea to fix the buildings before the treasures inside pay the price of neglect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-127: The national debt's books got an audit in 2007, and GAO's report grades the Public Debt bureau's schedules for 2006 and 2005. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows the trillions got their own tally. The debt's ledger had to add up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-27: Tax season services kept improving in 2007, and GAO's report says most filing services got better, though savings opportunities remained. The findings balance praise and prodding. The report shows the tax collector learning to serve. The service had to keep improving.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-627: The global AIDS fund's books got a review in 2007 — GAO's report says its funding decisions were better documented, with work left to do. The findings credit the progress made. The report's standard is high: billions for the dying deserve bulletproof books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-27: After years of flu-shot scares, GAO's 2007 report takes the vaccine pipeline apart: how shots get made, how they reach arms, and what the public is told. The supply chain proved brittle, and the health messages did not always land. The report points at the weak links — and asks whether official talk was building trust or burning it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-327: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on DOD Pharmacy Program: Continued Efforts Needed to Reduce Growth in Spending at Retail Pharmacies. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-427: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Logistics: Navy Needs to Develop and Implement a Plan to Ensure That Voyage Repairs Are Available to Ships Operating near Guam when Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gide-counterfeiters-bussy-1927:
André Gide called The Counterfeiters, published in French in 1925, his only true novel. Dorothy Bussy translated it into English in 1927. Schoolboys in Paris pass counterfeit coins, and the false money mirrors false selves all through the book.

At its center stands Edouard, a novelist keeping a journal for a novel of his own. Around him, students, teachers, and rogues drift into theft, despair, and suicide. Gide weaves diary, letters, and shifting viewpoints into one design. The book asks what counts as real in art and in life. It became a landmark of the modern novel in France and beyond.
haldane-possible-worlds-1927:
Possible Worlds, published in 1927, gathers Haldane's essays on science for general readers. He writes on the size of the universe, the oddness of life, and what future ages might bring. His humor and range made him a model for later popular science writers.

One famous line holds that the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we can suppose. Haldane moves from stars to microbes to human society without losing his plain, lively voice. The essays show a first-rate mind enjoying hard questions in public. Each piece stands alone, so the book can be read in any order.
hales-vegetable-staticks-1727:
Stephen Hales, an English clergyman with a gift for experiment, published Vegetable Staticks in 1727. Hales measured living plants the way others measured machines. His book is often called the founding text of plant physiology.

With gauges and tubes, Hales showed how sap rises and how leaves give off water. He measured root pressure and the air plants take in and release. His methods were new: count, weigh, and test, rather than guess. Much later lab work on plant water and gases still starts from Hales. Growers and gardeners read his numbers on how fast sap can rise.
handy-polynesian-religion-1927:
Edward Smith Craighill Handy synthesized Polynesian Religion in 1927 for the Bishop Museum, the great storehouse of Pacific learning in Honolulu. Tapu, the sacred restriction, mana, the spiritual power, gods great and small, and ritual form his themes throughout. Hawaii, Tahiti, Samoa, and New Zealand supply the evidence, drawn from the museum's unmatched collections and its field reports.

Handy set scattered island traditions into one comparative frame without flattening their real differences. Priests, temples, feasts, seasons, and prayers all find their place in his calm, orderly survey of the whole region. The book remains a standard Bishop Museum synthesis of how Polynesians understood the sacred world around them.
hemingway-men-without-women-1927:
Ernest Hemingway published Men Without Women in 1927, his second book of stories, written in the wake of The Sun Also Rises. The fourteen stories circle men in worlds where women are absent, lost, or kept at the edge of the frame. It is the essential early Hemingway collection.

The Killers puts young Nick Adams in a lunchroom where two hitmen wait for their victim. Hills Like White Elephants stages a whole strained relationship in one station-bar conversation. Other tales cover bullfighting, boxing, soldiers, and an old fisherman's trade in Italy. Hemingway's dialogue does nearly all the work, with feeling buried under plain talk. Few story collections have influenced later writers more.
hesse-steppenwolf-1927:
Hermann Hesse published Steppenwolf in 1927, here in Basil Creighton's first English translation of 1929. Harry Haller's divided self and the Magic Theater make the novel Hesse's darkest work of fiction. Creighton's version was the book's English debut, two years after the German original stunned readers at home.

Harry, a writer of fifty, calls himself a wolf of the steppes, torn between bourgeois comfort and savage solitude in himself. Hermine, a dancer, tutors him in jazz, love, and laughter, and lends him Pablo and the Magic Theater's doors. In the theater, mirrors, chessmen, and a stabbed Hermine stage the selves he must learn to laugh at, not obey. Mozart's laughter closes the book's vision of humor as the soul's way out of its private hell. The novel found its mass audience forty years on, among the young of the sixties.
holmberg-finno-ugric-siberian-mythology-:
Uno Holmberg wrote this survey of the faiths of Finland, Hungary's kin groups, and Siberia for the Mythology of All Races set, and it came out in 1927. The set aimed to cover the myths of the whole world in plain English. His part deals with the far north of Europe and Asia.

The book maps gods, spirits, and the shape of the world as those peoples held it. Shamans hold a large place, as links between men and the spirit world. It served for years as the main English guide to faith in the cold north.
hortulus-hermeticus-flosculis-philosopho: Hortulus hermeticus, 1627. The hermetic garden. This book preserves that alchemy. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
hurston-cudjos-own-story-1927:
In 1927 Zora Neale Hurston published an account of her interviews with Cudjo Lewis in the Journal of Negro History. Lewis was the last known survivor of the Clotilda, the last slave ship to reach the United States. Hurston visited him in Alabama and recorded his memories in his own words.

Cudjo tells of his youth in Africa, his capture, and the middle passage in 1860. He recalls slavery, freedom, and the founding of Africatown by the Clotilda's survivors. His grief for his lost homeland runs through the whole account. The piece became a key source for Hurston's later book Barracoon and a rare firsthand record of the slave trade.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-27:
A fragile peace holds through Volume 27, from 1898, on the Hurons of 1645 and 1646. Between storms, the mission breathes and gathers its strength once more. Thwaites prints reports that sound, for once, almost hopeful in tone.

Baptisms continue in the towns, and new ventures westward take shape. Priests repair chapels, plant fields, and teach with fresh energy each day. Yet every calm page carries quiet dramatic weight for modern readers. They know the peace will break and the storm will return. That knowledge gives this gentle volume its deep, sad pull. Calm, here, feels more fragile than any storm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maas-joseph-102:
Joseph Maas, an English singer, receives a biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Dartford, Kent, on January 30, 1847, he sang as a chorister at Rochester Cathedral for five years. When his voice broke he worked as a dockyard clerk at Chatham. In 1869 he went to Milan to train. He died in London in 1886.

The article follows his rise on the English stage. Back home in 1871 he sang in concert, then in opera at Covent Garden. His reputation was made in America, where he spent years as a leading tenor. Returning to England, he joined Carl Rosa's company and sang Rienzi at Her Majesty's Theatre in 1879. In ballad opera his popularity was unmatched, and few rivaled him in Handel. The entry preserves the career of a cathedral chorister who became a star of English opera.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-samuel-10:
Samuel Marks is the subject of an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906 and written by Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind. Marks was a South African pioneer born in Sheffield, England, about 1850. He went out to Cape Colony around 1868, started as a country trader, and then moved into the diamond trade.

Working together, Marks and his brothers bought diamond claims and built a large fortune. In 1884 he moved to the Transvaal, lent money to President Kruger's government, and bought farms that turned out to hold rich coal deposits. His firm, Lewis and Marks, supplied coal to the Cape railways and opened mines, factories, and a distillery near Pretoria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mecklenburg-103:
Mecklenburg, the north German territory on the Baltic, has its Jewish history surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and Isidor Warsaw. Since 1701 the land had been split into the grand duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz, which in 1900 held 1,763 Jews in thirty-six congregations and 331 in six. Settlement may reach back to Brandenburg's expulsion of 1243, but documents begin in 1266, when Wismar received the Lübeck law and its Jews are already mentioned.

The article then walks town by town: Boizenburg in 1267, Rostock in 1279, Schwerin about 1340, Neubrandenburg not until 1440. Everywhere the pattern holds. Jews paid heavily each year for the right to live and for the prince's protection, could not own land, and were penned into neglected streets. When Henry the Pilgrim spent twenty-four years a captive in Palestine, the Jews of Wismar were expelled outright.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-jac:
Menahem ben Jacob was a German synagogal poet. He died at Worms on April 16, 1203. Joseph Jacobs and Max Schloessinger profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came of an old Worms family of scholars. His great-grandfather Simson, surnamed the Preacher, lived through the First Crusade and is quoted by Rashi. Menahem's own epitaph gives him three titles. It calls him teacher of the Law, preacher, and payyetan.

Zunz credits him with thirty-one poems. They span the liturgical forms. He wrote penitential hymns besides. The article singles out his elegies. One entered the German rite for the Ninth of Ab. One mourns the martyrs of Blois in 1171, another those of Boppard in 1195, and a third the ten martyrs of Roman times. A tone of gloom runs through the work. The writers see it as answering his age. It answers the condition of the Jews in his time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mikweh-rabbinic:
Miḳweh, a Hebrew word for a gathering of water, came to mean the ritual bath of Jewish law, as Cyrus Adler and Julius H. Greenstone explain in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible uses the word for collected waters in Genesis and Exodus. Leviticus ties it to purification, and the rabbis built detailed rules around it.

Every kind of ritual impurity once required immersion, the article says, but since the Dispersion most purity laws have lapsed in practice. One survives widely: the laws of niddah, still kept in most Orthodox communities, which keep the mikweh a necessary institution there. The bath must cover an average man's whole body, a volume the rabbis fixed at forty seahs in a pool three cubits long.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mortality-11027:
Mortality, the Jewish Encyclopedia's article on death rates among Jews, was written by Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg. It opens with a puzzle. Jews mostly lived in the most crowded and unsanitary parts of European and American cities. Yet wherever figures existed, their death rates ran lower than those of their neighbors.

The article piles up numbers, above all for infants, from Prussia, Baden, Posen, Amsterdam, Vienna, and other places. In Prussia, for example, 129 Jewish infants per thousand died in the first year, against 174 Christian infants. Similar gaps appear in the figures for Germany, France, Italy, and England. As a period source it shows how Jewish scholars around 1900 used statistics to argue about health, poverty, and Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-menah:
Moses ben Menahem, called Präger, was a cabalist of Prague in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was a disciple of Rabbi David Oppenheim. His writings work on the Zohar and on the ascetic life.

His Wa-Yakhel Mosheh, printed at Dessau in 1699, gives cabalistic treatises on passages of the Zohar with a double commentary. His Zera Kodesh treats asceticism in a cabalistic sense. To it he appended a story: a young man at Nikolsburg possessed by an evil spirit, which Moses himself drove out. That tale was also printed in Judeo-German at Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munz-sigmund-11:
Sigmund Münz was an Austrian writer born at Leipnik in Moravia on May 7, 1859, brother of Bernhard Münz. Isidore Singer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Vienna and Tübingen and took his doctorate in 1883. Years in Rome, Milan, Venice, and Florence made Italy his subject.

From 1891 Münz settled in Vienna and wrote on foreign politics for the Neue Freie Presse, above all on Italy. His books gather Italian studies, sketches, and letters: From Modern Italy, From Quirinal and Vatican, and Italian profiles. He also wrote on the historian Gregorovius and a set of biographical sketches, Modern Statesmen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nascher-sinai-s:
Sinai Simon Nascher was a Hungarian writer born in 1841 at Szent Miklos. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied at Baja and Berlin and in 1866 was chosen preacher at Berlin. Repeated attacks of insanity forced him to resign, and he lived retired at Baja.

From that retirement came a shelf of German books. He wrote on pulpit exegesis, on Hai Gaon and Semitic language study, and on the proverb among Jews and Arabs. Later works treat German philosophy's reach, the Judaism of the Enlightenment, and the community's past and future. He also rendered a Hungarian poet into German verse. He died at Baja in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehemiah-ben-ko: Nehemiah ben Kohen Zedek held Pumbedita's gaonate by a trick. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served from 960 to 968. While Aaron b. Sargado still held the office, Nehemiah schemed against him. The college kept Sargado, judging him better in every respect. After Sargado died, Nehemiah seized the post anyway. Most of the college, led by Sherira, refused to own him. Only a few members and rich laymen backed him. Nothing is known of his learning or deeds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunez-11627:
Nuñez is a Marano family name of sorrow. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Four of its women are named in the record. Each met the Inquisition in Spain's power. Their stories survive in autos and in elegy.

Beatriz Nuñez burned at sixty years of age. The auto da fé was at Madrid in 1632. Clara Nuñez was martyred at Seville with Francisco Lopez. His father, a physician, burned a few years after. Barrios wrote an elegy in her memory. Violante and Helena, of the Gradis branch, fared otherwise. The same Madrid day sentenced them both in 1632. Imprisonment and the galleys for life was their doom. Persecution, not achievement, is this family's chronicle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-abrah: Abraham Hayyim Oppenheim was a rabbi at Péczel, in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died there young, at the age of twenty-eight. His death came at some date before the year 1825. He wrote a book on rites for the sick and the dead. He wrote a second book on the soul that lives on past death. A kin judge at Budapest brought both books out in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-owl-11827:
The owl is a bird of the night named in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Three Hebrew words are rendered as owl in English texts. Those words are kos, yanshuf, and tinshemet. All three stand in the lists in Leviticus.

Kos is a small owl that lives among ruins, by the Psalms. Men link it to a kind still known in that land. Arabs call that kind by the name bumah there. It is the most oft seen owl in Palestine. Yanshuf is a great owl of ruins and caves. It is found through Palestine, most near Petra of old. More kinds live in that land, the piece notes. White, horned, wood, and fish owls are all found there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pascheles-wolf-:
Wolf Pascheles was an Austrian publisher of Jewish books in Prague. He was born there in 1814 and died there in 1857. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Pascheles began poor, earning his living as a tutor.

His break came during the cholera outbreak of 1831. He printed prayer books that Prague Jews badly needed. The books sold well, and he became a traveling book seller. In 1846 he launched Sippurim, a series of tales and lives of famous Jews. He later published a popular Jewish calendar. His small Pentateuch with a German translation went through many editions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perez-ben-elija:
Perez ben Elijah was a French tosafist of Corbeil. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father was Elijah of Tours, a Talmudist.

Perez studied under Jehiel of Paris and Samuel of Evreux. He traveled through Brabant and Germany on his studies. In Germany he met Meir of Rothenburg. Back home his lectures drew the next age's great rabbis. His comments covered most of the Talmud. Students reworked them so much that few stayed pure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prag-joseph-123:
Joseph Prag was an English worker for Jewish causes, born at Liverpool in 1859. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was schooled at the Liverpool Institute. He studied at Queen's College, Liverpool, as well. For long he has led in Zionist circles in England.

Prag does not follow the movement of Herzl, though. His loyalty stays with the Chovevei Zion. He founded the English branch of that body himself. He wrote in the reviews on settling Jews in Palestine. He sat on the council of the Anglo-Jewish Association. In 1901 it sent him to a Berlin meeting on the Jews of Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-macron-:
Ptolemy Macron was a general of King Antiochus Epiphanes of Syria. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The prefect Lysias sent him against the Jews. Nicanor and Gorgias went with him on that march. Their foe was the band of the Maccabees. Three books name Macron as a son of Dorymenes.

Menelaus sent Macron rich gifts at one point. He sought the general's good word with the king. That act alone shows Macron's high rank at court. In Second Maccabees he is called governor of Coele-Syria. The article builds his role from these scant records. He stands where Syrian power met Jewish revolt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raffalovich-art:
Arthur Raffalovich was a Russian economist of a banking house. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Odessa in 1853. He studied matters of trade and state at Paris and Bonn. From 1876 he served Count Schuvalov in London. He was that envoy's private secretary for three years.

At the same time Raffalovich wrote for the French press. He served the Journal des Débats and later the Temps. His own books treat trade and finance most of all. One treats the tax on spirits in depth. Russia named him to its high council of commerce. The entry shows a banker turned public voice on money.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ree-anton-12627:
Anton Ree was a Danish pianist born on October 5, 1820. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Aarhus in Jutland. He died in Copenhagen on December 20, 1886.

The article traces his piano study in Hamburg, Vienna, and Paris. He settled in Copenhagen in 1842. Many pupils gathered around him there. His fine technique ranked him among Denmark's leading pianists. In 1866 he became a first teacher at the new conservatory. He composed piano pieces and wrote for music journals. His book on piano technique came after his death. A second work sketched the history of music. The entry is distinct from the Hamburg teacher's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rhodes-12727:
Rhodes is a Turkish island in the Aegean Sea. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Galante wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It is the largest island in the Sporades group. The Bible knew it under an older name form.

The article gives the island about thirty thousand people. About four thousand Jews live in its capital town. Jews were established there in remotest times, they say. First Maccabees mentions Jews dwelling there in 140 B.C. Benjamin of Tudela found five hundred Jews on his visit. A Jew of Emesa bought the fallen Colossus debris in 656. Spanish refugees later settled there after fleeing persecution. A village street still bears a name from Jewish settlement. The entry traces a community older than its rulers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosanes-jacob-1:
Jacob Rosanes was a German mathematician born in Brody, Galicia, on August 16, 1842. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He rose from a clerk's job in Breslau to full professor at its university.

Rosanes started out in a business house, then prepared himself for university study. He earned his doctorate at Breslau in 1865 and became professor there in 1876. In 1903 the university elected him its rector, a rare honor for the time. His papers deal with conic sections, triangles in perspective, and systems of points. He also wrote on how people picture space itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubo-julius-129:
Julius Rubo was a German jurist born at Halberstadt on June 9, 1794. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. After war service against Napoleon, he took his law degree in 1817.

Rubo's learning won notice in a pamphlet war over Jewish doctors of law. Yet practice stayed closed to him in Hamburg, Holstein, and Brunswick, for his religion. He settled at Halle as a privat-docent to teach instead. An 1822 law then barred Jews from academic posts and cost him that office. He turned to legal writing in Berlin, on Roman law of obligations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saliva-hebrew-r:
Saliva, in Hebrew rok, is spittle, treated here in law, custom, and folklore. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. To spit in a person's face meant the utmost contempt in Scripture.

Spitting before someone also showed disrespect, so none might spit in the Temple. Mosaic law, unlike the law of Manu, counts saliva pure in itself. Only the saliva of one with an impure issue defiled others under it. Healing power, above all for eye diseases, was widely ascribed to spittle. Jews, early Christians, Greeks, and Romans all shared that belief then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-mart: Samuel ben Marta was a Palestinian amora of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He explains the word mishkan, twice used in Exodus for the sanctuary, by its likeness to mashkon, a pledge. The sanctuary, on his reading, was twice taken as a pledge, in the first and second destructions. Simeon ben Marta of Genesis Rabbah seems to be the same man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-abba-b-bat:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Abba Saul ben Baṭnit. He was a tanna of the second and first centuries B.C. Derenbourg thought his mother was a proselyte from Batanea. The name Baṭnit, though, seems to be a man's proper name. Abba Saul traded in business with Eleazar ben Zadok.

With Eleazar, Abba Saul issued a ruling on Sabbath law. It is recorded in the Mishnah's tractate Shabbat. He also filled his liquid measures with wine before feast days. That let him give the wine to children on the feasts themselves. A sharp saying about corrupt priestly families passes under his name. It condemns the outrages of some high-priestly houses. Bacher's study of the tannaim supplies most of the evidence here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulman-kalman:
Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Kalman Schulman. He was a Russian author, historian, and poet. Schulman was born at Bykhov in 1819. He died at Wilna on January 2, 1899. He studied at the Volozhin yeshibah for six years. The strain hurt his eyes, and he moved to Wilna. Poverty there forced him to divorce his wife.

Schulman aimed to spark a Jewish rebirth in Russia. He believed only Hebrew could carry that revival. The language had slept for centuries. He wrote in pure Biblical Hebrew with rare mastery. Hardly any modern idea escaped his expression. He became the most widely read Jewish author of his world. His fame began with a petition to Sir Moses Montefiore in 1846. It pled for Jews expelled from the border districts. Its beauty of style won him the Progressivists' circle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sens-hebrew-etc:
Sens, a town in France's Yonne department, held a Jewish community by the sixth century. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its Jews lived on streets named for their quarter and synagogue. They kept two cemeteries within the town.

An archbishop expelled the Jews of Sens in the ninth century. Louis VII let them return in 1146. Later, a pope complained that their synagogue outshone the nearby church. That fine building stood until 1750, when it was razed for a salt warehouse. The entry gives a long, uneven history of one French Jewish community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shepherd-13527:
Shepherding was the chief work of the Israelites in their early days in Palestine. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the shepherd. A shepherd led flocks to pasture and to streams. He guarded them from wild beasts and robbers.

Sheepdogs sometimes helped with that guarding work. At night shepherds kept watch in the open air. They also used tents, stone towers, caves, or stone folds. A sick or lame lamb was carried in the shepherd's bosom. He wore a single garment and walked before his flock. The entry shows daily flock care behind the Bible's beloved shepherd images, from Psalm twenty-three onward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simferopol-1372:
Simferopol was the capital of the government of Taurida in Russia, on the Salghir river near Sebastopol. Joseph Jacobs and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews made up about a fourth of its roughly 50,000 people. The community had nine synagogues and prayer houses in all.

Its Jews fell into three groups: Mitnaggedim, Hasidim, and Krimchaks. The city had a Russian school and two Talmud Torahs. A Jewish hospital dated from 1845, and a home for the aged opened in 1887. The entry ends with the riot of May 14, 1905. In that riot, 140 Jewish stores burned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sodom-13827:
Sodom was the first city of the Pentapolis, a group of five cities. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The other cities were Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Zoar. All stood in the vale of Siddim. God vowed to destroy them for their wickedness.

Abraham pleaded for Sodom to be spared for ten righteous men. He could not find even ten righteous there. Fire and brimstone then rained on the whole Pentapolis. Prophets later used Sodom as a sign of dire disaster. Rabbinic tales name four corrupt judges of the city. Giving bread to the poor there was punished by death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-basilius-:
Basilius Stern was a Russian educator born at Tarnopol, Galicia, in 1798. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He got a thorough Talmudic education as a young man. At Joseph Perl's school he became a teacher at age twenty. He died at Odessa on March 15, 1853.

In 1828 Stern became director of the Jewish school in Odessa. Under him the school prospered greatly. He even won over Orthodox opponents of its modern approach. In 1837 he gained leave to open a school at Kishinef. The government often sought his advice on Jewish matters. He proposed a seminary in Russia to train rabbis. The entry shows his lasting mark on Jewish education in South Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tang-abraham-14:
Abraham Tang was an English author in London in the 1700s. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He flourished in the century's second half. In 1773 he published a commentary on Ecclesiastes. The work shows real classical scholarship throughout.

Tang explained Greek and Roman mythology in his commentary. He presented the myths clearly and briefly for readers. He cited the Greek Anthology often in the notes. Ovid, Vergil, and Seneca appear again and again. A year earlier he published a Talmud exposition. It treats passages quoting the Ancients of Athens. He dedicated that work to Moses of Minsk. The brief entry preserves a learned London Jew's two books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-meir-be:
Meïr ben Samuel Te'omim was a Polish Talmudist of the 1700s. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He was a grandson of Joseph Te'omim. At Lemberg he worked as a preacher. He died on July 10, 1773.

Meïr's work Nofet Zufim survives inside his son's book. His son Joseph printed it at Frankfort in 1782. Another work of his appeared at Zolkiev in 1750. His son reports a larger book called Emek Halakah. It explained a large part of the Talmud. Later Talmudists cite Meïr's decisions in their works. The entry keeps a preacher's voice alive through his family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-ben-isaa:
Todros ben Isaac was a Talmudist in Italy or southern France around 1300. Isaac Broydé wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He wrote novellae on the Talmud treatise Nazir. The work survives only in manuscript at Oxford. Todros dated its finish to 1322.

That year brought heavy persecution to the Jews. The lepers' massacre had just swept the region. The Pastoureaux rising followed with more violence. The Talmud itself was burned in those years. Grätz linked Todros' note to Emperor Frederick, Louis of Bavaria's rival. An elegy by a certain Joab mourned the same burning. The entry ties one scholar's book to a dark season.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-troy-n-y-14527:
Troy, New York, on the Hudson above Albany, gained its first Jewish resident around 1842. Joseph Jacobs and Louis Loewenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Emanuel Marks settled there from Albany for business. Herman Levy followed in 1843, and Charles Wolf in 1845. Emanuel Gratz organized worship in rented rooms in 1851.

A permanent congregation, Anshe Chased, formed in 1853. Quarrels split it within two years of founding. Aaron Ksensky reunited the factions in 1857. The merged flock took the name Berith Shalom, covenant of peace. It built the Third Street Temple in 1870. Orthodox members left to form Beth Israel Bickur Cholim. Another Orthodox congregation, Sharah Tephilah, arose in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valence-14627:
Valence, chief town of the Drome in France, sheltered Jewish refugees in 1323. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Families expelled from the Comtat-Venaissin fled to Valence then. Bishop Guillaume brought more Jews into his diocese in 1330. He granted them important privileges for settling.

By 1441 eighteen Jewish families lived in Valence. Each paid the bishop one gold florin yearly. The same bishop forced them to wear the wheel badge. The dauphin Louis showed the Jews much good-will later. He confirmed their privileges and invited more settlers. His terms promised protection like other Dauphiné towns enjoyed. An anonymous local writer commented on Bonfils' astronomical tables. The entry is short but dense with such detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-karl-14827:
Karl Weil was an Austrian doctor and surgeon. He was born at Altsattel, Bohemia, on March 19, 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at Prague and Vienna. He took his degree in 1867. He then assisted at Vienna's surgical hospital.

From 1873 to 1879 Weil worked at Prague's German university. He became a lecturer there in 1877. In 1879 he rose to assistant professor of surgery. His writings treat knock knee and the thyroid gland. For a handbook of forensic medicine he wrote on wounds. He also judged scars for legal purposes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilkesbarre-149:
Wilkesbarre is a Pennsylvania city in Luzerne County. Cyrus Adler and Marcus Salzman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first Jewish settlers arrived about 1838. Martin Long, a Bavarian, was the most prominent. In 1840 a society formed for occasional worship. Services met in rented rooms for nine years.

In 1849 the group dedicated its first synagogue. In 1857 it incorporated as Congregation B'nai B'rith. Reader Herman Rubin served it for thirty years. Reform practice grew with the younger generation. Orthodox Jews organized separately in 1871. Their offshoots built synagogues in 1886 and 1887. A fourth synagogue opened in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worship-idol-15:
Idol worship is the foe that the Bible sets against the worship of God alone. Kaufmann Kohler and Ludwig Blau wrote the study for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Ten Words open with a ban on all other gods. The first books of the Bible press that ban from all sides.

The prophets spent their force in a fight with idol cults. Those cults were deep in the hearts of the folk. To own the true God meant to live a clean life too. So the fight was a fight for right acts as well. The study says the cults were not crushed till late. That end came after the return from exile in Babylon. A long list of linked entries shows the cults one by one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yudan-15127:
Yudan was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century of this era. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name does not stand in the Babylon books at all. It stands oft in the old Palestine tale books and Talmud.

He was a pupil of Abba in his school days. He rose to be a peer of Jose of Tiberias. That man led the school in that lake town then. The two oft fell to debate on points of law. He seems to have served as a judge with Jose. One tale says Jose ruled on a case of cash law. He ruled alone since Yudan had fled to Nawe then. That flight is the sole life fact known of the man.
joyce-pomes-penyeach-1927:
Joyce issued this small book of poems in 1927 and priced it, as the title jokes, at a penny each: pomes penyeach, poems a penny each. It holds thirteen short lyrics written across many years of his exile.

Among them are 'Tilly', 'A Flower Given to My Daughter', and 'On the Beach at Fontana'. The poems are plain, tender, and often sad, far from the dense puzzles of his prose. Several grieve for his mother or watch his children with a father's ache. The little volume shows Joyce the lyric poet persisting beside Joyce the novelist.
kafka-der-verschollene-1927:
Der Verschollene, The Man Who Disappeared, is Kafka's unfinished first novel, published after his death in 1927 under the title Amerika. Karl Rossmann, a boy of seventeen, is sent to the United States after a scandal with a servant girl.

Karl passes through a rich uncle's house, roadside inns, a great hotel, and stranger episodes, always falling downward through kindness and confusion. Kafka never saw America; his version is a dream of elevators, desks, and vast indifferent systems. The surviving chapters end in the Nature Theatre of Oklahoma, which hires everyone. Even unfinished, it is a major, haunting work.
keble-christian-year-1827:
John Keble was an Oxford scholar and country parson whose verse cycle The Christian Year appeared in 1827. It gives a poem for each Sunday and holy day of the church calendar. Families across England kept it beside the Bible.

The poems follow the seasons of worship through the year, matching scripture readings with quiet scenes of nature and village life. Keble's calm devotion, and his later famous sermon at Oxford, helped launch the Oxford Movement in the church. The book stayed a devotional bestseller for the rest of the century. Its sales rivaled those of popular novels for decades.
kendrick-druids-1927:
T. D. Kendrick, a British scholar of old remains, wrote this study of the druids in 1927. The text here is from the 1928 printing. He aimed to test the old tales of druids against hard proof from the ground. By then wild claims about druids filled shelf after shelf of books.

Kendrick weighed Greek and Roman texts, then turned to graves, stones, and finds from Celtic lands. He split firm fact from the wild claims built up since the 1700s. The book set the base line for all sound druid study that came after it.
labor-s-martyrs-haymarket-1887-sacco-and:
Vito Marcantonio wrote Labor's Martyrs, linking two famous American labor cases. William Z. Foster supplied a framing piece. The book marks fifty years since the Haymarket executions of November 1887.

Foster names Parsons, Spies, Fischer, Engel, and Lingg, leaders of the eight-hour strike. They were hanged after the Haymarket bomb deaths in Chicago. Marcantonio pairs their fate with Sacco and Vanzetti, executed in 1927. He argues that the same forces crushed both groups. The book is a passionate labor history, written from inside the movement. Foster's angry tone matches the book's purpose as a memorial. It asks readers to remember the dead as heroes, not criminals.
lawrence-mornings-mexico-1927:
Mornings in Mexico, published in 1927, collects Lawrence's sketches from his stays in Oaxaca and the southwest. He called them mornings because each catches a place in fresh, early light, before his theories woke up.

He writes of Indian markets, fiestas, dancers, and the slow theater of a Mexican town waking. Other pieces describe Hopi and Pueblo ceremonies he witnessed, with respect and argument both. The prophetic Lawrence is here, but so is the watcher, content to record a dog, a servant, a dance. Many readers rate these pieces his best travel writing: vivid, humane, and strange.
lemaitre-univers-homogene-1927:
Georges Lemaître was a Belgian priest and physicist who studied Einstein's theory of gravity. His 1927 paper, printed here in French, asks what that theory says about the whole universe. The answer was bold: space itself is growing.

Lemaître shows that a universe of fixed mass and growing radius fits the math of general relativity. He also links the flight of distant galaxies to that growth, using data on their speeds. At first few noticed, but the paper became the seed of the Big Bang idea and modern cosmology. Einstein at first resisted the claim, then came to accept it.
lenin-materialism-empirio-criticism-kvit:
Lenin defended materialism in Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, written in 1909 and Englished by David Kvitko in 1927. Followers of Ernst Mach had recast matter as bundles of sensation. Lenin saw that Machist turn as a threat to Marxist philosophy. His book answers the revision, thinker by thinker.

He insists that the world exists apart from our minds and that knowledge reflects it. Matter, in his phrase, is what acts on our senses and is copied by them. The work became the epistemological base of dialectical materialism in Soviet teaching. Philosophers still argue over its bluntness and its force. It shows Lenin as polemicist in philosophy.
lewis-elmer-gantry-1927:
Sinclair Lewis published Elmer Gantry in 1927 after months of research among ministers, including attending services across Kansas City. Lewis had already skewered business in Babbitt and medicine in Arrowsmith. Now he aimed at professional religion, and the result caused a national uproar.

Elmer Gantry, a college football star with a golden voice, stumbles into preaching and discovers he is a magnificent fraud. He rises through Baptist and Methodist pulpits, joins the flamboyant evangelist Sharon Falconer, and schemes toward a national ministry. Scandal, blackmail, and revival tents fill his climb. Lewis's satire made religious hucksterism an American archetype. Ministers denounced the book from pulpits, which only widened its fame.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The January 1873 Lippincott's builds iron bridges first. Edward Rowland explains their construction to general readers. A search for the quinine-plant in Peru begins here. Caroline Chesebro introduces Probationer Leonhard and the Happy Valley.

Our hero takes his test across the serial's first chapters. Reginald Wynford tours the Irish capital for readers. Marie Howland recalls reminiscences of Florence. Will Wallace Harney profiles the Southern planter to close the list. Gray Eyes, babes in the wood, and a life-guards charge follow. An unpublished Nelson letter to Lady Hamilton joins the gossip.
literature-ancient-egyptians-erman-black:
Adolf Erman gathered The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians in a comprehensive anthology, Englished by Aylward M. Blackman in 1927. Erman, the great Berlin Egyptologist, chose poems, tales, hymns, and wisdom texts from three thousand years of writing. Scribes of the pharaohs speak here in love songs, shipwreck tales, and counsels for kings.

The collection showed general readers that Egypt had a literature, not just monuments and tombs. Humor, grief, pride, and tenderness survive in these translations from hieroglyph and papyrus. Erman's volume remains a rich first shelf of ancient Egyptian writing in English, arranged by a master of the field.
manzoni-betrothed-1827:
Alessandro Manzoni published The Betrothed in 1827, Italy's national novel of Lombardy under Spanish rule. The tale sends Renzo and Lucia toward a wedding blocked by plague, war, and a tyrant's lust. Manzoni revised the book for years, washing its language in the Arno toward a national Italian tongue.

A village priest, bullied by Don Rodrigo's bravos, refuses to marry the young silk weaver and his Lucia. Flight splits the pair: Lucia to a convent and a kidnapper's castle, Renzo to riots in Milan. The Unnamed, a great outlaw, converts in a night and frees Lucia from his own plot. Plague empties Milan, and the lovers meet again among the sick at the lazaretto in 1630. The novel taught Italians a common language and a conscience about power and the poor.
mctaggart-nature-existence-vol-2-1927:
J. M. E. McTaggart completed The Nature of Existence with Volume 2, published after his death in 1927. This volume applies his system to the world as a whole. McTaggart argues that reality is a timeless community of selves bound by love. Matter, sense perception, and time are shown to be appearances that mislead us.

His denial of time's reality is the book's most debated claim. Selves, he holds, are eternal and perceive each other directly in the Absolute. Few readers accept the whole system today. Yet its logic and ambition command respect. Together the volumes form one of the boldest metaphysical works in English.
mitchell-business-cycles-problem-setting:
Mitchell restated his life's program in Business Cycles: The Problem and Its Setting, published in 1927. The book opened a fresh, multi-volume attack on the cycle problem for the National Bureau of Economic Research, the institute he directed. Fourteen years after his first treatise, Mitchell took stock of what had been learned.

He surveys the many rival theories of the cycle and finds each too narrow for the facts. His own answer is method before doctrine: measure the cycle in all its parts, then let explanation grow from the record. The volume is the mature statement of American institutionalism's research agenda. It shows economics as organized fact-finding on the grand scale, and it framed the studies that followed from his bureau for decades.
noel-through-tibet-to-everest-1927:
John Noel climbed toward Everest with a camera on the famed attempt of 1924 and wrote his road book in 1927. Through Tibet to Everest tells the long trek through the hidden land to the foot of the peak. Noel was the photographer of the famed 1924 Everest attempt.

One chapter takes up the Legendary Hairy Man of the Mountains, as the Tibetans told of him. Noel treats the tale with care, as a climber who has heard it in high camps. His is an early, grave hearing for yeti lore from a man of the peaks. The book joins hard travel to a soft-footed mystery.
ohm-galvanische-kette-1827:
Georg Simon Ohm works out the math of the galvanic circuit in his German treatise of 1827. Current, voltage, and resistance fall into one clear law. A humble schoolteacher reached the result alone, and the learned world shrugged at his book for years before granting its worth at last.

His law became the ground rule of all electrical engineering in time. Every circuit drawn since rests on the relation he proved here. Ohm endured neglect and mockery with quiet patience in Cologne. The treatise gives the fruitful equation in its first form, a modest volume whose single idea now runs the wired world entire.
openalex-w2016455427:
Jacklyn Wong, Steven Stoddard, Helvio Astete and colleagues studied egg laying in the dengue mosquito. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. The mosquito Aedes aegypti spreads dengue. With no vaccine then available, mosquito control was the main defence. Where females lay eggs shapes control plans.

The team studied hundreds of water containers in Iquitos, Peru. They checked which containers females chose for eggs. They also measured food for larvae in each container. Females were drawn to sites holding young mosquitoes. Food levels alone did not explain their choices. Container size, lids and sun exposure also mattered. The authors suggested traps that exploit this attraction. Killing late-stage young could turn chosen sites into egg sinks.
openalex-w2115862827:
Yukio Ando, Teresa Coelho, John Berk and colleagues wrote a clinician's guide to a hereditary amyloid disease. Their paper appeared in Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases in 2013. The disease slowly damages nerves and the heart. Faulty transthyretin protein forms harmful deposits. Its varied symptoms make it hard to recognise.

Misdiagnosis is common in this condition. Patients may wait years for the right answer. The guide explains how to confirm the diagnosis. It covers staging and tracking of progression. Symptom relief options are reviewed in detail. Liver transplant and newer drugs are discussed. Some drug treatments showed promise in trials. Early recognition can slow irreversible decline.
openalex-w2119008227:
Lilian Beatriz Aguayo Rojas and Marilia Brito Gomes reviewed metformin's place in type 2 diabetes care. Their paper appeared in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome in 2013. Metformin is an old, cheap diabetes drug. It remains the accepted first treatment worldwide. Newer drug classes raised questions about its role.

Beyond lowering blood sugar, metformin helps blood vessels. It improves insulin resistance and blood lipids. It also shifts body fat in favourable ways. Heart outcomes improved in ways beyond sugar control alone. Studies hint at anti-cancer and brain-protective effects. Low blood sugar risk is negligible when used alone. Slow dose increases improve tolerance, they advise.
openalex-w2119191227:
Arnaud Bertrand, Alexis Chaigneau, Salvador Peraltilla and colleagues argued that oxygen shapes fish life off Peru. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. Anchovy and sardine numbers there swing over decades. Food and temperature were the usual explanations. The authors suspected oxygen mattered more.

The Peruvian upwelling system is naturally low in oxygen. Fish evolved under those anoxic conditions nearby. A large dataset linked fish patterns to oxygen levels. Oxygen set the depth limits of fish habitat. It also structured the wider food web. Temperature alone could not explain the patterns. Ocean oxygen is changing worldwide now. Fisheries models should include it, they argue.
openalex-w3045526727:
Estela Aquino, Ismael Silveira, Júlia Pescarini, and colleagues published this narrative review in Ciência e Saúde Coletiva in 2020. Written in Portuguese, it examines social distancing as a tool against COVID-19 in Brazil. The pandemic challenged leaders to find measures that could keep health systems from collapse.

The authors gathered evidence on distancing effects from medical and preprint databases. They also analyzed federal and state laws to map what Brazil actually put in place. Distancing adopted by the population appears effective, they conclude, above all when joined with isolating cases and quarantining contacts. The review then discusses the likely social costs and the practical hurdles of holding such measures in a large, unequal country.
openalex-w3099237227:
Adriane Esquivel-Muelbert, Oliver Phillips, Roel Brienen, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It asks how Amazon trees die, and which risk factors drive their deaths. Tree mortality shapes how much carbon the forest can store, yet its main drivers stayed largely unknown.

Trees die in two broad modes: standing, after internal failure from stress or water transport collapse, or broken and uprooted by storms and falls. Long-term monitoring plots, where deaths are logged in a standard way, offer the best large-scale evidence. The team read those records across the Amazon to map each mode and its links to regional climate. The patterns help forecast how the forest's carbon store will weather change.
openalex-w3165658327: Felipe Naveca, Valdinete Nascimento, Victor Souza, and colleagues at Fiocruz and partner institutes in Brazil studied the COVID-19 epidemic in Amazonas state. Their paper appeared in Nature Medicine in 2021. It reports that long-lasting local virus lineages drove the epidemic, along with the rise of the P.1 variant. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author list, with no readable abstract or results.
openalex-w4391232927:
Mariachiara Di Cesare, Pablo Perel, Sean Taylor, and colleagues present a global portrait of cardiovascular disease in Global Heart in 2024. Heart and vessel diseases remain the world's leading killer. Of the twenty and a half million such deaths in 2021, about four fifths occurred in low- and middle-income countries. The authors drew on the Global Burden of Disease study and World Health Organization data.

Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia face the highest death rates. Raised blood pressure is still the top risk factor, linked to nearly eleven million deaths in a recent year. The paper scores countries on a policy index for prevention and treatment. Sub-Saharan Africa had the most countries with very low scores. The authors urge each nation to read its own risk profile and act on it.
openalex-w4411194627:
Tomohiro Hattori, Hirotaka Irie, Tadashi Kadowaki, and Shu Tanaka study a trick for making quantum annealers solve bigger problems. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. Quantum annealers are limited by qubit counts, wiring patterns, and energy scales.

One workaround fixes some spins in advance, shrinking the problem. The authors examine how that fixing interacts with energy rescaling. Rescaling adjusts the problem's energy units to fit the hardware. Done well, fixing spins lets a small machine attack larger optimisation tasks. Done badly, it distorts the problem and harms answers. Their analysis guides when the trick helps. That matters as users push annealers toward real industrial problems.
openalex-w4416665727:
Yi Yang and Takahiro Mori review recent progress in lincosamide biosynthesis. Their review appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2026. Lincosamides are antibiotics made by Streptomyces bacteria. Lincomycin A and celesticetin are the best-known members.

These drugs are built by unusual gene clusters. The clusters lack the standard signature genes found in similar pathways. Since the lincomycin pathway was fully mapped, work has shifted to control and redesign. Researchers now adjust the regulatory elements that switch production on. They also engineer the pathway's enzymes and study how their shapes drive function. Such control could yield improved lincosamide drugs and steadier production.
openalex-w7163524827: Schizophrenia runs in families, and genes may hold clues. This study tested a set of genes, the inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitors, for links to the disorder. The team hunted DNA hot spots in a strongly inherited illness. A mind-gene study chasing a promising lead.
openalex-w7163998427: Salty seas may hide tomorrow's antibiotics. This paper reports that salt stress pushed a Streptomyces strain to make 7-deoxypactamycin and oligomycin, two germ-fighting compounds. The team studied how the sea microbe's chemistry woke up under stress. A germ study of pressure unlocking hidden drugs.
openalex-w7204188927: Children are not just adults-in-waiting; they are social actors with their own worlds. This article studies the sociology of childhood and what it offers for understanding atypical childhoods, those lived outside the expected scripts. The authors map contributions, challenges, and new directions. A theoretical piece that takes children's agency seriously.
openalex-w7212146527: After heart surgery, fluid balance is critical. This study tested giving intravenous tolvaptan, a water-shedding drug, right when patients reached the ICU. The team checked whether early dosing was safe and feasible. A cardiac-care study of a new drug's first hours.
openalex-w7214604527: Some blood infections whisper of hidden colon cancer. This paper studied the tie between two germ blood infections and later colon cancer finds. The team probed timing and how it happens. A cancer-germ study of infections as early alarms for tumors.
openalex-w7220678127: Children with malaria only get better if they finish their medicine. This study measured how well caregivers stuck to antimalarial treatment in kids and what the caregivers reported. The authors linked adherence to outcomes. A global-health study of the last mile of malaria care.
parrington-main-currents-vol-1-1927:
Vernon Louis Parrington set out to trace the growth of American thought from the colonial years to his own day. The first volume, published in 1927, covers the colonial mind, from Puritan New England to the age of Jefferson. The full work won the Pulitzer Prize for history.

Parrington reads sermons, pamphlets, laws, and poems as signs of a long fight between freedom and control. He favors the voices that pushed for wider rights and faults those that guarded wealth and rank. His bold, opinionated style made the book a landmark of American literary history. It set the pattern for later histories that read books as records of their times.
parrington-main-currents-vol-2-1927:
The second volume of Parrington's history of American thought appeared in 1927 and takes up the years of the early republic. He calls this stretch the Romantic Revolution, when older habits of thought gave way to bold new hopes. Writers from Emerson to Whitman stand at its center.

Parrington follows poets, essayists, and novelists as they praised nature, self-trust, and the common man. He ties their work to farms, towns, and trade, not just to books. Readers get a sweeping story of how a young nation learned to think in its own voice. Together the volumes made Parrington the best-known American literary historian of his day.
pavlov-conditioned-reflexes-anrep-1927:
Ivan Pavlov's Conditioned Reflexes appeared in English in 1927, in G. V. Anrep's translation. Pavlov, a Russian scientist, reports decades of experiments on digestion and reflexes in dogs. A bell paired with food soon makes a dog salivate at the bell alone. Pavlov calls this a conditioned reflex and maps its laws with care.

He studies how such reflexes form, fade, and return, and how the brain's cortex governs them. Sleep, inhibition, and nervous types receive long treatment. The book is Pavlov's own account of classical conditioning. It founded a branch of learning theory used worldwide. Psychologists and neuroscientists still build on its findings.
plos-pbio-0020327:
Cecile Martinat, Shoshana Shendelman, Alan Jonason, and their team built a Parkinson's cell model in PLOS Biology in 2004. A gene called DJ-1, when broken, causes a rare early form of Parkinson's disease. The team made dopamine neurons from stem cells that lack DJ-1 and stressed them with oxidants.

Those neurons died more readily than normal ones under the same stress. That result links DJ-1 to protection against oxidative damage, a long-suspected factor in Parkinson's. A stem-cell model that can be grown in a dish lets labs test protective drugs fast. The study is thus both a clue about the disease and a tool for hunting treatments.
plos-pbio-0020427:
Graham E. J. Rodwell, Rebecca Sonu, Jacob M. Zahn, and a large team profiled the aging kidney in PLOS Biology in 2004. They measured gene activity in human kidneys across adult ages. Aging organs change slowly, and the kidney's changes affect how well it filters blood and handles drugs.

Their profile shows a clear age signature: sets of genes that rise or fall steadily with age. Such a signature can act as a clock for organ health, more precise than years alone. It also points to the processes that drive kidney aging, like shifts in immune and metabolic genes. That gives researchers targets for keeping kidneys working longer.
plos-pone-0000027:
Colin A. Russell, Leslie A. Real, and David L. Smith modeled rabies spread in PLOS ONE in 2006. Rabies moves through wildlife like raccoons and foxes, and its front advances across the land in waves. Real landscapes are patchy, with rivers, towns, and forests that speed or slow the virus.

Their model asks how such patchiness changes where control works best. Barriers and vaccine zones placed with the land in mind can beat uniform plans. Rabies control is costly and long, so smarter placement matters. The work is a case study in spatial disease control, useful for other infections that spread across mixed terrain.
plos-pone-0000127:
Matthew R. E. Symonds, Neil J. Gemmell, Tamsin L. Braisher, and colleagues published this research-policy study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It compares the publication output of men and women scientists. The goal is a fair metric of research performance, one that does not bake in bias from career breaks or part-time work.

Raw paper counts can mislead when judging who performs well. The authors look at how gender gaps in output are measured and propose a less biased yardstick. The work speaks to hiring, funding, and promotion decisions across science, where a skewed metric can quietly hold back whole groups of researchers.
plos-pone-0000227:
Xuhua Xia, Huang Huang, Malisa Carullo, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vertebrate mitochondrial genomes, the small DNA circles inside cells' power plants, run under tight size limits. The authors describe a conflict between translation initiation and elongation, starting and continuing protein production, inside these compact genomes.

In a cramped genome, signals for starting a gene can collide with the machinery reading the previous one. The authors analyze how that conflict plays out across vertebrates. The work explains odd features of mitochondrial gene layout and adds to the picture of how these ancient genomes are organized.
plos-pone-0000327:
Xinyan Lu, Chad A. Shaw, Ankita Patel, and colleagues published this clinical genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Chromosomal microarray analysis scans a patient's genome for missing or extra chunks too small for a microscope to see. The authors summarize the clinical implementation of the test across 2513 postnatal cases, children tested after birth for developmental problems.

A summary that large shows the test's real-world yield: how often it finds an answer. Microarrays were then becoming the first-line test for unexplained developmental delay. The paper documents that transition with numbers clinics could plan around.
plos-pone-0000427:
Massimo Buvoli, Ada Buvoli, and Leslie A. Leinwand studied how muscle cells handle faulty messages, using a mouse model of muscular dystrophy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The mdx mouse carries a defect in the dystrophin gene. The team examined how exonic splicing enhancers, DNA-letter motifs that help splice a gene's message, interact with mRNA processing and mRNA surveillance.

Surveillance systems destroy garbled messages before they make harmful proteins, but they can also destroy messages the cell could have used. In a dystrophic muscle, that balance affects how much working protein the cell can salvage. The work speaks to therapies that coax cells to skip damaged exons and keep more of the message.
plos-pone-0000527:
Simona Ozden and colleagues showed that a mosquito-borne virus can infect human muscle's repair cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chikungunya virus causes fever and severe joint pain, and its 2005–2006 outbreaks reached new regions. The team found that human muscle satellite cells, the stem cells that repair muscle, are targets of chikungunya virus infection.

Muscle pain and weakness are major features of the disease, yet the virus's targets in muscle were unclear. Infection of the repair crew itself could explain slow recovery: the cells needed for healing are under attack. The finding directs attention to muscle as a site where the virus may persist.
plos-pone-0000627:
Jason W. Locasale used computation to probe a short-term memory inside T cells, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. T cells are immune cells that meet antigen-presenting cells, which show them fragments of invaders. Recent studies had found that T cells can add up signals across interrupted meetings. The total behaves as if the cell remembers the earlier encounter.

Locasale built a simple mathematical model of that signal integration. The model hunts for the chemical steps that could hold a trace between meetings. A clear model gives experimentalists specific predictions to test in real cells. It also frames a general puzzle: how brief molecular events store information, even briefly.
plos-pone-0000727:
Laurence Fiévez, Christophe Desmet, Emmanuelle Henry and colleagues called a signaling protein a two-faced regulator of neutrophil balance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. STAT5 promotes the survival of the progenitor cells that make blood. Yet mice lacking STAT5 develop mild neutrophilia, an excess of neutrophils, the most common white blood cells. That paradox drives the study.

The authors show that in these mice, liver endothelial cells autonomously secrete large amounts of G-CSF, a growth factor for neutrophils. Progenitors then overcompensate for their own handicap. An ambivalent regulator indeed: STAT5 both supports blood cell survival and holds their numbers down through distant signals.
plos-pone-0000827:
Veronika Hartmannsgruber, Willm-Thomas Heyken, Michael Kacik and colleagues showed that arteries' answer to blood flow hinges on one channel protein. In blood vessels, the endothelium is the inner lining. It is a key signal interface that controls vessel tone and blood pressure. That control ensures energy and oxygen supply matches organs' needs. The lining answers vasoactive factors and the shear stress of flowing blood.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title states the critical dependence: the arterial response to shear stress depends on endothelial TRPV4 expression. TRPV4 is a channel that senses mechanical and chemical cues. A single channel carrying the flow signal makes it a candidate lever for blood pressure control.
plos-pone-0000927:
John Azevedo, Emily Tietz, Tashena Two-Feathers and colleagues compared how cyclists burned the sugars in two sports drinks, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Riders took either a drink with lactate polymer, fructose and glucose, or a leading rival drink built on fructose. Six male cyclists in the top amateur classes rode through steady exercise while the team measured fuel use.

The question was practical: which mix of sugars actually gets burned during hard effort. Drinks often promise more than the body can use. Measuring oxidation profiles, how each sugar is taken up and burned, gives riders and makers real numbers. Small trials like this keep sports claims honest.
plos-pone-0001027:
Marta Szulkin and Ben Sheldon studied how the cost of inbreeding shifts with conditions in wild birds, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inbreeding depression is the fitness loss in offspring of relatives. It is usually blamed on harmful recessive gene copies showing themselves when inherited from both parents.

The open question is how much that loss depends on the environment. Hard years might expose inbred young more than easy ones. A wild bird population gives the test real setting: pedigrees, weather and survival all recorded. The answer matters for small populations, where inbreeding is forced and managers must know when it hurts most.
plos-pone-0001127:
Head lice are usually treated with insecticide liquids, but there were signs the standard drug was losing its punch. Ian Burgess, Peter Lee, and Geraldine Matlock ran a clinical trial, reported in 2007 in PLOS ONE, comparing two treatments. One was 4 percent dimeticone lotion. The other was 0.5 percent malathion liquid, the most prescribed head louse treatment in the United Kingdom for about ten years.

The trial was randomized and controlled, and the people judging results did not know which treatment each patient got. Anecdotal reports had suggested malathion worked less well than before, but that had not been confirmed in a clinic. The study put both options to a fair head-to-head test.
plos-pone-0001227:
The axolotl, a Mexican salamander, can regrow a whole limb perfectly after amputation, something no mammal can do. Mathieu Lévesque and colleagues asked which signals that regrowth requires, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The axolotl limb is the most widely used model for studying vertebrate regeneration.

The authors report that signaling by transforming growth factor beta is essential for limb regeneration in axolotls. Block the signal, and the celebrated regrowth fails. Knowing a required signal in an animal that regenerates is a clue for the much harder question of why mammals mostly cannot.
plos-pone-0001327:
Some neurons do not fire spikes; the retinal rod bipolar cell is one. Lorenzo Cangiano and colleagues studied how such a cell filters its inputs, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. These cells carry the eye's signals for dim light, mediated by a current called Ih, which flows through HCN channels.

In spiking neurons, Ih mostly supports rhythmic activity. The authors report high-pass filtering of input signals by the Ih current in the rod bipolar cell: slow signals are damped, faster ones pass. That filtering shapes what the retina tells the brain about changing light.
plos-pone-0001427:
Carmela Palermo and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a guard protein that halts cells when DNA is hurt. The protein, Chk1, is a core part of the damage checkpoint. It is switched on in yeast when DNA harm is sensed. The team asked what role its tail end plays in that guard work.

They found that a kept region at the tail of Chk1 is key for full checkpoint action. Without it, the guard is weak even if the rest is intact. The result refines how labs think this switch is built. It may matter for cancer drugs that aim to break the guard in tumor cells.
plos-pone-0001527:
Xiaolin He and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on gut harm that spreads to the lungs. When gut blood flow is cut and then restored, the lungs can fail in a grave state. Clotting and swelling cross talk drives that spread. The team tested an antibody against a clotting factor in mice bred with the human form of the factor.

The antibody eased the lung harm that followed the gut insult. That backs anti clotting care as a route for this lung state. Mouse tests with the human factor give the result more weight for clinics. It is still early, but the path is now marked.
plos-pone-0001627:
Benjamin Dewals, Christel Boudry, Frédéric Farnir, and their co-authors studied a deadly animal disease called malignant catarrhal fever in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The disease is caused by Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1, a virus that wildebeest carry with no signs of illness. When the virus crosses into cattle and other hoofed animals, it can kill them. In the lab, rabbits can be given the disease to study it.

Dewals and his team report that the disease in rabbits comes with fast growth of CD8-positive T cells, a type of immune cell. Their results support the idea that the virus hides in these cells in a latent, quiet state. The full text gives the cell counts, the tissue damage they saw, and their reading of how the virus and the immune system interact.
plos-pone-0001727:
Amr H. Sawalha, Ryan Webb, Shizhong Han, and their co-authors reported a gene link to lupus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, is an autoimmune disease that mostly strikes women and can damage many organ systems.
