The gene is MECP2, on the X chromosome at position Xq28, which fits the female skew because women carry two X chromosomes.

MECP2 makes a protein that binds methylated DNA and helps control gene activity. The team reports that common variants within MECP2 confer risk of SLE. The full text gives the patient and control groups and the variant comparisons. A gene that regulates other genes could explain wide, body-wide symptoms, and it points lupus research toward gene-control faults.
plos-pone-0001827:
Yanlan Mao, Martin Kerr, and Matthew Freeman studied how the fly eye keeps its surface intact in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Development of the Drosophila eye imaginal disc requires complex epithelial rearrangements. Cells of the morphogenetic furrow are apically constricted, indenting the epithelium, and cells behind the furrow rearrange into distinct clusters that become facets.

The team examined how the adhesion proteins Capricious and Tartan modulate retinal epithelial integrity during this process. The full text gives the mutant eyes and cell behavior data. Adhesion tuning is a general problem in organ building: too little and tissues fall apart, too much and they cannot rearrange.
plos-pone-0001927:
Lisa van Baarsen and co-authors studied why a standard drug helps only some patients with multiple sclerosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The drug is interferon-beta, and the illness varies a great deal from person to person. The team asked whether the gene activity pattern a patient starts with sets how they respond.

They profiled gene activity in blood from sixteen patients with the relapsing-remitting form of the illness. As the title states, the starting interferon signature set apart how patients reacted to the drug at the gene level. A blood test of that kind could one day sort patients toward the drug most likely to help them.
plos-pone-0002027:
Stephen Todryk and co-authors hunted immune signs of protection from malaria in Kenya, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In regions where malaria is endemic, people gain immunity with time, but the steps that protect them are poorly known. Many vaccine plans aim to raise T cells against parasite stages before the blood phase, called pre-erythrocytic antigens.

One such antigen is TRAP. The team linked memory T cell responses against TRAP to protection from clinical malaria, and a class of regulatory T cells to susceptibility instead. Field correlates like these tell vaccine makers which responses to aim for.
plos-pone-0002127:
Joung Woul Kim and co-authors built a new way to watch chemical signals inside living tissue, reported in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their focus was the pancreatic islet, the small cluster of cells that releases insulin. Two messengers, cyclic AMP and calcium, carry signals inside these cells after hormones and other cues arrive at the cell surface.

Calcium could already be tracked with glowing dyes that are easy to load into cells. The team used mice bred to carry a reporter that lights up when cyclic AMP levels change, letting them film those shifts in whole islets. The method opens a window on how islet cells time their signals.
plos-pone-0002227:
Matthew Cairns, Ilona Carneiro, Paul Milligan, and co-authors asked how long malaria protection lasts in infants given preventive treatment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The method, called IPTi, gives babies anti-malaria drugs at set visits during their first year. It had been shown to protect safely and well in Navrongo, Ghana, and other sites.

Some hoped the benefit might last long after the doses end, but in most settings protection fades fast. The team measured the duration of protection against both malaria and anemia in Navrongo. Knowing the true window of protection tells health programs whether extra doses or other tools must fill the gap.
plos-pone-0002327:
Douglas Fudge and co-authors stretched the fiber networks of human skin cells and found them surprisingly tough, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Intermediate filaments are 10 nanometer ropes inside cells. The standard model held that their networks behave like soft gels and that single filaments never bear direct pulling load.

Working with cultured human keratinocytes, the main cells of the skin surface, the team pulled on the network and measured its response. They found it remarkably extensible and resilient, stretching far without breaking. The result revises what these filaments do for skin: they act as safety ropes that keep cells whole under strain.
plos-pone-0002427:
Pattyn joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Els Pattyn, Annick Verhee, Isabel Uyttendaele, among others. Its subject is hyperISGylation of Old World Monkey ISG15 in Human Cells. ISG15 is an Ubiquitin-like protein, highly induced by Type I Interferons.

Upon the cooperative activity of specific Ubiquitinating enzymes, ISG15 can be conjugated to its substrates. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002527:
Urich led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Tim Urich, Anders Lanzén, Ji Qi, among others. Its subject is simultaneous Assessment of Soil Microbial Community Structure and Function through Analysis of the Meta-Transcriptome. Soil ecosystems harbor the most complex prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbial communities on Earth.

Experimental approaches studying these systems usually focus on either the soil community's taxonomic structure or its functional characteristics. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002627:
Thomas Nowotny and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on probing the dynamics of identified neurons with a Data-Driven modeling approach. Authorship is credited in the record to Thomas Nowotny and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In controlling animal behavior the nervous system has to perform within the operational limits set by the requirements of each specific behavior. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002727:
Ross J. Davidson and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was antimalarial therapy selection for quinolone resistance among escherichia coli in the absence of quinolone exposure, in tropical south america. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ross J. Davidson, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Bacterial resistance to antibiotics is thought to develop only in the presence of antibiotic pressure. It goes on to note a further point. Here we show evidence to suggest that fluoroquinolone resistance in Escherichia coli has developed in the absence of fluoroquinolone use. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002827:
Kim T. E. Olde Dubbelink and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on increased Resting-State functional connectivity in obese adolescents; a magnetoencephalographic pilot study. The catalog record names Kim T. E. Olde Dubbelink first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Obesity is not only associated with metabolic abnormalities, but also with cognitive dysfunction and changes in the central nervous system. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002927:
Ira Surolia, Sharmistha Sinha, Debi Sarkar and co-authors linked Danish dementia and cataract in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Familial Danish dementia is an inherited disease marked by gradual loss of vision, deafness, unsteady gait, and dementia. Cataract, clouding of the eye lens, is its first sign.

The team studied how peptides tied to the dementia interact with alpha-crystallin, a main protein of the lens. They report a specific link between the poisoning of that lens protein and disease. The work helps explain why the eye fails first in this rare inherited condition. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003027:
Hideaki Kawabata and Semir Zeki scanned brains viewing desired and undesired images in 2008. In their fMRI study, eighteen healthy subjects viewed pictures of events, objects, and persons. Each picture was classified by the viewer as desirable, indifferent, or undesirable.

Each category produced activity in a distinct set of areas, the excerpt reports. The study maps the neural correlates of desire, the brain patterns that track wanting. Published in PLOS ONE, the work speaks to how value is assigned in the brain, a base process behind choice and addiction. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003127:
Hong-Lian Shao, Wei-Wei Zheng, Peng-Cheng Liu and colleagues report a new insect cell line in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. When an insect molts, its outer old cuticle is shed and a new one forms beneath it. Skin cells carry out that work under control of two hormones, 20-hydroxyecdysone and juvenile hormone.

The team set up a cell line from the epidermis of a moth or butterfly type insect, then studied how those hormones regulate its genes. A stable line lets researchers watch molting steps in the lab. Readers interested in insect growth and hormone control will find the setup and gene results most useful.
plos-pone-0003227: Jean-Claude Dreher and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on brain injury and multitasking, the skill of handling several tasks at once. The title states its claim: damage to the fronto-polar cortex, at the front of the brain, goes with impaired multitasking. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no patient or test details are added.
plos-pone-0003327: Rukia S. Kibaya and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 setting reference ranges for a clinical laboratory. The ranges come from a rural population in Kericho, Kenya, rather than from imported standards. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record lists no values; local ranges matter because healthy values can differ by population.
plos-pone-0003427:
Daniela Puiu and Steven L. Salzberg rebuilt a bacterial genome in this 2008 paper. The bacterium, Francisella tularensis, causes tularemia and infects people with ease. It counts as a major biodefense concern. The team worked on a type B strain called OSU18, kin to a live vaccine strain.

The older genome assembly for that strain held errors. A fresh assembly gave a cleaner, more reliable sequence. Good reference genomes anchor all later work on a germ. The rebuilt map helps labs study how this dangerous microbe lives and harms. Other labs build their tularemia work on maps like this one.
plos-pone-0003527:
Christiane Hertz-Fowler and co-authors studied disguise sites in a parasite genome in this 2008 paper. Trypanosoma brucei causes African sleeping sickness. It survives by switching the coat proteins on its surface. The switchboard sits in expression sites near chromosome ends, called telomeres.

Those end regions are often missing from genome sequences. The team found the expression sites highly conserved across the parasite. Such stability in a restless region hints at an essential system. Guarding the disguise factory seems worth the parasite's trouble. Coat switching is the trick that lets this parasite outlast the immune system.
plos-pone-0003627:
Ilaria Roato, Patrizia D'Amelio, Eva Gorassini, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at prostate cancer that has spread to bone and forms new bone there. The team asked whether osteoclasts, the cells that break bone down, are active in these growths.

Working with tissue from patients, the authors found that bone-breaking activity is present in these bone-forming metastases. That finding was not expected, since these lesions were seen as mainly bone building. It shows both sides of bone turnover at work, which matters for treating the pain and damage this spread causes.
plos-pone-0003727:
Hong Sun, Geir Skogerbø, Zhen Wang, and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many short DNA stretches have stayed nearly unchanged across vertebrate evolution. These highly conserved elements often sit in or near genes that control gene activity and early development.

The authors mapped how the elements are arranged in relation to genes across vertebrate genomes. The layout shows set structural relationships rather than random scatter. That pattern hints at why evolution froze these regions: they likely help control the important genes beside them. Such maps are a base for asking what these elements do.
plos-pone-0003827:
Glen John Mcintyre, Jennifer Lynne Groneman, Anna Tran, and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Building DNA vectors with restriction enzymes gets harder as constructs grow more complex. Gene silencing studies often need many shRNA pieces in one vector. Repeats in those pieces also trip up standard PCR.

The authors offer a cloning strategy that can expand without limit, plus a repeat-proof PCR method. Together they let labs assemble vectors carrying multiple shRNAs cleanly. The kit removes a bottleneck from large-scale gene knockdown studies. Gene silencing with many targets at once is the use in view.
plos-pone-0003927:
Isora V. Sernández, Virginia G. de Yébenes, Yair Dorsett, and co-authors tested what happens with half the normal amount of an immune enzyme in 2008. Antibodies gain variety through two reshaping processes in immune cells. Both processes depend on an enzyme shortened to AID. The team asked whether one working gene copy is enough.

Their PLOS ONE article reports that half levels of AID fall short. Antibody reshaping weakened in cell cultures and in living animals. Misplaced reshaping also raised chromosome breaks that swap DNA segments. The work shows antibody variety needs the enzyme at full strength.
plos-pone-0004027:
Fengyu Wang, Jingfa Xiao, Linlin Pan, and co-authors surveyed very small proteins across microbes in 2008. Mini-proteins carry no more than one hundred amino acids. They occur in prokaryotes and eukaryotes alike. Many play regulatory roles that scientists keep discovering.

Their PLOS ONE article systematically catalogued mini-proteins in bacteria and archaea. Small size makes these proteins easy for gene finders to miss. A proper survey reveals how widespread they are across species. It also flags candidates for experiments on gene regulation. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004127:
Martin Richer and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It focuses on Toll-like receptor 3, a sensor that spots double-stranded RNA, a sign that a virus is copying itself inside cells. Earlier reports disagreed on whether this sensor helps, does nothing, or even harms the host during infection.

The team studied mice infected with coxsackievirus B4 and asked whether signals from this receptor on macrophages, a type of white blood cell, affect survival. They show that this signalling on macrophages is required for the mice to survive the infection. The paper helps sort out when a virus sensor protects and when it does not.
plos-pone-0004227:
Jared Young and colleagues published this test development paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Poor sustained attention, or vigilance, is tied to disability in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and Alzheimer's disease. Vigilance is among the leading targets for new cognition drugs, yet tests rarely translate between humans and animals.

The authors present the 5-choice continuous performance test as a version that mice can perform. Evidence that the mouse test measures the same vigilance as human versions would let drug candidates be screened in animals first. A shared test bridges the gap between lab discovery and clinic.
plos-pone-0004327:
Siem van der Laan, E. Ronald de Kloet, and Onno Meijer published this stress hormone study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Glucocorticoid hormones switch off the stress axis partly by directly repressing gene transcription in cells bearing the glucocorticoid receptor. The team investigated the cross-talk between the two main signalling pathways involved in activating the CRH gene, which starts the stress response.

They report that timing is critical for effective repression of the cAMP-induced CRH gene by the receptor. The same hormone signal can succeed or fail depending on when it arrives, a subtlety that matters for stress disorders.
plos-pone-0004427:
Gene chips can read thousands of genes at once, but mixed cell samples muddy the picture. Penelope Bryant, Gordon Smyth, Roy Robins-Browne, and co-authors tackled that problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. A core design choice is whether to study one pure cell type or a blend. Blends are easier to get, yet signals from one cell type can be drowned out.

The team used monocytes, a type of white blood cell, stirred into a mixture. They measured how many of the genes switched on by a bacterial signal in monocytes could still be detected. Their counts show what is lost, and what survives, when one cell type must be read through a crowd. That helps researchers design gene studies they can trust.
plos-pone-0004527:
The tail end of a gene message can itself change how organs stick together, report Daniel Lee, Tatiana Shatseva, Zina Jeyapalan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mature microRNAs are short RNAs that repress genes after they are read. Whether their work can itself be regulated was unknown.

The authors studied the tail region, called the 3 prime untranslated region, of a gene named versican. Expressing that tail alone induced organ adhesion in their experiments. The effect ran through a microRNA called miR-199a star, whose functions the tail regulates. A message tail acting as a regulator in its own right was a surprise. It adds a new layer to how genes control body structure.
plos-pone-0004627:
Brain cells and blood vessel cells take up Alzheimer's amyloid by different routes, compare Karunya Kandimalla, Olenych Scott, Smita Fulzele, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease is marked by degeneration in the cortex and hippocampus, tangles of tau protein inside neurons, and accumulation of beta-amyloid proteins. Amyloid builds up both in brain tissue and in the cerebral vasculature, the brain's blood vessels.

The team studied the mechanism of uptake of amyloid beta by neuronal cells versus endothelial cells, which line the vessels. Different doors into different cells matter for drug design: a therapy that clears amyloid from vessels may not reach amyloid in neurons. Mapping both routes gives Alzheimer's research a more exact picture of the target.
plos-pone-0004727:
Poh Chee Ong and colleagues studied a shape change in a protein that packs DNA into a silent form, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tight packing of DNA is a main way cells switch genes off for good. A protein called MENT helps drive that packing and locks cells in a mature state.

MENT belongs to a family of proteins that block cutting enzymes. The team tracked how its shape shifts as it works. A shape change may be the switch that lets it grab DNA and hold it tight. Knowing that switch helps explain how cells lock in their final identity.
plos-pone-0004827:
Klaus Pechhold and colleagues showed that blood glucose regulates pancreatic beta cell proliferation in autoimmune diabetes in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 1 diabetes is caused by immune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to insulin deficiency and elevated blood glucose. At onset a limited number of beta cells persist, but their replication capacity in a high glucose, inflammatory environment was a key open question.

Glucose itself signals remaining cells to divide. That feedback could aid recovery if immunity is controlled. It also complicates interpretation of regeneration studies. Metabolic state shapes cell fate. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004927:
Campylobacter jejuni is a major cause of food poisoning. Strain 11168 was the first of its kind to be sequenced. It became a widely used lab model. Christopher Day and colleagues studied it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how the strain reads sugar patterns on surfaces. They also asked whether temperature and growth conditions change that reading.

Long passage in the lab is known to alter this strain. Its colonizing behavior drifts away from wild bacteria. The team compared carbohydrate recognition under different conditions. Their findings warn of a real risk. Results from lab-kept strains may not match the germs that actually infect people.
plos-pone-0005027:
A stretch of chromosome 9p21 keeps appearing in genome studies. Its variants are linked to atherosclerosis and type 2 diabetes. The region sits near the INK4/ARF tumor suppressor genes. Yan Liu and colleagues explored the mechanism in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured INK4/ARF transcript expression in cells.

Expression levels were associated with the 9p21 variants. The genetic signal connects to a real molecular effect. The variants change how much message the cells produce. That moves a statistical hotspot toward biology. It also links heart disease risk to a famous cancer locus. Understanding the link may explain why these diseases cluster in the same families.
plos-pone-0005127:
Self-poisoning with pesticides is a serious public health problem. Older compounds, like organophosphorus chemicals, are commonly fatal. Fahim Mohamed and colleagues described cases of a newer poison in PLOS ONE in 2009. The compound is imidacloprid, a neonicotinoid insecticide. Its clinical effects after deliberate swallowing were not well described.

The study tracked patients who poisoned themselves with it. The clinical picture was milder than with the old poisons. Most patients survived with supportive care. Such information guides emergency treatment. Doctors in agricultural regions meet these cases often. Knowing the expected course helps them act fast. It also informs debates about which pesticides should stay on the market.
plos-pone-0005227:
Skin's outer barrier depends on a family of proteins made in a gene cluster for skin development. Faults in one family member, filaggrin, are known to cause skin disease. Wu and colleagues identified a related protein, filaggrin-2, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team described the new gene and analyzed where and when it is switched on. Filaggrin-2 belongs to the S100 fused-type protein family, whose members help keep surface tissues stable. Adding this member to the family portrait helps explain how the barrier is built and where it can fail.
plos-pone-0005327:
A family of five genes called adiponutrin codes for proteins that both break down and build fats. One member, PNPLA3, was already tied to adult obesity. Johansson and colleagues tested variants across the family for links to childhood obesity in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Childhood obesity has strong genetic roots and lifelong health effects. Checking the whole gene family at once shows whether the adult link extends to children and to sibling genes. Any confirmed link could flag at-risk children early and refine how obesity genes are understood. Child weight has risen fast in rich lands, and genes set part of that risk long before school age. So a firm gene link could help aim food and play advice where it counts most.
plos-pone-0005427:
Alberto Cagigi and co-authors reported a 2009 PLOS ONE study on antibody-making cells during long-term HIV infection. Healthy B cells improve their antibodies by swapping parts and adding small changes after they meet a germ. HIV infection harms the memory B cells that normally carry out that work.

The team found that one group of B cells, lacking a marker called CD27, still made improved antibodies during chronic infection. That result surprised many workers, since those cells were not thought to do this job. It changes how scientists picture the immune system coping with HIV over time.
plos-pone-0005527:
Michael Schmid and co-authors studied vision areas of the monkey brain in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Damage to the main vision area is thought to cut off the next vision areas from input. Earlier work found that most cells in those next areas stop firing after such damage.

The team made small, precise lesions and then tested whether the next areas still reacted to sights. Some activity driven by vision remained, pointing to side routes into those areas. Those routes may underlie the blind-sight some patients show after similar damage.
plos-pone-0005627:
Zijun Xiao, Cuiqing Ma, and Ping Xu studied chemical production by a Bacillus species in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Small alcohol-like chemicals called diols are used to make plastics and many other products. Making them with microbes instead of oil has drawn growing interest.

The team traced how Bacillus pumilus breaks down one compound, acetoin, and forms a related diol in a defined lab broth. Mapping the steps shows where the process can be sped up. Such maps are the basis for cleaner factory strains. Defined broths matter because every input is known, letting engineers assign each step to the right enzyme.
plos-pone-0005727:
Erik Kvam and co-authors aimed a probe at the harmful folded form of proteins in living cells in 2009. In Parkinson's, Huntington's, and Machado-Joseph disease, certain proteins misfold and clump. They pass through many shapes on the way, some toxic, some less so.

The probe locks onto the fiber-like form of these proteins inside live cells. To the team's surprise, forcing that form made clumping and cell harm worse, not better. That result warns that not all clumps are alike, and some shapes actively drive disease. It also gives labs a tool to force and study the risky shape.
plos-pone-0005827:
Muhammed Murtaza and co-authors reviewed headache cases in Pakistan in 2009, classifying them by type and symptoms. Headache disorders affect nearly half of all people, with migraine and tension headache the most common. Yet headache is barely studied as a health burden in developing countries.

The team reviewed clinical records to map which disorders Pakistani clinics actually see. Local data matter because triggers, care access, and drug use differ by country. Their classification gives Pakistan a baseline for planning headache care and training. It also shows how much morbidity hides behind a symptom often dismissed as minor.
plos-pone-0005927:
People name what they see at different speeds, and the level of the name matters. Marc Macé, Olivier Joubert, Jean-Luc Nespoulous and colleagues timed that process in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They asked how fast viewers sort pictures in natural scenes into broad groups and into narrower ones.

The title gives the twist: viewers spot the animal faster than the bird. A broad label can thus beat a basic one, against the usual rule from older work. The timing data show how the visual system ranks categories, and they give vision science a sharper test of how seeing turns into naming.
plos-pone-0006027:
Hard exercise that lengthens a muscle, like lowering a weight slowly, tears tiny fibers that must be rebuilt. Bryon McKay, Michael De Lisio, Adam Johnston and colleagues studied the rebuilding crew in people in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper links interleukin-6, a signal released during exercise, to the response of muscle stem cells, also called satellite cells.

Those stem cells wake after damage and supply the parts for repair and growth. How they are regulated in humans was largely undefined before work of this kind. Tying IL-6 to their response names one of the signals that rallies the repair crew, a step toward training and recovery plans built on the body's own rules.
plos-pone-0006127:
Emergency departments choke on their own queues, and two kinds of model can show where. Marek Laskowski, Robert McLeod, Marcia Friesen and colleagues applied both in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper builds agent-based models, which simulate each patient and worker, and queuing models, which use the math of waiting lines, to study patient access and flow through emergency departments.

Each model sees what the other misses, so running both gives a fairer picture of waiting times. The comparison itself is the contribution: managers learn which tool to trust for which question. Shorter, safer waits are the end goal, and this dual approach shows its work before any department is rebuilt on a model's say-so.
plos-pone-0006227:
The adult brain and spinal cord heal badly, partly because injured tissue forms a glial scar. Mathieu Desclaux and colleagues tested a new gene transfer strategy in lab-grown cells, reported in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The scar is built mainly by reactive star-shaped cells that raise two scaffold proteins.

Their method calmed glial reactivity while improving neuron survival and axon growth in the dish. Taming the scar and feeding the nerves at once is the key advance. Many past attempts did one or the other. The combined result supports gene-based strategies for spinal cord repair research.
plos-pone-0006327:
Naming a musical note without a reference is a rare gift called absolute pitch. Alfredo Brancucci and colleagues probe its basis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The simplest account says skilled matching between a heard pitch and a verbal label sits at its origin.

People without absolute pitch were confused when note labels shared vowel identity, the title reports. The vowel inside the label itself tripped pitch identification. That quirk supports the label-matching account of the ability. It also shows language sounds leaking into music perception in measurable ways.
plos-pone-0006427:
Yonghua Qi and colleagues described a lab method in PLOS ONE in 2009 for making cheap antibody tools. Their target was sulfadimidine, a drug whose traces in food need checking. They used ribosome display, a platform for building low-cost antibody-based tests. From a hybridoma cell line they selected small antibody fragments called scFvs.

The fragments were chosen because they bind sulfadimidine in a specific way. Such binders can form the heart of tests that screen food for drug residues. A cheaper route to these tools could widen routine food safety checks. The study shows the display method can supply them.
plos-pone-0006527:
Parthav Jailwala and co-authors studied the death of guard T cells in type 1 diabetes for PLOS ONE in 2009. In this disease, the immune system attacks the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. Guard cells called regulatory T cells should stop such attacks. The team looked at apoptosis, the built-in death of cells, among these guard cells.

Their title says that lack of IL-2, a growth signal, may drive part of this death. If starved guard cells die off, the attack on the pancreas can flare. That idea points to IL-2 support as a way to treat the disease. It also helps explain why the guards fail in the first place.
plos-pone-0006627:
Ricardo Águas and co-authors used computer models to weigh malaria prevention plans in PLOS ONE in 2009. Care of malaria is a major health issue in sub-Saharan Africa. New plans based on intermittent preventive treatment give drugs to people at set times to stop illness before it starts. The team assessed the impact of IPTi for infants and IPTc for children on malaria's clinical burden, all in silico, that is, in models.

Models let planners compare plans before costly field work starts. They show where preventive care pays off most in fewer sick cases. Such models now sit at the heart of malaria planning for whole regions. The work is a guide for those who must choose between good options.
plos-pone-0006727:
Muhan Chen and co-authors tested a candidate cancer gene in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is CHD1L. A chromosome region called 1q21 is amplified in many liver cancers. That amplification is the most frequent genetic change in hepatocellular carcinoma. The group had earlier isolated CHD1L from that region as a candidate driver.

They built transgenic mice expressing CHD1L. The mice developed spontaneous tumors. Spontaneous tumors mean no extra carcinogen was needed. That outcome supports CHD1L as a real driver of cancer growth. It strengthens the case for targeting the gene in liver cancer. It also gives researchers a mouse model driven by this gene.
plos-pone-0006827:
Yao-Zhong Liu and colleagues ran a two-trait genome scan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Standard genome-wide studies analyze one trait at a time. That approach ignores genetic correlation between traits. Obesity and osteoporosis are two traits that may share genes. Studying them jointly could reveal those shared influences.

Their bivariate analysis suggested the gene SOX6 influences both traits. The signal appeared in males. A gene affecting both body weight and bone strength fits known links between fat and bone. Joint analysis proved more powerful than separate scans. The work argues for multi-trait designs in genome-wide association research.
plos-pone-0006927:
Robert Nudds, Jonathan Codd, and William Sellers re-examined how animals move on land in PLOS ONE in 2009. An old rule held that transport efficiency rises steadily with body size. Their reanalysis of existing data suggested that rule needed a second look. The best statistical model told a different story.

Instead of one smooth trend, the data split into two groups. Smaller animals and larger animals followed different patterns of efficiency. That step-change challenges a long-standing tenet of locomotion science. It also changes how researchers should compare the walking and running costs of animals of very different sizes.
plos-pone-0007027:
Oscar Diaz-Ruiz, Agustin Zapata, Lufei Shan, and colleagues deleted a tumor suppressor in mouse brain cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. PTEN is found widely across the nervous system. It brakes a growth pathway run by the kinase Akt. That braking role suggests PTEN shapes many brain functions.

The team removed PTEN only from dopamine neurons. Those neurons grew larger, a trophic effect. The striatal neurons they connect to adapted in response. The experiment shows how one signaling brake shapes a whole circuit. It may inform work on brain disorders tied to this pathway.
plos-pone-0007127:
Alfonso Arribas, Guiomar Garrido, César Viseras, and colleagues reported a fossil find in PLOS ONE in 2009. Europe's mammal faunas turned over near the Pliocene-Pleistocene boundary. That shuffle, about 1.8 million years ago in rough terms, drew intense research interest. Chronology, spread, and taxonomy of the mammals all mattered, early humans included.

Their site in southwest Europe held a mammal community unlike others of its age. They call it a lost world from the late Pliocene. Isolated refuges can preserve odd survivors. Such pockets rewrite the map of which animals lived where, and when.
plos-pone-0007227:
Kim A. Caldwell, Michelle L. Tucci, Jafa Armagost, and colleagues looked for environmental contributors to Parkinson disease in 2009. Parkinson disease involves progressive loss of dopamine neurons from a brain area called the substantia nigra. Rare inherited forms point to cell pathways that handle damaged proteins.

The authors investigate whether bacterial toxins could contribute to that neuron loss. They frame toxicity as an environmental factor alongside genetics. Their PLOS ONE study uses simple model systems to test the idea. It may help explain why dopamine neurons are so vulnerable in this disease.
plos-pone-0007327:
Rickie Patani, Alastair Compston, Clare A. Puddifoot, and colleagues improved conversion of stem cells into nerve cells in 2009. Turning human embryonic stem cells into neural cells had been shown in several systems. Some used defined suspension culture, while others used dual SMAD inhibition with added signals on adherent cells.

The authors test Activin and Nodal inhibition alone. They report highly efficient neural conversion from human embryonic stem cells. They also find the treatment imposes a caudal, or rearward, positional identity on the cells. Their method simplifies production of specific nerve cell types for research.
plos-pone-0007427:
John Milton and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 using a classic balance test: keeping a stick upright on a fingertip. The task is a standard way to study how the nervous system controls balance. The team added an unexpected twist. The person balancing stood on a platform that vibrated, sending small shakes up to the fingertip.

Vibration roughly doubled how long subjects could keep the stick balanced. The authors explain the gain with a strategy they call drift and act. The nervous system lets the stick wander a little, then steps in with a correction. Vibration seems to sharpen those corrections. A simple parlor trick thus becomes a useful window on how the brain manages balance.
plos-pone-0007527:
Roy Salomon, Rafael Malach, and Dominique Lamy published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how the brain recognizes its own movements. Telling self from world is a basic task the brain performs constantly. Recent work links the default system, a network active during self-reflection, to self-related processing. The team used a movement-recognition task to test that network's role. Volunteers judged whether motions they saw were their own.

The intrinsic default system engaged when people recognized their own movement. That ties the sense of self to the brain's quiet background network. The network is not idle downtime machinery; it helps mark what belongs to the self. Movement offers a clean test because the body is always moving. The study connects philosophy's oldest question, selfhood, to a measurable brain circuit.
plos-pone-0007627:
Amir Qureshi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 profiling the proteins of resting human blood platelets. Platelets sit quietly until a vessel is injured. Then signals like thrombin flip them into clotting mode. A key event is the activation of integrin alpha-IIb-beta-3, a surface receptor that lets platelets grip and clump. The team mapped the platelet's proteins and their chemical tags in the basal, resting state.

A full inventory of the idle state is the reference for everything that follows. Changes during activation show up only against a known baseline. The profile also maps the integrin signaling network before it fires. That network is the target of several anti-clotting drugs. The study supplies the parts list and wiring of a resting platelet. It is groundwork for understanding how clotting begins, and how to stop it safely.
plos-pone-0007727:
Vladimir Novitsky and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks a basic question about HIV: when do mutations appear during a new infection? The team focused on subtype C, the most common form worldwide. They tracked changes in the virus's Gag protein.

Their group included people with very early and recent infections. They recorded when each Gag mutation first showed up. They also noted how fully each mutation took over the virus population. The timing map helps explain how HIV adapts under immune pressure, and it informs vaccine design.
plos-pone-0007827:
Takuya Kobayashi and Takashi Murayama published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches a molecular motor at work inside mammalian cells. The motor, cytoplasmic dynein, hauls cargo along microtubule tracks. It positions organelles, moves vesicles and helps cells divide.

How dynein's placement changes with the cell cycle was unclear. The authors tracked its dynamic transport across the cycle's phases. The motor's routes and timing shift as the cell prepares to divide. Understanding that traffic control matters for basic cell biology. Errors in such transport are tied to disease. Its maps show where the motor goes, and when.
plos-pone-0007927:
Roberto Amato and colleagues scanned the human genome for signs of local adaptation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most gaps between groups arise by chance drift, which should touch all DNA in a fairly even way. Spots shaped by selection should stand out from that plain background.

The team hunted for those stand-out spots and checked what they do. Some fell in gene pathways with clear jobs, and some linked to known disease risk. By sorting chance change from selected change, the scan helps explain how groups diverged and where genes may have helped people thrive in new settings.
plos-pone-0008027:
Dmitry Ayollo and colleagues watched how cells change their grip as they turn cancerous, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Healthy lining cells hold each other through junctions built on a protein called E-cadherin, backed by a web of actin fibers. That grip keeps tissue neat and still.

Early in the shift to cancer, both the web and the junctions rearranged. Cells held each other in new, looser ways. Looser grip is a first step toward invasion, since a cell that lets go can wander. The work maps that step in close detail.
plos-pone-0008127:
Jenny Leitz and colleagues tested alcoholic drinks for a plastics-linked chemical in PLOS ONE in 2009. The chemical, diethyl phthalate, is added to some alcohol to make it unfit to drink, and it also keeps plastics soft. Unrecorded alcohol, made and sold off the books, skips every safety check.

Lab measures across many drinks let the team judge how much of the chemical drinkers actually take in and what risk that poses. Off-record liquor carried the worst loads. The numbers give health officials a firm base for rules and raids aimed at the riskiest supply.
plos-pone-0008227:
Allison L. Weber, Qiong Zhao, and Michael D. McMullen used teosinte genetics in PLOS ONE in 2009 to study maize history. Large screens had found dozens of maize genes bearing marks of artificial selection. Farmers shaped those genes during domestication and later improvement. Such genes may control trait differences between wild and cultivated maize. Teosinte is the wild ancestor of maize.

By mapping associations in teosinte, the team tested what these candidate genes actually do. Working in the wild relative avoids effects bred into modern corn. Their results help separate true selection targets from bystanders. That sharpens the story of how maize was domesticated.
plos-pone-0008327:
Mark W. Perlin and Alexander Sinelnikov wrote about forensic DNA evidence in PLOS ONE in 2009. Crime scene DNA often mixes several people's contributions. Sometimes only a tiny amount of DNA is present. Read with simple inclusion methods, such signals can look uninformative. A sample is then reported only as matching or not matching.

The authors argue an information gap hides in that practice. The same data can yield much more when analyzed quantitatively. Computers can extract probabilities that simple methods discard. Closing the gap could change how DNA evidence is presented in court. It matters for both convictions and exonerations.
plos-pone-0008427:
Shamik Sen, Meimei Dong, and Sanjay Kumar wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on glioblastoma, a fast brain tumor with low survival. Tumor cells spread deep into brain tissue. The authors studied a protein called alpha-actinin, which links actin fibers in cells. Its levels had been tied to how far the tumor spreads.

The paper asks what each form of the protein does in glioma cells. It looks at how the forms change cell shape, pull, and movement. The work helps explain why some tumor cells push into brain tissue so well. It may point to new ways to slow that spread.
plos-pone-0008527:
Adam Whelan and co-authors revisit host preference in tuberculosis in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In the late nineteenth century, experiments defined which animals each TB form infects. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the human tubercle bacillus. Smith, Koch, and von Behring each showed it to be avirulent in cattle. That is, it did not cause disease in cows. The team test that classic claim with modern methods.

They experimentally infect cattle with the strain H37Rv. The strain again proves avirulent in cattle in their hands. Confirming the old result matters for animal models and vaccine trials. It sharpens the line between human and bovine tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0008627:
Geoffrey Horwitz and co-authors test a channel hypothesis in mouse ears in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Sensory hair cells in the inner ear convert sound into nerve signals. The molecular composition of their transduction channel had not been identified. The team explore a novel hypothesis that HCN channel subunits form part of it. HCN channels are a family of four ion channels first found in heart and brain pacemaking. They test hair cells lacking HCN function.

They find HCN channels are not required for mechanotransduction in those cells. Sound conversion proceeds without them. A clear negative result narrows the search for the true channel. Future work must look to other channel families.
plos-pone-0008727:
Meser Ali, Branislava Janic, Abbas Babajani-Feremi, and colleagues tracked blood vessel changes in rat brain tumors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gliomas are deadly brain cancers fed by abnormal vessels. Drugs that block vessel growth signals are in early patient trials. One such drug targets receptors for VEGF, a growth signal. What it does to leakiness inside real tumors needed watching.

After treatment, the team measured how leaky tumor vessels became. They also read levels of several vessel-growth factors. The measures show whether the drug normalizes vessels or merely starves them. Such detail helps set doses for glioma therapy.
plos-pone-0008827:
Alexey Karpushev, Daria Ilatovskaya, Tengis Pavlov, and colleagues showed a salt channel needs the cell skeleton to switch on. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The channel, ENaC, controls how much sodium crosses surface linings. That control sets body fluid volume and airway wetness. Small G proteins can activate the channel. The cytoskeleton, the cell's inner scaffolding, was suspected to help.

Breaking up the scaffolding blocked the G proteins' activating effect. An intact skeleton proved necessary for the switch to work. Cell structure and channel control are thus tightly linked. The link matters for blood pressure and lung fluid balance.
plos-pone-0008927:
Francesco Caruso and co-authors examined the disinfectant taurolidine in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Taurolidine is made from taurine, an amino acid, and it kills many kinds of bacteria and some fungi. Doctors use it to prevent infections, but its exact way of attacking germs was not fully clear.

The researchers watched how taurolidine stops E. coli bacteria from sticking to surfaces. They also tracked how the compound changes once it sits in body-like fluids. Their tests showed it binds to the bacterial cell wall and damages that outer shell. Knowing this helps explain why the drug works against such a wide range of microbes.
plos-pone-0009027:
Hongqi Xin and co-authors traced how stem cell treatment helps mouse brains regrow nerve fibres after stroke, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The treatment uses multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells, given after a blocked brain artery. Recovering brains sprout new neurites, the fibres nerves use to connect. An enzyme called tPA, famous for dissolving blood clots, turned out to be involved.

The stem cells raised tPA activity in astrocytes, the brain's support cells. With more tPA at work, neurites grew out more readily. tPA's own inhibitors pushed the other way, slowing growth. The pathway explains part of how these cell transplants aid stroke recovery.
plos-pone-0009127:
Farhan Baluch and Laurent Itti trained volunteers for ten days to see whether attention itself can be coached, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Practice improves scores on the very task being practised. The open question was whether top-down attention improves more broadly. Their test task was a hard triple-conjunction search through cluttered scenes.

Training sharpened performance on the search well beyond the drilled items. The gain looked target-nonspecific, a general boost to guided search. Attention, like a muscle, appears trainable in its own right. That matters for jobs from airport screening to reading medical scans.
plos-pone-0009227:
Lane Yoder published this brain theory study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It builds on two earlier papers that proposed an explicit model of brain wiring. In that model, families of logic circuits made from synapses do the processing. The circuits were shown to match known effects in several senses.

Here Yoder shows the same circuit model predicts local features of the neocortex. The predictions cover both how the tissue works and how it is built. A model that forecasts anatomy and physiology, rather than just fitting them afterward, is a strong test. The study argues this explicit circuit scheme deserves that test.
plos-pone-0009327:
Abderrahmane Tagmount and co-authors published this crab genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Crustaceans, from shrimp to crabs, had few large DNA resources at the time. A completed genome for the water flea Daphnia made comparisons possible. Porcelain crabs, genus Petrolisthes, were a promising next subject.

The team built the porcelain crab's transcriptome, the set of all messages its cells produce. They also launched PCAD, a database pairing those sequences with microarray tools. Such a resource lets researchers compare gene use across crustaceans and spot what changed in evolution. It also supports studies of how crabs cope with stress in their shore habitat.
plos-pone-0009427:
Tsuyoshi Iwata and co-authors published this prostate cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mice engineered to overproduce MYC in the prostate develop pre-cancer and then cancer. The model is widely used, yet exactly when MYC switches on, and in which cells, was not pinned down. Timing matters because early changes are the easiest to treat.

The team used staining to follow MYC in the mouse prostate over time. Excess MYC brought on prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a pre-cancerous state. It also caused loss of Nkx3.1, a protective gene, in the luminal cells lining the glands. The sequence shows two early steps on the road to prostate cancer.
plos-pone-0009527:
Balaji V. and colleagues studied drug resistant tuberculosis at a large hospital in India in PLOS ONE in 2010. India bears a heavy load of tuberculosis that resists standard drugs. The hardest forms resist many drugs at once. Data on those extreme forms, called XDR-TB, were scarce in India. The team reviewed cases at a tertiary referral hospital.

They identified factors that raised the odds of resistant disease. Prior treatment and its gaps stood out among the risks. Such findings give health officials clear targets. Catching resistant cases earlier can slow their spread. Making sure first treatment is completed helps too, since unfinished courses breed harder to cure forms.
plos-pone-0009627:
Michel Levesque and co-authors designed RNA tools against hepatitis C in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ribozymes are RNA molecules that act like enzymes. They can be built to find a matching RNA and cut it. That makes them a possible weapon against viruses, whose genomes are RNA or are read into RNA. The team investigated a new generation of ribozymes aimed at hepatitis C virus.

The new designs aim for better targeting and cutting than earlier versions. A tool that strikes only the virus would spare the patient's own cells. Hepatitis C infects millions and can cause liver failure and cancer. Work like this explores whether RNA scissors can become a real treatment.
plos-pone-0009727:
After the Wenchuan earthquake, surveys found a strange pattern in how people felt. Shu Li and colleagues tracked that pattern and its changes over time. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The earthquake struck Sichuan province in China in 2008.

The pattern is called the psychological typhoon eye. Like a storm's calm center, people nearest the disaster reported less anxiety than people farther away. The team charted how that gap evolved as time passed after the quake. The paradox matters for planning mental health aid after disasters. Later surveys let the team watch the effect fade or shift.
plos-pone-0009827:
Genes carry marks of the pressures that shaped them over evolution. Eduardo Tarazona-Santos and colleagues read those marks in a gene for moving glucose into cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glucose is the main sugar cells burn for fuel.

The gene is SLC2A4, which builds the glucose transporter-4 protein. Its diversity in humans reflects natural selection acting along the Old-World primate line. Selection leaves patterns that drift alone would not produce. Reading those patterns shows how diet and energy shaped primate evolution. Old-World primates include monkeys and apes of Africa and Asia.
plos-pone-0009927:
The mosquito Anopheles gambiae spreads malaria and lymphatic filariasis across Africa. Dziedzom de Souza and colleagues mapped where it lives in Ghana and what shapes that map. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Environmental factors include rainfall, temperature, water, and land use. Knowing where the vector thrives tells control teams where to strike first. Ghana carries a heavy burden of both diseases. The species named is Anopheles gambiae sensu stricto, the most dangerous of its sibling group. Distribution maps turn mosquito control from guesswork into targeting. The work covered Ghana in West Africa.
plos-pone-0010027:
The authors were Andrew Marshall, Oliver Barrett, Timothy Cullingford, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used heart cells from newborn rats. It asked how two signal routes shape early gene changes. A compound called endothelin-1 triggered those changes in the cells.

One route runs through enzymes called ERK1 and ERK2. The other runs through a protein called RhoA. The title states the finding plainly: ERK signaling dominated RhoA signaling in this early response. That ranking helps explain how heart cells grow larger under stress, a step toward heart disease. The work reads that contest in the earliest hours of change.
plos-pone-0010227:
Puran Sijwali and Philip Rosenthal tested how malaria parasites ship their proteins in 2010. Malaria parasites grow inside red blood cells, within a bubble called a vacuole. To change their host cell, they must export many of their own proteins across that bubble. Those proteins end up in the cell fluid and its membranes, reshaping the red cell.

Working in a mouse malaria species, Plasmodium berghei, the pair evaluated export signals on proteins. Their PLOS ONE results suggest more than one mode of export exists. Multiple routes would give the parasite flexible ways to remodel its host cell.
plos-pone-0010327:
David Eriksson, Sonata Valentiniene and Stylianos Papaioannou explored how the visual brain reacts to sudden change in PLOS ONE in 2010. When an image flips at once, neurons in the first visual areas fire at their fastest rate soon after. That early burst also carries the most detail about which image is shown. It is tempting to treat the burst as the whole story.

The authors instead asked how firing relates to coding and to later adjustment. They decoded the joint firing of cell groups in areas 17 and 18 as a stimulus changed. Their work separates three ideas often blurred together: raw information, how it is encoded, and how responses fade with exposure. Vision, they show, must be read over time, not from one peak.
plos-pone-0010427:
Aseefhali Bankapur and colleagues combined a light trap with a laser method to read single blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Raman spectroscopy reads the chemical fingerprint of a cell from scattered light. Holding one live cell still long enough to read is the challenge. An optical trap, focused light that grips tiny objects, solved it. The team trapped single red and white blood cells under near-body conditions.

The trapped cells gave clean, detailed spectra one at a time. Red and white cells could be told apart by their fingerprints. Single-cell reading could one day flag sick cells without dyes or destruction. Blood is the easiest tissue to sample, so the use case is wide. The study is a step toward label-free cell diagnosis.
plos-pone-0010527:
Sabine Hermans and co-workers showed that catching tuberculosis during HIV treatment harms later immune recovery in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antiretroviral therapy cuts TB risk over time, yet TB rates spike in the first months of treatment. The team followed patients at a large urban HIV clinic in sub-Saharan Africa. They measured how TB during treatment affected long-term outcomes. Risk factors for that early TB were also examined.

Patients who developed TB on treatment regained immune strength more slowly. Their long-term HIV control suffered as well. Early TB is thus not a brief detour but a lasting setback. Preventing it in the first months deserves extra effort. The study quantifies the stakes with real clinic data.
plos-pone-0010627:
Ruth Chia and colleagues studied misshapen proteins in ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2010. ALS kills motor neurons and usually proves fatal within a few years. Damage often starts in one spot, then spreads along the spinal cord.

The team took clumps of a protein called SOD1 from the spinal cords of sick mice. Those clumps seeded fresh clumps when mixed with normal SOD1. Seeding is how prions spread their shape from protein to protein. If ALS spreads the same way, blocking the seed could slow the disease. That idea now needs testing in living animals.
plos-pone-0010727:
Felix Bonowski and colleagues built a robot-run assay for enzyme studies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enzymes behave differently as acidity, salt, and food supply change. Measuring that behavior by hand is slow, so models of living systems often rest on thin data.

Their computer-controlled setup ran many enzyme tests in sequence without human handling. It recorded full reaction curves across changing conditions. Steady automation produced the dense, even data that model builders need. With better numbers, computer models of metabolism can be tested instead of merely tuned to fit.
plos-pone-0010827:
Yu-Fang Pei, Lei Zhang, Jian Li and co-authors published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genetic studies often miss some variants, and imputation fills those gaps by estimating untyped genetic markers from known patterns. The authors set out to compare seven popular tools that use imputed data to test links between genes and disease.

Using simulated and real data sets, they tracked how linkage patterns, the rarity of a hidden causal variant, and imputation accuracy changed each method's power. Tests built on imputed data could sharpen signals and raise power when linkage was moderate or strong, and gains grew as linkage grew stronger. Their head-to-head results give researchers practical guidance on which approach to trust, and when imputation helps a gene hunt rather than muddying it.
plos-pone-0010927:
Ursina Tobler and Benedikt Schmidt published this amphibian disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chytridiomycosis, a fungal skin disease, is driving frog and toad declines worldwide, but species differ hugely in how hard it hits. Whether populations of one species also differ, the raw material for evolving resistance, was largely unknown.

The authors raised midwife toads from several populations under shared conditions, all naturally carrying the fungus, and measured deaths after metamorphosis. Mortality ranged widely, from about a quarter to nearly all animals, depending on the source population. Within populations, survival also hinged on body mass and the timing of metamorphosis. Tobler and Schmidt show that variation in disease toll exists within a single species. That variation is exactly what natural selection would need to build tougher populations.
plos-pone-0011027:
Eduardo Undurraga, Dan Eisenberg, Oyunbileg Magvanjav and co-authors published this human behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Evolutionary theory predicts people can read useful information about others from faces, but almost all tests ran in wealthy Western countries. The authors took the test to the Tsimane', a forager-farmer people of the Bolivian Amazon.

Forty women and forty men in their late teens and twenties rated photographs of nearly a hundred Tsimane' men on four traits relevant to mate choice and rivalry. Comparing ratings with measured traits checks whether face reading works outside industrialized settings, and whether women and men differ at it. Undurraga and colleagues ask whether a celebrated human skill is a cultural habit or a shared inheritance. Their field design, using raters judging their own community, avoids the usual cross-cultural shortcuts.
plos-pone-0011127:
Mastrolorenzo, Petrone, Pappalardo and colleagues revisited Pompeii in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Roman town was buried by a volcanic blast in ancient times. At the edge of the flow, scholars had debated whether heat alone could kill, or whether other causes explained the deaths there.

Evidence from the site showed that even at the outer edge, the hot surge reached lethal heat levels. That finding reshapes how the final moments at Pompeii are understood. It also matters for modern hazard planning near volcanoes. People far from the center of a surge may still face deadly heat, not just ash and dust.
plos-pone-0011227:
Bojang, Milligan, Conway and colleagues followed Gambian children in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children treated in hospital for severe anemia often fall ill again soon after going home. The team tested preventive drug treatment after discharge to stop anemia from returning.

A working prevention plan could protect children during their most fragile weeks. Severe anemia kills many young children in malaria regions, and relapse wastes hard won recovery. The study offers a practical strategy hospitals can apply at discharge. Its results can guide programs that aim to cut child deaths after hospital care ends.
plos-pone-0011327:
Li, Ali, Wang and colleagues studied the chickenpox virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. This virus, varicella zoster, also causes shingles later in life. A human enzyme best known for breaking down insulin was found to interact with a key surface protein of the virus, changing that protein's shape.

The reshaped protein made the virus more infective and more stable. A human protein thus helps the virus break into cells, an unexpected partnership. Blocking that helper interaction is a possible antiviral route. The finding adds a host factor to virology's map of how this common virus succeeds.
plos-pone-0011427:
Beverly Duncan and co-authors reported in 2010 that an unusual immune cell from young mice can protect against type 1 diabetes for a long time. In the NOD mouse, the standard model of the disease, immune cells destroy the insulin-making cells of the pancreas. The team isolated a rare spleen cell type that lacks both of the usual T-cell markers.

Transferring those double-negative cells into mice at risk gave lasting protection against diabetes. A small, overlooked cell population acting as a durable guard is a striking result. It suggests the immune system carries its own brakes that could be boosted on purpose. If a human counterpart exists, cell therapy built on it might prevent diabetes in people at high risk, rather than only managing blood sugar after the disease has taken hold.
plos-pone-0011527:
Erik Maronde and co-authors reported in 2010 that two clock genes pull bone formation in opposite directions. Bones are rebuilt constantly, and the body's daily clock helps set the pace of that renewal. The team studied the clock genes Period 2 and Cryptochrome 2 in the skeleton, where their roles had been unclear.

The two genes differentially balanced bone formation, one restraining and one permitting, so the clock acts on bone as a matched pair of pushes rather than a single switch. That pairing ties the timing system of sleep and waking directly to the skeleton. It suggests that chronic clock disruption, as in shift work, may carry a skeletal cost worth measuring. For bone medicine, the clock becomes a factor to record alongside diet and hormones when judging why a skeleton is thinning.
plos-pone-0011627:
Philomena Mburu and co-authors studied the protein machinery that builds hearing structures, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sound is picked up by hair cells in the inner ear, whose tiny bristles, called stereocilia, are built from the protein actin. A scaffold complex at each bristle tip is vital for growing and lengthening them correctly.

The team showed that gelsolin, a protein that shapes actin strands, works within that tip complex in hair cells. Placing gelsolin in the assembly helps explain how bristles reach their precise stair-step heights. Faults in such machinery cause deafness, so each part identified sharpens the search for its genetic causes.
plos-pone-0011727:
Sergio Almécija, Salvador Moyà-Solà and David Alba compared fossil thumb bones across early human relatives, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tip bone of the human thumb closely reflects our refined precision grip, holding objects pad to pad. Similar features in fossil hominins have been linked to human-like hand proportions and tool use.

The authors measured these thumb bones in fossils and living primates. Their comparison pushes the origin of human-like precision grasping surprisingly early. Tool-ready hands may have evolved long before modern humans, reshaping the story of how manual skill developed in our lineage.
plos-pone-0011827:
Xianyao Li and co-authors read gut gene activity in chicken lines with unlike resistance, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Campylobacter jejuni is one of the top causes of human gut infection in the world, most often through tainted poultry. The team had found a marked gap in how much of the germ settles in the ceca of two broiler lines with distinct genes.

By profiling the local cecal response in each line, they picked out gene-use patterns tied to being prone or resistant. Their readout shows what holds the germ back in the bird's gut. Breeding or care that boosts those responses could cut taint at its source.
plos-pone-0011927:
Ted Cranford, Petr Krysl, and Mats Amundin opened in 2010 a new window into how toothed whales hear. Concern over ocean noise grew after whales stranded during intense sound events, yet the mechanics of the toothed whale ear remained poorly known. The ear sits in a dense bony structure called the tympanoperiotic complex.

The team describes an acoustic portal, a route by which sound reaches that ear complex, and analyzes how the complex vibrates. Understanding the route sound takes is the first step toward judging which human-made noises can injure whale hearing. It also recasts the whale head as an acoustic instrument shaped by evolution for underwater listening.
plos-pone-0012027:
Jianrong Yao and co-workers used PET imaging in 2010 to pin down where high blood sugar strikes during pregnancy. Diabetes and obesity in pregnancy harm fetal outcomes, but the mechanisms are hard to isolate in a living mother. Their approach isolated one element: raised glucose itself, in defined places.

Positron emission tomography gave a spatial and time-resolved picture of localized fetomaternal hyperglycemia, showing where glucose piles up between mother and fetus and how fast. A map in space and time replaces the vague statement that sugar is high. That precision helps separate glucose's own harm from the other problems that travel with diabetes.
plos-pone-0012127:
Maria Ledesma, Sara Ochoa, Ariadnna Cruz, and co-authors studied a dangerous gut bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. This E. coli strain causes bloody diarrhea and can trigger kidney failure, especially in children. It grows long bundles of thin pili, hair-like anchors that help it grip the gut and do harm, and the team asked what those bundles do to gut cells.

They found the pili push intestinal cells to release pro-inflammatory signals, the chemical alarms that bring swelling and immune attack. So the same structures that help the bacterium hold on also stir up the gut's defenses. Knowing this helps explain the severe gut damage in these infections and suggests targets for blocking them.
plos-pone-0012227:
Margaret Pullen, Nick Clark, Fatemeh Zarinkamar, and co-authors studied vein formation in mutant flowering plants in PLOS ONE in 2010. A plant's veins carry water and food to every leaf, and their pattern is set during development by interacting hormone signals. The mutants used here, called hydra, cannot make their normal sterols, the fatty molecules that also carry signals in plant growth.

By reading vein development in these sterol-poor plants, the team traced how sterols and hormones together steer the plumbing's layout. Errors in this system stunt the whole plant, so the rules matter for crop growth. The work also shows how one chemical family can serve as both building material and messenger.
plos-pone-0012327:
Brittany Huntington, Mandy Karnauskas, and Elizabeth Babcock worked to separate marine reserve effects from natural variation, in PLOS ONE in 2010. No-fishing reserves are judged by comparing their reefs with fished ones, but reefs differ naturally in layout and habitat mix, and those differences can hide or fake a reserve's effect. Their landscape approach treats the coral reef seascape itself, the arrangement of its habitats, as a variable to measure.

Accounting for seascape variation lets the true management signal show through. Without that accounting, good reserves can look useless and useless ones successful, and policy follows the mirage. The method travels to any protected-area debate where the land or sea refuses to be uniform.
plos-pone-0012427:
Christopher Bagwell, Kim Hixson, Charles Milliken and colleagues mapped how a tough soil bacterium handles copper, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Copper kills most cells, so all life keeps it under tight control. Kineococcus radiotolerans shrugs off radiation and also tolerates metals, making its defenses of interest for cleaning polluted sites.

The team read the bacterium's protein response to copper loads. It reshaped transport and stress proteins to keep copper in safe bounds. Learning its tricks could help build microbes that survive metal waste and perhaps extract valuable metals from it. The study also adds to the portrait of a famously hardy organism.
plos-pone-0012527:
Pia Steensland, Jeffrey Simms, Carsten Nielsen and colleagues tested a craving-blocking drug in animals, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The obesity epidemic is fed in part by overconsumption of sweet drinks and foods, and the drive to seek them shares circuitry with drug addiction. The team targeted the neurokinin 1 receptor, a receiver for a stress-and-reward peptide.

Its blocker, ezlopitant, reduced how hard animals worked for sucrose and for ethanol. One drug trimming appetite for both sugar and alcohol hints at a shared reward lever. Such compounds interest researchers seeking treatments for overeating and alcohol use disorder alike.
plos-pone-0012627:
Yao, Yoon, Kalie and co-authors studied how calcium inside a cell shapes a growth signal. The signal runs through ERK5, part of a chain that carries growth and stress messages. A growth factor called EGF can set that chain off, but the steps were not fully mapped.

Their 2010 experiments raised and lowered cell calcium and watched ERK5 respond both ways. They traced the effect to a meeting between two proteins, Lad1 and MEKK2. Working out such wiring helps explain how cells read growth cues, a process that goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pone-0012727:
Godmann, May and Kimmins studied how chemical gene tags control two genes in a male germ cell line. Sperm develop under tight epigenetic control, and faults may sit behind falling male fertility. Their 2010 paper covers Pou5f1, a stem cell gene, and Gfra1, both active in the cells that give rise to sperm.

They map the tag patterns that switch these genes in this cell line. The environment can rewrite such tags while sperm form, linking lifestyle and fertility. Groundwork like this is needed before those links can be tested in men.
plos-pone-0327927:
María del Carmen Sanjuán and James Byron Nelson test how seeing one pattern alone sharpens later learning to tell patterns apart. Perceptual learning of this kind sits behind skills from reading X-rays to telling wines apart. Their 2026 paper reviews rival theories and runs two online game-style experiments where players first meet blended shapes and later learn which blends predict outcomes.

Earlier solo exposure changed how one part of the blend behaved in later tests. In the second experiment, that part picked up new learning faster, which favors the idea that solo exposure restores its punch rather than tying it to disappointment. The results help sort out why practice with a single cue can sharpen the senses.
plos-pone-0335327:
Cynthia Mubanga and a team of researchers looked beyond simple antibody counts to judge a diarrhoea vaccine given to Zambian toddlers. The vaccine, ETVAX, targets a toxin-making E. coli that kills young children in poorer countries. Counts alone can mislead, so the team measured avidity, how tightly antibodies grip their target, in sixty children given three small doses over three months with a booster ingredient.

Blood taken before vaccination already showed gripping antibodies, evidence that these children had met the germ naturally. Surprisingly, grip strength against one target eased slightly by the end of the course rather than rising. The authors argue that vaccine trials in places where the germ circulates should weigh antibody quality alongside quantity, since natural exposure reshapes what the vaccine can add.
plos-pone-0339427:
Stephanie Wied and colleagues ask how much the way patients are split into trial groups matters when diseases are rare and patient numbers tiny. Random splitting guards against bias, but with few patients, some splitting methods guess easily or stack groups unfairly. The team offers guidance built on an evaluation framework and a free software tool that scores splitting methods on bias, predictability, and error rates for a given trial design.

Judged one measure at a time, different methods can look best, which the authors warn is misleading; the full scorecard must be read together. No single method wins for every design. Wied and colleagues aim their guidance at trial designers who must defend their choice to regulators when every patient counts.
plos-pone-0343227:
Hassan Gharayagh Zandi and colleagues ran a school trial for inactive teenage girls. Many teens lose drive for exercise as confidence falls. Girls aged thirteen to eighteen joined seven group sessions. Sessions taught acceptance skills and values based action. A control group kept normal school routines. Tests covered drive, activity, skill, and fitness.

Girls in the sessions gained inner drive for exercise. They also felt more choice and less outside pressure. Activity time rose. Fitness scores rose too. Both felt skill and tested skill improved. A mind based programme can move the body. Schools could use such sessions to build habits that last past childhood.
plos-pone-0344827:
Etienne Kouokam, writing solo, built a hybrid tool to predict the epidemic threshold in networks of linked communities. The threshold is the tipping point where a disease can take off. Classic graph formulas estimate it fast but roughly. His network learns from graph features and disease settings. It is punished when it breaks basic epidemic theory. Heavy simulation supplied the true values, with uncertainty ranges, across hundreds of networks.

Kouokam then benchmarked seven methods on the same ground. He reports plainly where deep learning wins. He also reports where simple tree models match or beat it. That honesty is the spine of the work. Modelers gain a theory-guided tool, a trusted yardstick, and a map of when the fancy option is not worth its cost.
plos-pone-0346027:
Nadun Salinda and Tharaga Sharmilan built a portable robot that tests raw milk quality on the spot, a job that normally needs a slow laboratory visit. Their machine uses a jointed arm to dip sensors into each sample, checking acidity, dissolved solids, temperature, density, and colour in under five minutes. Then a trained computer judge grades the milk.

The computer judge graded samples correctly far more often than simple fixed cut-offs, especially for borderline milk. Trials at rural collection centres in Sri Lanka matched laboratory verdicts closely, and the whole check ran about a third faster than manual testing. The authors pitch the system, cheap to maintain and free of chemicals, as a way to cut spoilage and unfair rejections in village dairy chains.
plos-pone-0346627:
Jian Zhang and co-authors ran a computer pipeline to find new blockers of an enzyme that worsens brain damage after stroke. The enzyme chews through the scaffolding that holds tissue together, letting swelling and bleeding spread, yet existing blockers travel poorly in the body. Starting from the enzyme's shape, the team screened a compound library in stages, checking fit, drug-like properties, and safety flags at each gate.

One candidate compound survived every filter. Long molecular simulations showed it gripping the enzyme stably, and energy calculations confirmed a snug, favourable fit. No animal or human testing is reported; the value is a well-vetted shortlist of one, ready for laboratory chemists to synthesise and try. The authors present the pipeline itself as reusable for other hard drug targets.
plos-pone-0348127:
Jin-Sung Yuk and Sang-Hee Yoon used South Korea's national health insurance records to ask whether removing the uterus changes later risk of ovarian cancer. Hysterectomy is one of the most common operations on women, yet its long-term effect on this rare but deadly cancer has been unclear, especially in Asian populations. Their 2026 study matched about thirteen thousand women who had the surgery with the same number who did not.

Over a median of eleven and a half years, ovarian cancer appeared at slightly higher rates in the surgery group, but the difference was small and statistically uncertain. The authors are explicit: with so few cases, the data fit both a real increase and a real decrease. The question stays open.
plos-pone-0348427:
Philemon Mohammed Seid and colleagues compared kidney health markers between dry cleaning workers and hotel laundry workers in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Dry cleaners breathe perchloroethylene, a solvent suspected of harming kidneys. One hundred sixty-four workers from dozens of shops gave blood and urine samples and answered questions about their work habits.

Dry cleaners showed significantly higher urinary protein, creatinine, and calcium, a pattern pointing to early kidney stress, though several other markers did not differ significantly. Years on the job, spills, frequent handling, and poor ventilation tracked with symptoms. The authors urge protective measures and regular health monitoring for dry cleaning workers.
