plos-pone-0348527:
Kurşunel and colleagues asked whether parenting a child with special needs blocks parents from exercise in a 2026 study. More than two hundred parents answered surveys on activity, care burden, and barriers, and some sat for short interviews. Families often shape their whole lives around the child's needs, leaving little time for themselves.

Higher barrier scores went together with higher body weight in the survey data. Interviews named four barriers: heavy responsibilities, the child's needs themselves, parents' mental state, and poor sports facilities. Numbers alone missed some of these pressures, the authors note. Support programs need to ease time and facility problems, not just urge parents to move more.
plos-pone-0349027:
Lauren A Rutter, Prabhvir Lakhan, and Laura Germine asked in 2026 whether two personality traits change how well young adults read faces. Spotting subtle shifts between anger, fear, and happiness is a core social skill, and past findings on trait effects were mixed.

Nearly three hundred students took a test built to measure fine feeling discrimination without guessing bias, plus questionnaires on traits, mood, and stress. Women reported higher levels of both traits studied. Trait scores tracked mood symptoms closely, yet neither trait predicted face reading accuracy in the final models. The null result usefully narrows where personality does, and does not, shape social perception.
plos-pone-0349227:
Shruthi Venkataraman and colleagues interviewed thirty-one first-year medical students from Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous backgrounds across the United States about what pulls them toward or pushes them from research careers. Physician-scientists from these groups are scarce, and the first year is when intentions form. Four themes ran through the conversations.

Structured research experience before medical school proved pivotal in sparking interest. Many students framed research as a tool for social justice and community benefit. Mentorship mattered most when mentors invested genuinely and shared the student's background. Yet students also described a research arms race for residency spots that amplifies inequality and can squeeze out the very motivations that drew them in, a tension schools could relieve.
plos-pone-0349527:
Sadia Tabassum and Naushin Nower present DG-LLM, a traffic forecasting framework that borrows the pattern-finding power of large language models. Traffic data entangle daily rhythms with road-network effects across many time scales, defeating simpler predictors. Their method first decomposes the traffic signal into simpler modes, then learns a changing map of which sensors influence each other within each mode.

Those structured inputs feed a pre-trained language model, which handles the long-range time patterns. Across six real-world datasets, from city streets to highways, the framework beat leading graph-based and language-model forecasters, including at long horizons where errors usually snowball. Cities use such forecasts to time signals and pre-empt jams, so durable long-range accuracy is the prize.
plos-pone-0349627:
Jingke Wu and Fuxing Xie present this 2026 PLOS One lab study on how fast loading changes the way rock-like material breaks. They cast artificial rock cylinders from sand, cement, and gypsum in three mixes. They crushed the cylinders at varied loading rates, under two loading styles. They recorded strength and stiffness. They also tracked how absorbed energy split between stored elastic energy and energy lost to damage.

Strength and stiffness rose in a logarithmic pattern as loading sped up. The strain at failure fell. All samples failed by splitting into columns. Faster loading shattered them more fully. Force-controlled loading did more damage than displacement-controlled loading. The stored-energy share also grew with rate. The authors offer these links as a reference for support design in deep, soft rock work.
plos-pone-0349827:
Wen-Chao Zhang and colleagues mined intensive care records in 2026 for patterns in a type of white blood cell after heart attack. Earlier studies disagreed on whether eosinophil counts predict death or kidney injury in these patients.

About fifteen hundred critically ill heart attack patients were grouped by how their counts moved over time: steady low, slowly rising, or quickly rising from a middle start. The rising groups fared better than the steady low group on survival. Kidney injury partly carried the link to death. Watching the trend, not a single count, may sharpen risk judgments after a heart attack.
plos-pone-0350027:
James I Mullet, Amy Pruden, and co-authors went hunting through public genome databases for a curious kind of mobile DNA that lives a double life. These phage-plasmids can persist quietly like plasmids inside bacteria, yet also behave like viruses that infect bacteria. Little was known about where they occur or what jobs their genes do. Their 2026 search used a machine learning classifier to spot them among virus and plasmid sequences.

The search recovered more than five thousand unique elements from a striking range of settings, from human and animal hosts to soil, rivers, wastewater, and seawater. Elements from host-associated settings carried the most defense and antibiotic resistance genes, while those from open waters leaned toward making chemical compounds. Some traits, including systems that block viral defenses, appeared more often in these hybrids than in plain plasmids or viruses.
plos-pone-0350127:
Jiguang Yu and Louis Shuo Wang rebuilt the classic predator-prey model from first principles to fix a mathematical shortcut that misrepresents chance in ecology. Modelers usually sprinkle randomness onto population equations as independent noise for each species. Their 2026 derivation starts instead from the actual random events of birth, death, and predation, and proves what the true noise structure must be.

Events that couple predator and prey, like a kill that feeds a predator, force the two species' fluctuations to move against each other, something the standard shortcut cannot express. The authors also separate two modeling worlds that are often confused: one conditioned on survival, another allowing extinction. They supply a rigorous proof framework so future models can keep noise honest and boundaries sound.
plos-pone-0350727:
A J A Al-Gburi designed a very small dual band antenna for 5G phones in 2026 and checked its safety against the head. Phones at these high frequencies pack antennas near the ear, so radiation absorbed by tissue must stay well under legal limits.

The antenna works at the two main high bands planned for handsets. Three realistic head models, a full head, a skull, and a brain alone, were used to measure absorbed radiation in simulation, and a built prototype matched the simulated behaviour closely. Absorption stayed well below international limits in all three. Compact and compliant designs clear a key hurdle for high band phones.
plos-pone-0350827:
Angelo Maria Sabatini revisited a famous experiment in 2026: the mathematician Markov counting vowels and consonants in Pushkin's verse novel Eugene Onegin. Sabatini applied modern time series tools to the poem and to an Italian translation.

Letters were coded simply as vowel or consonant, and a compact chain model reproduced the poem's patterns of memory and repetition well. The Russian text lost memory gradually as it unfolded, while the translation stayed more even. Short letter patterns also tracked shifts in the story. The study shows how much structure a very simple code can reveal in a literary classic.
plos-pone-0351127:
Zhang and Chen, in a 2026 study, chart a whooping cough outbreak among children in Chengdu, China, across one year from May 2024. Whooping cough has resurged in many places despite vaccines. The team reviewed genetic test results for about nineteen thousand children at a large children's hospital, looking at season, age, sex, and where care was given.

About one in five tests came back positive. Summer dominated, with the peak month, June 2024, alone producing more than a thousand cases. School-aged children, roughly six to eleven, made up the largest share of cases and tested positive most often. Sex made no clear difference. Outpatients tested positive more than inpatients, especially in spring and summer, which may reflect who gets tested in each setting. The authors aim their findings at regional prevention, with school-age children and the summer surge as the clear targets.
plos-pone-0351327:
Jingting Zeng, Tianchi Qiu, and Linmin Shan analyse how today's readers receive a famous translation of a Chinese classic. Their 2026 study concerns Arthur Waley's 1942 Monkey, his shortened English Journey to the West. Nearly eight hundred reviews from Amazon and Goodreads were gathered. Topic modelling grouped what readers talked about. A sentiment classifier scored their feelings. A large language model helped validate the qualitative reading of themes.

The verdict leans warm. About forty-three percent of reviews were positive, against eighteen percent negative. Readers loved Waley's chatty prose. They adored Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, as a trickster hero. The book's philosophy and humour crossed cultures well. Complaints clustered elsewhere: story structures that clash with Western expectations, too little guidance on cultural background, and a poorly received British-accented audiobook. An eighty-year-old abridgement, it turns out, still wins readers, provided nobody promises them the whole epic.
plos-pone-0351627:
Irene Vianini and a large team tracked how world media covered Russia and Ukraine across more than a decade. They gathered over twenty-two million article titles from thousands of sources in nearly two hundred countries and many languages. Human reviewers worked with automated clustering to group the titles and follow story lines over time.

Coverage spiked around the Euromaidan protests, the seizure of Crimea, and the full-scale invasion of twenty twenty-two. Recurring themes included tension between Russia and the West, energy security, and false-information campaigns. Early clusters centered on gas disputes and protests, while later ones centered on the invasion and its worldwide effects. Attention kept returning to the same leaders and institutions. The dataset gives researchers a map of how a conflict's story was told globally.
plos-pone-0351727:
Yandong Song and colleagues engineered a vision model, MCCA-YOLO, to spot rice leaf diseases early, when the marks are faint and farmers' routine spraying either wastes pesticide or arrives too late. Rice feeds more than half the world, so small accuracy gains scale enormously. Their design gives the detector two feature-extracting backbones, a module that sharpens leaf texture in the frequency domain, and a feedback loop that checks its own work across scales.

The architecture targets exactly the failure mode of field photos: tiny, low-contrast lesions on cluttered leaves. Cross-scale fusion lets a pinhead spot borrow context from the whole leaf before the model commits. For extension services and drone scouts, a detector tuned for the earliest, faintest stage is the difference between spot treatment and blanket spraying, with the chemical savings and yield protection that follow.
plos-pone-0351927:
Dennis Acheampong, Kwaku Adomako, and Bismark Kyei raised three hundred broiler chickens under Ghana's humid tropical heat. Three commercial breeds took part: Hubbard, Cobb 500, and Ross 308. All birds ate the same feed and lived under the same care for six weeks. The team weighed growth, meat yield, health, and cost. A growth curve model added a second view of the same birds.

By the final weighing, the breeds were statistically tied. Weight, feed use, and cost per kilo of gain all matched. The curve model gave Cobb 500 the fastest growth path. Ross 308 died least and grew the largest gut organs, signs of toughness in heat. With headline results tied, breed choice turns on survival and local fit.
plos-pone-0352327:
Julie Agel and three colleagues borrow a chart from oncology to display young athletes' sporting lives. Their 2026 methods paper concerns sports specialisation: children dropping other sports to train year-round in one. Specialisation is suspected of raising injury risk. The data behind that debate are usually squeezed into tables that hide timing. Swimmer plots give each athlete one bar, marked with events along a timeline. The team built a dataset from recall survey patterns to demonstrate.

Two clocks were compared. One plot runs on chronological age, the other on years of participation. Each exposes different structure in the same sporting histories. Injuries appear as markers against the single-sport and multi-sport years that preceded them. Standardising a dataset matters as much as the picture. With shared variables and a visual language everyone reads at a glance, studies from different clinics could finally be compared without translation losses.
plos-pone-0352427:
Paolo Boldi and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One mathematics paper about distance-count matrices, tables recording how many nodes in a network sit at each distance from a given node. Such tables underpin measures of how central a node is, and researchers sometimes need to know whether a made-up table could come from a real network when hunting for counterexamples.

The authors prove that deciding this question is strongly NP-complete, meaning no efficient general method is likely to exist. On the brighter side, they show that many common ways of combining networks preserve the ability to compute the combined table directly from the parts. The result closes one door for counterexample hunters while opening a compositional route for structured networks.
plos-pone-0353127:
Noriko Yoshida and seven co-authors describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for the SACLA trial. The trial is a phase II study of surgery for bleeding under the center of the retina. Such bleeding can blind patients with macular degeneration. Twenty patients will have a vitrectomy, then an injection of a clot-dissolving drug under the retina. The trial runs partly in decentralized form. Later check-ups can happen at partner sites, to spare patients travel.

As a protocol, the paper sets out the design, not results. The main measure is change in the thickness of the retina's center, one week after surgery. Vision and safety will be tracked for twelve weeks. No drug is yet approved for this use. The authors aim for the first prospective proof on whether this approach is feasible and safe.
plos-pone-0353227:
Readers should treat this entry with caution: it is a formal Expression of Concern issued by the PLOS One editors in 2026 about an earlier review article. The review in question surveyed machine and deep learning methods for classifying white blood cells from blood smear images. After publication, the editors found serious citation problems in it.

Several works the review cited had themselves been retracted, some before the review even appeared, and other citations did not support the statements attached to them or were missing entirely. The authors replied that some citations were meant only as background on model designs, but the editors state the matter is not fully resolved. The notice corrects the missing citation locations and advises interpreting the review's conclusions carefully.
plos-pone-0353527:
Ahmed and colleagues trialed a rapid on-farm culture kit for udder infection in dairy cows in a 2026 study. Usual care gives antibiotics at once, a habit that fuels drug resistance. Sixteen commercial farms assigned sick cows either to instant treatment or to treatment guided by a three-plate culture read after one day.

Culture guidance removed antibiotics entirely for nearly half the guided cases, where no growth or a certain germ class appeared. Cure rates were then compared between groups. Cutting needless doses while holding cures steady would help farms, milk safety, and resistance control at once, which is why farm-side testing draws wide interest.
plos-pone-0353827:
Maialen Zabalza-Zudaire and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for VOICE-DEP, a Spanish hospital study testing whether the voice can betray depression. Diagnosis and follow-up for major depression rest on interviews and rating scales, yet speech may carry measurable signs of severity. Past voice studies were mostly one-off snapshots, rarely in non-English speakers. This protocol sets out a standardized, repeatable way to record and analyze speech during ordinary medical interviews.

The study will follow twenty-five adults with moderate or severe depression monthly for four months, alongside fifty healthy controls recorded once. Each visit pairs the recording with the standard clinician rating scale, so voice features can be checked against accepted severity measures over time. The authors aim to learn whether speech markers move in step with recovery or relapse. If they do, voice could become a cheap, remote support for depression monitoring.
plos-pone-0354027:
Brennan-Tovey and colleagues, in a 2026 study, evaluate a peer support service for breastfeeding in Newcastle upon Tyne, in North East England. Health guidance says babies should be fed only breast milk for the first six months, yet many mothers in the United Kingdom stop within weeks. Trained volunteers who have breastfed themselves offer advice and encouragement through the service.

The team interviewed twenty-two people: mothers who used the service, plus the staff, volunteers, and health workers around it. Four themes came out, covering how the service works, the support it gives, what it achieves, and where it struggles. Mothers said the emotional support raised their confidence, and making breastfeeding seem normal mattered a great deal. Reaching mothers under twenty-five and those who speak English as a second language remained hard. The findings will guide how the service grows.
plos-pone-0354127:
An and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, teach a neural network to read the texture of asphalt roads from photographs. How rough a road surface is decides how well tires grip, and the classic field test, spreading sand and measuring the patch, is slow. Their method first builds a three-dimensional model of a pavement, then works backward to produce exact black-and-white teaching images.

A U-Net model, a design good at separating regions in images, learned to split road photos into stone and void. Its sorting quality was solid on held-out images. Texture depth computed from its output tracked the sand test closely, and a shape measure called fractal dimension tracked it too. Both links were statistically firm. The authors offer the pipeline as fast technical support for judging skid resistance from a camera instead of a sandbag.
plos-pone-0354427:
Jiarong Wang, Roxana Dev Omar Dev, and Nurhidayah Yaakop published a 2026 survey study in PLOS ONE on the mental side of stand-up paddleboarding, a balance-demanding sport. Just over one hundred seventy athletes completed three surveys covering mindfulness, coping skills such as focus under pressure, and mental toughness. They examined how the three qualities hang together, and whether coping sits between mindfulness and performance.

Athletes scored moderate to high on everything, with no meaningful gender differences Mindfulness tracked with coping skills, and both with stronger mental performance. Coping skills showed the tightest link to performance expression of all. The mediation test supported an indirect path: mindful athletes seemed to perform mentally better largely because they regulated themselves better. As a one-time survey, the authors stress these are associations, not proof of cause, but coaches get a hint that mindfulness work may pay off through coping skills.
plos-pone-0354527:
Qiu Haifei and colleagues tackled a narrow but costly problem in textile mills. The heald frame is a loom part that lifts warp threads thousands of times a minute. Their 2026 engineering study built a replacement frame as a layered sandwich. It combined carbon fiber, epoxy resin, honeycomb, and wood cores. Computer models then tuned how the carbon layers are angled and stacked.

The tuned design raised the frame's natural vibration frequencies well above the steel frame it replaces. Bench tests then confirmed less vibration, less noise, and less wear on the loom's cams. Energy use fell too. For loom builders, the work offers a tested recipe for frames that let modern machines run faster without shaking themselves apart.
plos-pone-0354727:
Jinzhi Bai, Hanlin Xia, and Lin Zhang examine an underappreciated channel through which China's central bank policy reaches the real economy, in this 2026 economics paper. Local governments there borrow heavily by issuing bonds, so their borrowing costs shape local spending and, in turn, national output. The authors first present empirical evidence that this bond channel exists, then build a multi-region economic model with layered governments to measure its strength.

In the model, monetary stimulus worked more than twice as powerfully when local governments could borrow at the risk-free rate, compared with the baseline. Spillovers between regions complicated the picture: average responses shrank, but areas facing certain bond rates responded especially strongly, and competition among local governments blunted transmission overall. The authors say the channel creates distinctly geographic effects of national policy.
plos-pone-0354827:
Kazuhiro Hayashi led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of personality and chronic low back pain in Japan. Just over a hundred clinic outpatients completed a standard personality inventory alongside scales for pain, mood, sleep, self-confidence, and quality of life. The authors traced how a neurotic tendency score flowed through these measures.

Neurotic tendency did connect with worse scores across the pain-related measures, but its effect was small next to pain intensity itself. A small share of patients also scored as prone to giving biased answers. Hayashi's takeaway is measured: personality shades how back pain feels, without driving it.
plos-pone-0354927:
Hai-jie Li and co-authors ran a three-factor greenhouse experiment to tune water and fertiliser for spring tomatoes. Greenhouse production often wastes water and nitrogen, threatening both profits and the environment. Their 2026 trial crossed two irrigation floors with two manure rates and three nitrogen top-dressing levels, including cuts of a fifth and two-fifths below convention.

The team measured leaf photosynthesis, yield, fruit quality, and how efficiently water and nitrogen were used. Combined statistical and component analyses sorted the treatment effects. The goal was a recipe that holds yield and quality while spending less water and synthetic nitrogen. Li and colleagues frame the design as a template for sustainable greenhouse practice beyond tomatoes.
plos-pone-0355727:
Wanlong Huang and co-authors analysed why drill pipe joints fail and how a redesigned joint could last longer. These threaded connections must seal and bear load deep underground, where conditions are harsh. Their 2026 study modelled single-shoulder and double-shoulder joints in three dimensions and checked the models against tests.

The double-shoulder design carried clearly lower stress than the single-shoulder one and sealed better. The team then proposed an extended thread joint that spreads stress more evenly along the thread. Contact pressure on the shoulder also spread more sensibly in the new design. Huang and colleagues present the redesign as a route to fewer joint failures during difficult drilling work.
plos-pone-0355827:
Valerie Kilders and co-authors mapped foreign farmland purchases against United States military interest points. Public and lawmaker concern about adversary-linked land near bases has surged since 2020. Their 2026 study combined social media listening with farm transaction records spanning nearly three decades.

Discussion volume spiked alongside a wave of state laws after 2022. In the records, China-linked deals, excluding one famous meat company purchase, landed in military-interest counties far more often than other foreign deals. Statistical models with state and year controls still found a small positive link. At the same time, most foreign transactions showed no such pattern. Kilders and colleagues separate measurable geography from the louder public debate.
plos-pone-0356727:
Saeed Pirmoradi and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on grading prostate cancer risk from gene activity instead of relying only on biopsy Gleason scores. Biopsy is invasive and can cause pain, infection, or worse. Their framework feeds patients' gene expression profiles and a network of gene interactions into a dual-branch graph neural network, sorting patients into low, medium, and high risk. An explanation method then shows which genes drove each call.

Distinct gene sets marked each risk tier, underlining the disease's different molecular faces. On a held-out test set, the model separated tiers well, most strongly for high risk, with accuracy around four in five patients. Pairing network-aware learning with explanations, they argue, makes predictions sharper and auditable. The main limit is plain: everything rests on one public cancer atlas, so outside cohorts must confirm the signature.
plos-pone-0357027:
Ahmed H Mohammed and seven colleagues tried to make gypsum, a cheap but weak and water-shy building binder, tougher by feeding it waste. Their 2026 study mixed nine recipes combining reactive silica, sodium silicate solution, and ground orange peel powder, then tested strength, water absorption, setting time, and internal structure under the microscope.

One blend stood clearly ahead: a tenth reactive silica, a fifth sodium silicate, and a small dose of orange peel. It reached the highest crushing and bending strengths with low water uptake, and the peel usefully slowed setting so the mix could densify. Microscopy confirmed tighter, less porous interiors. Construction gains twice here: better plaster from peels and industrial leftovers that might otherwise be dumped.
plos-pone-0357127:
Readers should treat the entry here as a formal retraction notice from the editors of PLOS One, issued in 2026. It withdraws a paper on an enhanced algorithm for balancing a circular assembly line with splittable tasks. The editors found that the work leaned too heavily on material from a technology competition run by Huawei, without clear citation or explanation of the link.

Figures, equations, a results table, and parts of the code in the paper closely matched a competition task description and another group's competition entry, the notice reports. The lead author acknowledged taking part in that competition and creating some of the shared figures. Because the overlap strikes at the work's originality, the journal removed the paper from the trusted record.
plos-pone-0357227:
Ahmad Reza Ahmadi and four colleagues test a plant compound as a shield for kidney cells against a chemotherapy drug, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cyclophosphamide cures cancers but damages kidneys at high doses. The team exposed human kidney cells in the dish to the drug, with and without protodioscin. That compound is a saponin from yam family plants, known for antioxidant effects. They measured survival signals, cell death machinery, stress proteins, and injury markers.

The compound protected the cells on several fronts at once. Death promoting signals fell, a protective protein rose, and fewer cells entered programmed death. The strained protein folding system inside the cells, a hallmark of this drug's damage, calmed down. Antioxidant defenses strengthened while injury markers eased. Cell culture protection is a long way from a patient remedy, but the multi pathway rescue makes protodioscin a candidate worth animal testing.
plos-pone-0358227:
Tang He and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE that brings natural language processing to a classic of Chinese philosophy, the Analects of Confucius. Because its many English translations differ in wording and in how they handle key concepts, He's team built a computer framework for comparing them. It lines up five English versions sentence by sentence and measures how closely they agree in meaning.

Their method cleans up concept terms and proper names first, then trains a shared sentence encoder with contrastive learning so matched sentences sit close together in the model. Tested on finding matching sentences across versions and on flagging pairs that disagree, the full model beat the alternatives they tried. Higher model scores also lined up with pairs that human judges had rated as highly consistent. They offer the tool as an aid for scholars comparing translations, not an automatic judge of quality.
plos-pone-0358327:
Tuan Anh Phan, Seohyun Nam, and Jason J Jung compare why scientists cite each other across fields, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A citation can set background, supply motivation, borrow a method, or extend a result, and fields may favor different intents. Their dataset is large: over seventeen thousand papers and more than two million citation contexts across twenty-one subject categories, each classified by intent and examined for distribution, age, and predictability.

The cultures diverge sharply. Philosophy, sociology, area studies, and history lean on background and motivation, and rarely use or extend what they cite. Artificial intelligence research inverts the pattern, dominating in uses and extensions while citing least for background. Citation ages agreed least across intents in area studies and history. Intent counts proved most predictable in biotechnology and plant science, least in the humanities and sociology. One literature, the authors show, is really twenty-one citation economies.
plos-pone-0358427:
Toshihisa Nakashima and colleagues published a 2026 drug safety analysis in PLOS ONE on tendon injuries linked to levofloxacin, a widely used antibiotic. Tendon damage is a known rare risk of this drug family, but patterns by sex, age, and how the drug is given were poorly mapped in Japan. The team mined two large spontaneous reporting databases, one American and one Japanese, covering five related antibiotics.

All five drugs showed warning signals in the American data, but only levofloxacin showed strong, consistent signals in both Japanese sources. The signal was much stronger in men, especially those aged seventy and older, and stronger for the oral form than for intravenous use. Most tendon events were reported within about two weeks of starting the drug. The authors urge Japanese clinicians to prescribe levofloxacin cautiously for older men and to watch early for tendon pain.
plos-pone-0358627:
The PLOS One Editors publish this notice in 2026 as an Expression of Concern about an earlier article on iron in wastewater irrigated soils and food crops near Sargodha. Readers are advised to interpret that article with caution. The notice centers on compliance with the journal's authorship policy, a matter that goes to who stands behind the work and its claims. Such notices are not retractions, but they are a warning attached to the record.

Alongside the warning, the editors correct a series of errors in the article's methods and results text. plos-pone-0359327:

Ioannidis argues, in a widely cited essay, that most published research findings are likely to be false. Concern was already rising when he wrote in 2005. He explains that whether a claim is true depends on study size and power, on bias, and on how many teams chase the same question.

Kaplina and colleagues run a prospective study on feeding and growth in newborns with heart defects. Babies with congenital heart defects often need surgery in their first weeks. Carvalho and colleagues report a skin disease that imitated spreading cancer in a young man with a rare tumour. Wei and co-authors in China tracked whether a combined triglyceride and glycated hemoglobin index predicts diabetes in fatty liver patients. Nassau William Senior opened his Oxford professorship with an Introductory Lecture on Political Economy in 1827. Political economy still smelled of radicals and stockjobbers to many dons.

He promises conclusions that advise governments without dictating to them. The lecture's care about what economics can and cannot prove set the Victorian agenda for the subject's method. His friendship with Paul Watkins, a worker turned communist, pulls him between the two worlds. The novel sweeps through strikes, Hollywood sets, and Washington scandal. spence-history-of-atlantis-1927:

suzuki-essays-zen-buddhism-1-1927:

Suzuki explains koans, the riddles masters set their students, and satori, the sudden flash of awakening they aim to trigger. Its frame of ten storytellers may have fed later tale cycles far beyond India. Ryder's complete version remains the standard English one. Few Sanskrit prose works read with such pace.
thomas-life-buddha-1927:
Edward Thomas was a scholar of Pali who set out in 1927 to write a critical life of the Buddha, separating legend from history. His Life of Buddha as Legend and History reads the earliest texts with a detective's patience. It became the landmark scholarly biography of its generation.

Thomas weighs birth tales, miracles, and late embellishments against the older discourses that may record real memory. He rebuilds the teacher's career, his order of monks, and his death from that sifted evidence. Readers get both the man the records allow and the legend the centuries built around him.
thomson-new-guide-health-1827:
Samuel Thomson was a New Hampshire farmer who built a new scheme of cure. His New Guide to Health came out in 1827. He held that cold and blocked flow cause most ills. Plant drugs and steam baths, he said, could cure kin at home.

Lobelia, cayenne, and hot baths form the core of his plan. Thomson sold rights to use his scheme to homes all over the States. His revolt struck at high fees and harsh drugs of the trained trade. The book launched the first great wave of alt cure in the young republic.
tibetan-book-of-dead-evans-wentz-1927:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz edited the first Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927. The source text, the Bardo Thodol, is a Tibetan Buddhist guide for the dead. Lama Kazi Dawa-Samdup did the English rendering that Evans-Wentz shaped and framed.

The book tells what the soul meets in the forty-nine days after death. Bright lights, calm gods, and fierce forms test the dead person's mind. Priests read the text aloud to guide the soul toward a good rebirth. Its arrival gave Western readers a first full look at Tibetan belief. Carl Jung and other thinkers took its scheme quite seriously.
tob-0127:
COINTELPRO was the FBI's secret program of watching and disrupting groups it judged dangerous. Its White Hate files cover Bureau work against white supremacist organizations in the 1960s. This file, released through the Freedom of Information Act, holds the headquarters record in its second sub-file.

Field reports, memos, and informant material show agents tracking the Klan and kindred groups, sometimes to block violence, sometimes by dirty tricks of their own. The papers are raw history, with the texture of daily bureau work. As a United States government document, the file is public domain by law. It documents both the hate groups and the watchers.
tob-10827:
Volume one of H. P. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine, published in 1888 under the subtitle Cosmogenesis, unfolds her account of the universe's origin. Blavatsky claimed to comment on an archaic manuscript, the Stanzas of Dzyan. Seven rounds, root races, and cycles spanning millions of years structure her cosmos.

Hindu cosmology and Victorian science are stitched together into a vast evolutionary scheme, spiritual as much as physical. The prose is formidable and strange, full of Sanskrit terms and cosmic diagrams described in words. Whatever its truth, the volume is the founding scripture of modern Theosophy, and later occult movements have mined it ever since.
tob-13527:
A Hebrew text known as 3 Enoch tells how Rabbi Ishmael rose through the palaces of heaven. There he found Enoch himself, no longer a man but Metatron, the highest of angels. The work crowns the Jewish merkabah tradition, the mysticism of the divine throne.

Guides show Ishmael ranks of angels, rivers of fire, and the letters by which the world was made. Metatron explains his own rise from human scribe to prince of the presence. Strange and dense, the book preserves the boldest claims of early Jewish mysticism and shaped later Kabbalah.
tob-4027:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Social Contract, bound here with his Discourses, asks how free people can legitimately be governed. Man is born free, his famous opening declares, and everywhere he is in chains. Rousseau's answer is the general will: citizens obey laws they give themselves as a body, aiming at the common good.

The accompanying Discourses treat inequality's origins and the effects of the arts and sciences, arguments that made his name before the Contract. Together, the volume holds the ideas that electrified the French Revolution and still fuel arguments about democracy, representation, and freedom. Dangerous, brilliant, and endlessly contested, Rousseau writes as if the reader's chains were personal insults.
tob-4127:
Franz Cumont published The Oriental Religions in Roman Paganism in 1911, and the lectures defined a field. Eastern cults, Mithras from Persia, Isis from Egypt, Cybele from Anatolia, and the Syrian gods, spread through the Roman Empire's armies, ports, and slave routes. Cumont argued they conquered pagan Rome from within before Christianity triumphed.

Drawing on inscriptions, temples, and ritual remains, he traces a spiritual marketplace in late antiquity, where salvation religions promising personal immortality displaced civic cults. Later scholars corrected details and softened his grand claim, but the framing remains his. Readers get the classic account of how Rome's religious world changed before Constantine.
twelfth-night-pg1527: Shipwreck, disguise, and a drunk knight's revenge on a prig in this edition of Shakespeare's most beloved comedy. Viola loves her master, Olivia loves Viola, and Malvolio gets his comeuppance. Joyful confusion from start to finish.
un-ga-res-27:
Hunger stalked the world in the first winter after the Second World War. Resolution 27 of the General Assembly was passed on 14 February 1946. It lays out the cause in plain terms. War had cut farm output. Draft animals and farm hands were gone. Drought had shrunk the wheat crop in lands that once grew the most grain. Rice was so short that famine loomed in some areas.

The Assembly urges all governments and peoples to act at once, with drastic steps. Crops must be gathered in full from the farms, and stocks must be saved and shared through the world bodies at work on food. The aim was blunt: head off wide suffering and death, and keep hunger from wrecking the work of rebuilding.
un-ga-res-a-69-27:
New kinds of mass-kill arms, not yet built, are the worry behind Resolution A/69/27, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Assembly recalls a chain of votes on the ban since 1996. Its aim is to head off fresh classes of weapons whose power to destroy could match the arms named in the UN's own 1948 test for weapons of mass destruction.

Talks at the Conference on Disarmament on the point are noted with thanks. The text holds that science will keep opening new paths to harm, and that law must move first. A ban agreed before such arms exist, it argues, is far cheaper in lives than a ban chased after them.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 27, adopted on 14 February 1946, answered the world food emergency that followed the Second World War. War damage, lost farm workers and animals, short fertilizer, and drought had cut wheat output hard. Rice was so scarce that famine threatened in places. The Assembly feared wide suffering if the next harvest also fell short.

Governments were urged to act at once and firmly. They were urged to gather crops well, save food, and cut waste. They were urged to push grain growing to the most for the coming season. States were also asked to publish full figures on their stocks and needs. Food bodies were told to share world supply news openly.

General Assembly resolution 69/27 (2014) renews the Assembly's long-standing call to bar new kinds of weapons of mass destruction. No new type of weapon with destructive effect like those covered by the 1948 definition should emerge. Determined that this should hold, the Assembly reaffirms that sound preventive measures are needed. It asks the Conference on Disarmament to keep the question under close review. When necessary, it should recommend specific talks on named types. States are called on to look with favor on any such recommendations.
un-sc-res-1027:
Macedonia's preventive force gained six more months in November 1995. On 30 November 1995 the Security Council extended UNPREDEP until 30 May 1996. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission a week earlier. The Council restated its support for Macedonia's independence and borders. It recalled its worry about events that could shake the young state. The force's work so far drew praise in the text.

UNPREDEP had to keep cooperating with the European security mission in the country. Member states were asked to look kindly on requests for help. The mission watched the northern border for spillover from nearby wars. It was the United Nations' first attempt at preventive deployment. Its renewals were routine while the region stayed tense.
un-sc-res-127:
A disputed zone around Government House in Jerusalem was placed under truce supervision by the Security Council on 22 January 1958. Jordan had complained in September 1957 about Israeli activities between the armistice lines. The Acting Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization had reported on 23 September 1957. Neither Israel nor Jordan held sovereignty over any part of the zone.

The Council directed the Chief of Staff to regulate activities inside the zone under the Israel-Jordan Armistice Agreement. He was to survey property records and settle who owned what there. As a rule, Israelis could not use Arab-owned property, nor Arabs Israeli-owned property. Civilian activities were to be discussed through the Mixed Armistice Commission, and works begun by Israelis in July 1957 were to pause until the survey ended. The talks had two months to finish, and the Chief of Staff had to report the result.
un-sc-res-1327: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 1327 is catalogued here under 2000. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1427: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 1427, this formal text is catalogued under the year 2001. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1527:
Côte d'Ivoire's small United Nations mission gained a few more weeks from the Security Council on 4 February 2004. The Linas-Marcoussis Agreement of January 2003 was being put into effect, with recent progress noted. The Ivorian president had asked in November 2003 for the mission, MINUCI, to become a full peacekeeping operation. The Secretary-General's January report recommended a stronger United Nations presence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended MINUCI's mandate to 27 February 2004. It renewed for the same period the authority of the West African ECOWAS forces and the French troops supporting them. The signatories of Linas-Marcoussis were told to carry out their duties quickly. The Secretary-General was asked to prepare for a reinforced presence pending the Council's decision. The short extension held the line while the Council weighed turning a liaison mission into the full operation that followed weeks later.
un-sc-res-1627: Security Council Resolution 1627 dates to 2005, and the collection holds its official text through English Wikisource. The resolution is one link in a chain: it cites earlier texts and is cited by later ones. Preserved in sequence with its neighbors, it lets readers follow the Council's handling of its business number by number.
un-sc-res-1727: Under number 1727, a Security Council decision entered the official record, and this collection holds the record through English Wikisource. Resolutions are the paper trail of world security politics: each one small, the accumulation enormous. This entry preserves its one small piece completely, in the form in which it was issued and circulated.
un-sc-res-1827: Resolution 1827, adopted in 2008, survives here as a Security Council act in its official-record text. The transcription is English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. Inside, opening clauses carry the members' shared account of events; closing clauses carry their instructions. Both are preserved, so the decision can be followed from reasoning to result.
un-sc-res-1927: In 2010 the Security Council recorded Resolution 1927, kept here through a Wikisource copy of the official record. The document's authority is the Charter's, exercised by fifteen states in one vote. What that vote produced, findings and numbered decisions together, is preserved in this entry in the exact form in which it entered UN practice.
un-sc-res-227: Security Council business produced Resolution 227, catalogued in this library as a 1966 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-27:
Fighting between Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia drew the Council's first word on the conflict on 1 August 1947. Resolution 27 is short and plain. The Council noted with concern the hostilities in progress between the two sides. Indonesia was then fighting for independence from the Netherlands.

The Council called on both parties to cease hostilities at once. The dispute then had to be settled by arbitration or by other peaceful means. The parties had to keep the Security Council informed about the progress of the settlement. The text is a first step only. It did not judge the rights of either side, and it set no force in place. The Council's long involvement in the Indonesian question, which ran until independence, began with this call.
un-sc-res-327:
Zambia paid a heavy price for obeying sanctions on Rhodesia. It had cut its remaining trade ties with the illegal regime. That step closed routes Zambia's own economy depended on. On 2 February 1973 the Security Council praised the decision. It also recognized the special hardships Zambia now faced. A special mission of four Council members was already at work on the problem.

The mission, helped by six United Nations experts, had to assess Zambia's needs. New road, rail, and transport links were the focus. Neighboring states were asked to cooperate with the team. The text is a rare case of the Council counting the cost of its own sanctions. It tried to share a burden it had imposed.
un-sc-res-427:
Lebanon's new United Nations force needed more troops within weeks of landing. On 3 May 1978 the Security Council approved a rise from 4,000 to about 6,000 soldiers. The Secretary-General had asked for the increase by letter the day before. UNIFIL had been created that March to confirm Israel's withdrawal. The Council noted that some Israeli forces had already left. The rest had to go without further delay.

The Council also deplored attacks on the force. It noted attacks by irregular groups inside Lebanon as well. A closing paragraph restated the force's terms of reference. The build-up showed how hard the mission's ground would be. UNIFIL remains in south Lebanon to this day.
un-sc-res-727:
A deadly attack on European monitors sharpened the Council's push for a Yugoslav cease-fire on 8 January 1992. Five members of the European Community Monitoring Mission had died in an incident on 7 January. The parties had agreed an unconditional cease-fire at Geneva on 23 November 1991. An implementing accord on its terms had been signed at Sarajevo on 2 January 1992.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 5 January 1992. It endorsed his plan to send up to fifty liaison officers at once to help hold the cease-fire. All parties were urged to honor the Geneva and Sarajevo promises and bring about a full halt to the fighting. They had to take every step to keep United Nations staff and the European monitors safe. The Council restated the arms embargo of resolution 713 (1991). The liaison officers were the advance edge of the force authorized weeks later.
un-sc-res-827:
Reports of mass killings and organized rape in the war in Bosnia horrified the world in 1993. The Council had already decided, in Resolution 808, that a war crimes court should be created. A report from the Secretary-General set out how to build it. Resolution 827, adopted in 1993 and dated to 25 May of that year in later texts, is the founding act.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council approved the Secretary-General's report and set up the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Its one purpose was to prosecute people responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. The crimes covered were those committed there since 1 January 1991. All states had to cooperate fully with the court. They also had to change their own laws where needed, so the court's orders could be carried out. The tribunal's seat depended on arrangements to be made with the Netherlands.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Macedonia's preventive shield gained another six months under Resolution 1027. It was adopted unanimously on 30 November 1995. UNPREDEP troops watched the young republic's northern borders. Their presence aimed to stop the Yugoslav wars spilling over. The Secretary-General's report of 23 November 1995 backed renewal.

The mandate now ended on 30 May 1996. Members praised the force's calming role. They urged continued cooperation with European security observers in the area. States were asked to answer the Secretary-General's requests for support. A fuller review was also commissioned. He would report on every aspect of the mission by 31 January 1996, if possible. The Council would then judge the mission against regional events.

A strip of no-man's-land in Jerusalem is the subject of Resolution 127. It passed by a full vote on 22 January 1958. Jordan had charged Israel with acts in the zone by the old Government House. The zone lay between the truce lines of 1949. A UN truce chief had filed a report on the area in 1957.

The Council noted that no side held sway over any part of the zone. It told the truce chief to run all acts inside it under the 1949 pact. He had to weigh who owned each plot of land. Jews could not use Arab-owned plots, nor Arabs Jewish-owned ones, unless both agreed. He was also told to survey land records to fix who owned what.

How the United Nations runs peacekeeping is itself the subject on 13 November 2000. A major review of peace operations, known as the Brahimi report, had just landed, along with the Secretary-General's plan for carrying it out. An annex to the text spells out the changes the Council backed.

The annex promises missions clear, credible orders they can actually carry out, backed by real strength where deterrence is needed. It asks the United Nations to join peace talks early when a settlement may lead to peacekeepers being sent. Better planning, faster deployment, and closer work with regional groups are also promised, with the Council checking progress over time.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 29 July 2002, and the Abkhazia conflict is taken up again. As in January, the Council recalled the October 2001 shooting down of a UNOMIG helicopter, which killed nine people. Those responsible had still not been found, and talks on the core dispute remained stuck.

The lack of progress is again called unacceptable, and breaches of the 1994 Moscow ceasefire agreement are condemned. Both sides are urged to rebuild trust, restart joint work, and act on earlier confidence measures. Georgia is asked to improve security for joint patrols in the Kodori Valley, and both sides are pressed to improve law and order in the Gali district.

Resolution 1527, adopted unanimously on 4 February 2004, buys a few weeks for the UN political mission in Côte d'Ivoire. The mission, MINUCI, was helping carry out the Linas-Marcoussis peace agreement after civil war divided the country. Côte d'Ivoire's president had asked for MINUCI to become a full peacekeeping operation, and a January report from the Secretary-General supported a bigger deployment.

The Council extended MINUCI's mandate until 27 February 2004 and renewed the authorization for French and West African forces backing the peace process. The short fuse was deliberate: the Council was about to decide on a full operation, which arrived weeks later as UNOCI, with thousands of troops.

Sudan's mission, UNMIS, is extended until 24 March 2006 on 23 September 2005. The north-south peace agreement was being carried out, and a Government of National Unity had been formed, a historic step. The country's First Vice President had died in a crash in July, yet both parties kept working to hold the peace together.

The parties are urged to meet their remaining promises under the peace deal, above all setting up the Assessment and Evaluation Commission. Reports are asked for every three months on the mission's work. Troop-contributing countries are urged to study the Secretary-General's guidance closely. The extension kept international support behind the deal while Darfur remained a separate, unresolved crisis.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed until 31 October 2007 on 15 December 2006. Expert panel reports in October and December described a crisis that persisted and worsened, with heavy humanitarian costs and large-scale displacement. The measures renewed are the arms embargo, travel bans, and asset freezes first set in 2004 and added to the year after.

Acting under Chapter VII, all Ivorian parties, including the transitional government, are demanded to stop blocking the peace process and the work of the United Nations operation and French forces. The Secretary-General and France are asked to report on obstructions. States, above all in the region, must report on their enforcement, and the measures would be reviewed at the end of the period.

UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, is terminated on 30 July 2008, effective 31 July 2008. Eritrea's restrictions had made the mission's work impossible, forcing its troops out of the border zone that February. The two countries, the Council says, share responsibility for carrying out the Algiers Agreements they signed.

Ethiopia and Eritrea are demanded to meet their duties under those agreements in full, including respect for the Temporary Security Zone and the boundary ruling they accepted as final and binding. The Secretary-General is asked to explore further contacts with both countries and to keep the Council informed. The Council stands ready to help the two sides settle the border dispute and normalize their relations.

Five months after a huge earthquake devastated Haiti, the Security Council adopted Resolution 1927 on 4 June 2010. The quake of 12 January 2010 had wrecked government buildings and killed United Nations staff. Large camps of displaced people had formed, and they brought new risks. The resolution concerns MINUSTAH, the United Nations mission that was already working in Haiti.

The Council authorized 680 extra police as a temporary surge. That raised the mission's limits to 8,940 troops and 4,391 police in total. The extra police were to focus on building up the Haitian National Police. The mission also had to protect people in the camps and fight sexual violence and gang crime. It had to help Haiti prepare and run its coming elections. The surge was a short-term answer to the emergency, not a permanent increase.

Who would lead the United Nations into 1967 was the single question behind Resolution 227, adopted at a private meeting on 18 October 1966. U Thant, the Secretary-General named in the text, had said he was willing to consider serving until the end of the General Assembly's session that year. The Council recommended that the General Assembly extend his appointment to that point. The Council itself would finish considering the appointment question in the meantime. The text records one step in a handover, not a final choice.

One of the young Council's first acts backed Indonesia's break from Dutch rule. On 1 August 1947, it adopted Resolution 27. Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia were then at war. The republic had claimed freedom from the Netherlands after the Second World War. The text notes the fighting with concern.

Both parties must stop fighting at once, the Council says. They must then settle their dispute by talks or other calm means. They must keep the Council posted on progress. The vote was taken in parts, not on the whole text. The move was the Council's first step into a colonial war. That role grew as empires fell in the decades after.

Zambia paid a steep price for standing by the Rhodesia bans. Its trade ran south, through the banned land. In 1973 Lusaka chose to cut the last links. That meant new roads, rails, and ports had to be found fast. Resolution 327 passed on 2 February 1973 by fourteen votes to none. The Soviet team held back.

The Council praised Zambia's choice in warm terms. It took full note of the pain the move would cause. A team of four Council men would judge Zambia's needs. Six UN aides would help them weigh the task. New routes by road, rail, air, and sea were the goal. Near states had to help the team work. Its word was due by 1 March 1973. The file shows the bans' cost fell on friends too.

A young peace force in Lebanon needed more troops in 1978. UNIFIL had deployed that March after Israel invaded the south. The Secretary-General wrote on 1 May asking for a bigger force. Resolution 427 passed on 3 May 1978. Twelve members voted yes. Two Soviet bloc states held back.

The Council agreed to raise the force. It grew from four thousand troops to about six thousand. The text notes that some Israeli units had pulled out. It tells Israel to finish the pullout from all of Lebanon at once. Attacks on the UN force drew sharp words. All sides in Lebanon were told to respect the blue helmets in full.

On 8 January 1992 the Council passed Resolution 727 by a full vote. It deals with a weak truce in Yugoslavia and a grim attack. The day before, five men of a European watch team died when their craft was shot down. At the same time, the warring sides had signed a pact at Sarajevo on 2 January. It set out how to keep the truce agreed at Geneva in November.

The Council backed the UN chief's report of 5 January and praised his work. It cheered the Sarajevo pact. It also backed his plan to send up to fifty army liaison men to Yugoslavia at once. Their job was to help hold the truce. A much larger UN force came the next month.

War crimes in Bosnia drove the Council to build a court in 1993. On 25 May, it adopted Resolution 827 under Chapter VII. Reports spoke of mass killings and mass rape of women. Ethnic cleansing was still going on. The Council said it was set on ending such crimes.

The text creates an ad hoc court for the former Yugoslavia. The court will try those charged with grave breaches of the laws of war since 1991. The text also adopts the court's statute, its rule book. All states must help the court in full. They must shape their home laws to fit its demands. The seat was left open, pending a deal with the Netherlands.
undset-the-cross-kristin-lavransdatter-i:
Undset closes her famous trilogy with The Cross, in Archer's 1927 English version. Kristin, now widowed and old, looks back on a life of love, pride, sin, and loss. Norway in her last years faces the terror of the Black Death.

Seeking peace at last, Kristin leaves her estate and ends her days in a convent. There she serves the sick as plague sweeps the land. Faith, long resisted, becomes her final refuge and strength. The long arc from wilful girl to humble penitent ends here, and many readers count the trilogy among the great novels of its century.
vagbhata-rasaratnasamuccaya-1927-1927: Vagbhata Rasaratnasamuccaya, 1927. The Sanskrit rasa text. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
whitehead-symbolism-1927:
Symbolism: Its Meaning and Effect, published in 1927, prints Whitehead's Barbour-Page Lectures at the University of Virginia. In three lectures he asks how symbolism, in language, ritual, and art, mediates between perception and meaning.

Whitehead argues that we perceive the world in two modes: direct presentational immediacy, and causal efficacy, the heavy pressure of the past. Symbols fuse the two, and error enters when the symbol is mistaken for what it stands for. The lectures are among his most accessible. They form a bridge between his philosophy of nature and the great system of Process and Reality.
whitney-v-california-1927: Whitney v. California (1927) upheld a conviction but Brandeis' concurrence became free speech law. The Tower library holds the full opinion. It planted liberty. Conviction stood. Dissent grew. Speech won. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
woolf-to-lighthouse-1927:
Virginia Woolf published To the Lighthouse in 1927, drawing on her childhood summers in St Ives, Cornwall. Her parents stand behind Mr and Mrs Ramsay, the novel's central pair. Woolf considered it her best book, and many readers agree.

The Ramsays plan a boat trip to the lighthouse that bad weather cancels. Their young son James longs for the trip while guests, including the painter Lily Briscoe, watch the family's tensions. A bare middle section then sweeps ten years past: war, deaths, an emptying house. In the last part the trip finally happens, and Lily finishes her painting. Woolf turns time and memory into the real plot.
wurzburg-hexenverbrennung-1627:
Burnings at Würzburg and Bamberg fill a German pamphlet of 1627, written while the trials still ran. HexenVerbrennung Bistum Würzburg Bamberg reports the work of the two prince-bishops' courts. In those lands the hunt for witches burned as hot as anywhere in Europe.

The pamphlet tells who was seized, what was charged, and how the fires were lit, in the plain style of the day's news. It treats the burnings as just and needful work, and says so openly. That tone is the point for modern readers. The print shows how mass trials were sold to the public as they happened.
xenophon-ephesus-ephesian-tale-rooke-172:
The Ephesian Tale, by Xenophon of Ephesus, is one of the five ancient Greek novels that survive whole. It tells of Abrocomas and Anthia, a beautiful pair who marry at Ephesus and are then torn apart by fate. John Rooke's English version of 1727 was the first ever made of the tale.

Pirates, false deaths, cruel masters, and long sea roads keep the lovers apart across the Mediterranean world. Both stay faithful through every trial, and the gods of Ephesus bring them home at last. The plot of the Greek romance, with its storms and near misses, starts here in near-full form. Rooke's old English keeps its period charm.
